If anything looks suspicious, the urologist can use a small tool on the cystoscope to remove tiny tissue samples for testing (biopsy). A flexible cystoscope (upper left) is used for viewing and biopsy. A rigid cystoscope (bottom right) is more invasive, but it can also remove small tumors. In a very similar exam, called a ureteroscopy, the cystoscope goes a little farther to examine the upper parts of the urinary tract—the ureters and inner kidneys. A ureteroscopy is done only if something seems abnormal with the ureters or kidneys. After a cystoscopy After the procedure, you may have one or more of these side effects: Bleeding from your urethra, which can appear bright pink in your urine or on toilet paper A burning sensation during urination Urinating more often for the next day or two If a tissue sample was taken for a biopsy, it will be sent to a lab and tested for cancer. Imaging Imaging means taking detailed pictures (images) of the insides of the body. The images can show the size, location, and other features of cancer. Imaging can reveal where the cancer started and whether the cancer has spread (metastasized). After your scan, your images will be studied by a radiologist. A radiologist is a doctor who’s an expert in interpreting imaging tests. The radiologist will send the results to your doctor or care team. This information helps to plan the next steps of your care. Your doctor or other health care provider will discuss the results with you. Be sure to ask any questions you have. Is blue light cystoscopy better? Cystoscopy commonly uses a white light to see inside the bladder. Some newer cystoscopes now use a blue light. When combined with a special dye injected into the bladder, blue light cystoscopy can identify tumors a little more distinctly than white light. Another technology called narrow-band imaging also helps detect tumors more clearly during cystoscopy but doesn’t require a dye. While both blue light cystoscopy and narrow-band imaging may potentially detect tumors better than standard white light, they’re relatively new and still in the “testing phase.” More research will show whether they can replace or be used with white light as the standard detection method. Types of imaging include x-rays, computed tomography (CT), positron emission tomography (PET), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and ultrasound. CT scan A CT scan takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles. A computer combines all the x-ray pictures to make a series of cross-sectional images. To look for cancer that has spread beyond the bladder, you may have a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis. The pelvis is the area of the lower abdomen located between the hip bones; it contains reproductive organs as well as the bladder and rectum. A CT scanner is a large machine that has a tunnel in the middle. During the test, you’ll lie on a table that moves slowly through the tunnel. Pillows or straps may be used to help keep you still during the test. PET/CT scan A PET scan uses a radioactive drug injected into a vein to see where cancer cells are in the body. Cancer cells show up as bright spots on PET scans. When a PET scan is combined with CT, it’s called a PET/CT scan. PET/CT creates detailed images that are useful in certain clinical situations for finding cancer that has spread outside the bladder. A PET/CT scan can be done with one or two machines, depending on the cancer center. MRI MRI uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. An MRI is used to get a more detailed view of cancer within the bladder or urinary tract. It’s also used to see if cancer has spread to the liver, nearby lymph nodes, or the bones in your pelvis. Like a CT scanner, an MRI is a large machine with a tunnel in the middle. Unlike CT, MRI doesn’t use radiation (x-rays). An MRI also makes much more noise and takes longer than a CT scan. Tell your team if you get nervous in small spaces. You may be given a sedative (medicine) to help you relax. You’ll need to remain as motionless as possible during each scan. You may be positioned with pillows or bolsters to help you keep still. Imaging To look for cancer that has spread beyond the bladder, you may have an imaging scan of your abdomen and pelvis. Because an MRI uses magnets, you can’t bring any metal objects (such as a cell phone, wristwatch, belt with a metal buckle, or jewelry) into the imaging room. Other types of imaging CT and MRI are commonly used to see how far bladder cancer has spread. Other types of imaging are sometimes used to look for cancer in other parts of the urinary tract or other parts of the body: Urogram uses a contrast solution and either CT or MRI to see how well your entire urinary tract is working. The contrast makes the lining of your kidneys, ureters, and bladder easier to see. You may have a urogram if you’re feeling symptoms such as pain in your side or back, or if you have blood in your urine. Renal ultrasound shows your kidneys, ureters, and bladder in real time. It’s the same technology used to look at a baby in the womb. A renal ultrasound is a painless, non-surgical test that produces black and white images of your kidneys and other organs.

LG means that the cancer cells are low grade (slow growing). HG means that the cancer cells are high grade (fast growing). The inner lining of the bladder is made of urothelial cells. Most cases of bladder cancer start in the urothelial cells. So this type of cancer is called urothelial cancer. But in rare cases, urothelial cell cancer has features that look like other types of cells. These are referred to as subtypes. Some of them include: Glandular subtype Squamous cell subtype Micropapillary subtype Plasmacytoid subtype Sarcomatoid subtype Nested subtype Lymphoepithelioma-like subtype Microcystic and tubular subtype It’s important to investigate whether you have one of these or another subtype. In general, treatment for these uncommon subtypes is similar in the early stages to treatment for typical urothelial cancer. However, some subtypes might grow or advance faster than typical urothelial cell cancer. And faster growth might mean it needs more aggressive treatment. Key points An important thing about bladder cancer is whether it has or it hasn’t grown into the muscle layer. Cancer that has invaded the muscle needs more aggressive treatment. The stage of cancer describes how deep it has grown into the bladder wall and how far it has spread. Cancer stage is used to determine which tests and treatments will help you receive the best outcome. Bladder cancer at stage 0 and stage 1 haven’t invaded the muscle layer. Stage 0 means that abnormal cells have grown on the inside lining of the bladder. Stage 1 means that a tumor has formed and has invaded the layer of connective tissue in the bladder wall. Stages 2, 3, and 4 bladder cancers are muscle-invasive. The tumor has invaded the muscle layer of the bladder wall. In stage 3 bladder cancer, the tumor has grown into the fat layer around the bladder. There may also be cancer in nearby lymph nodes. Stage 4 is metastatic bladder cancer. This is cancer that has spread outside the bladder and to distant sites in the body. Cancer grade is an estimate of how fast the cancer is expected to grow. Low grade bladder cancer is slow growing. This chapter explains the different treatment options for bladder cancer. Many people with bladder cancer receive more than one type of treatment. Together, you and your care team will choose a treatment plan that’s right for you. Treatment for bladder cancer is based on many things. This includes the extent, severity, and type of cancer. It also includes your age, your ability to perform daily tasks, your other health issues, and the availability and affordability of drugs. Importantly, treatment is also based on your wishes and preferences. There are several ways to treat bladder cancer. It’s likely that you’ll need a few different types of treatment over months or years. Treatments include: Surgery – The goal of surgery is to take out the tumor and sometimes the surrounding tissue. Surgery procedures range from snipping a single tumor from the bladder lining to removing the entire bladder and other organs. Intravesical therapy – Intravesical therapy involves filling the bladder with a liquid medication that helps destroy cancer cells. Systemic therapy – Systemic therapy is typically an intravenous (IV) treatment that treats cancer anywhere in the whole body. Types of systemic therapy include chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy. Radiation therapy – Radiation therapy is a local therapy, which means it affects a specific area of the body. Sometimes chemotherapy or another therapy is added to radiation therapy to enhance treatment. Clinical trial – Clinical trials are done to test experimental treatments. You may be able to join a clinical trial at any time. Surgery Types of surgery for bladder cancer include tumor removal and bladder removal. Tumor removal For bladder cancer, a surgical procedure called a resection removes the tumor but leaves the rest of the bladder in place. The full name of the procedure is called a transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT, sometimes pronounced tur-bit). Even though it has a complicated name, the concept of TURBT is simple. It’s a procedure that removes tumors through the urethra without having to cut into the abdomen. The tumor can then be tested to provide a more detailed diagnosis. TURBT is done in an operating room in a clinic or hospital. You’ll be given anesthesia to put you to sleep. The urologist then guides an instrument with a small cutting device through the urethra and into the bladder. The instrument is used to examine and remove the tumor from the bladder lining. The goals of TURBT are to: Confirm the initial bladder cancer diagnosis. Take a sample of the bladder wall to see if the tumor has invaded the muscle layer. Remove all the visible tumor. After the procedure, most people can go home the same day. But you’ll need a few days to rest and recover. You may feel pain or burning when you urinate and have blood in your urine for the following 2 weeks or so. Another TURBT procedure may be needed about 2 to 6 weeks after the first one. The second TURBT is done to make sure all the tumor is removed. Or it may be done to get a deeper biopsy sample for the pathologist to examine. A treatment called intravesical therapy is often done in combination with TURBT.

entities.description: A tumor is an abnormal mass of tissue that forms when cells grow and divide uncontrollably, and it may be benign or malignant. Tumors can arise in virtually any part of the body, including the colon, bladder, brain, central nervous system, oral mucosa, prostate, kidney, cervix, lung, pancreas, skin, rectum, and anal area. They are central to cancer diagnosis and treatment planning, and their size (often measured in centimeters or millimeters), depth of invasion, and extent of spread are key components in staging various cancers, such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma, head and neck cancers, cervical cancer, prostate cancer, and anal cancer (using the TNM system). Tumors can be primary (the original site of cancer) or metastatic (spread from another location), and they may invade nearby tissues, block organs (e.g., the bowel), or spread to lymph nodes and other parts of the body. They are detected and characterized through imaging tests (e.g., x-rays, mammograms, PET scans), endoscopy, cystoscopy, and biopsy procedures, and samples may be analyzed for biomarkers (e.g., dMMR). Treatment approaches include surgery (such as TURBT for bladder tumors), radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, which aim to shrink, kill, or remove the tumor. In specific contexts, tumors may present as one or multiple masses (e.g., in primary CNS lymphoma) or as lesions (e.g., squamous cell skin cancer), and their behavior and management depend on the cancer type and stage.

Recurrence, also known as relapse, refers to the return of cancer after a period of treatment or remission. This phenomenon is common across various cancer types, including bladder, breast, cervical, ovarian, prostate, basal cell skin, primary CNS lymphoma, and head and neck cancers. Recurrence can manifest locally (at the original site), regionally (in nearby lymph nodes), or at distant sites in the body, depending on the cancer type.

For bladder cancer, recurrence is a frequent occurrence that necessitates ongoing monitoring and regular follow-up testing. In breast cancer, recurrence may be local or distant. Cervical cancer recurrence can occur locally, regionally, or at distant sites, and often requires imaging, exploratory surgery, and biomarker testing to guide further treatment. Ovarian cancer recurrence also demands further management and monitoring. Prostate cancer recurrence can be detected through imaging tests such as MRI or PSMA-PET scans, and is a key factor in risk assessment. Basal cell skin cancer recurrence involves the cancer returning to the original area or spreading to lymph nodes or distant parts of the body, indicating a need for continued surveillance.

Monitoring for recurrence typically involves imaging tests like MRI, PSMA-PET, and other surveillance methods, including regular physical exams and blood tests. In some cases, such as higher-risk thyroid cancer, TSH suppression is used as a monitoring strategy. Symptoms of recurrence can vary but may include pelvic pain, bloating, and fatigue, particularly in gynecologic cancers.

Treatment for recurrence depends on the location and extent of the disease and may involve additional therapies such as surgery, radiation therapy, radioactive iodine (RAI), or adjustments to chemotherapy regimens. Biomarker testing is often employed to guide treatment decisions. Certain cancer subtypes and features can increase the risk of recurrence, and radiation therapy may be used in high-risk patients to prevent it. Overall, recurrence requires vigilant follow-up and individualized management to address the return of disease effectively.

Cancer is a broad category of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells, which can potentially spread to other parts of the body. It encompasses numerous specific types, including head and neck cancer, colon cancer, breast cancer and its subtypes, cervical cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), bladder cancer, ovarian cancer, skin cancer, blood cancers, primary CNS lymphoma, lymphoma, differentiated high-grade carcinoma of the thyroid, and cancers affecting the ovaries, adrenal glands, and other organs. Cancer can develop from precancerous conditions like adenomas, spread through organ walls, cause bone damage, appear as tumors, and affect various bodily functions, including fertility and pregnancy. The disease may run in families, making family health history an important factor in risk assessment and genetic predisposition. Diagnosis and monitoring involve a range of procedures, including imaging tests such as PET scans, bone scans, mammograms, MRIs, and cystoscopy, as well as biopsies and biomarker, tumor marker, and genetic testing. Cancer appears brighter in PET scans due to increased sugar metabolism. Treatment options include radiation therapy, systemic therapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy, and participation in clinical trials for new treatments, with considerations for side effects, emotional and physical impacts, fertility and bone health, and the importance of quitting smoking to improve outcomes. The disease can be local or metastatic, and its staging, grading, and treatment are tailored to the specific type and context.

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a type of cancer that arises from squamous cells, which are thin, flat cells lining the surface of the skin, mucous membranes, and various internal organs. This cancer can develop in multiple locations throughout the body, and its characteristics, prevalence, and treatment approaches vary depending on the site of origin.

In the context of cervical cancer, squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type, originating from the squamous cells lining the ectocervix (the outer part of the cervix). Treatment decisions for cervical SCC are based on the cancer stage and tumor grade, among other factors. Ovarian transposition (surgically moving the ovaries out of the radiation field) may be considered as an option for some patients with this type of cervical cancer.

Squamous cell carcinoma is also the most common type of anal cancer, starting in the squamous cells found in the skin and other tissues of the anal region. Diagnosis is typically made via biopsy, and the disease can range from early stages (such as squamous intraepithelial lesions, including SISCCA) to more advanced stages. Additionally, SCC is the most common type of throat cancer and head and neck cancer, often caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, and it forms in the thin, flat cells of mucous membranes. It is also the specific type of nasopharyngeal cancer for which TNM staging information is provided.

In the lungs, squamous cell carcinoma is a subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that starts in the flat cells lining the bronchi (airways). It accounts for approximately 3 out of 10 lung cancers. In the bladder, SCC is a non-urothelial type of bladder cancer, which is less common than urothelial carcinoma and is considered rare.

Overall, squamous cell carcinoma is a versatile cancer type that can affect various organs, with its management and prognosis depending on the specific location, stage, and individual patient factors.

Imaging can reveal where the cancer started and whether the cancer has spread (metastasized). After your scan, your images will be studied by a radiologist. A radiologist is a doctor who’s an expert in interpreting imaging tests. The radiologist will send the results to your doctor or care team. This information helps to plan the next steps of your care. Cystoscopy commonly uses a white light to see inside the bladder. Some newer cystoscopes now use a blue light. When combined with a special dye injected into the bladder, blue light cystoscopy can identify tumors a little more distinctly than white light. CT scan A CT scan takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles. A computer combines all the x-ray pictures to make a series of cross-sectional images. To look for cancer that has spread beyond the bladder, you may have a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis. The pelvis is the area of the lower abdomen located between the hip bones; it contains reproductive organs as well as the bladder and rectum. A CT scanner is a large machine that has a tunnel in the middle. During the test, you’ll lie on a table that moves slowly through the tunnel. This chapter explains the different treatment options for bladder cancer. Many people with bladder cancer receive more than one type of treatment. Together, you and your care team will choose a treatment plan that’s right for you. Treatment for bladder cancer is based on many things. This includes the extent, severity, and type of cancer. It also includes your age, your ability to perform daily tasks, your other health issues, and the availability and affordability of drugs. Importantly, treatment is also based on your wishes and preferences. There are several ways to treat bladder cancer. It’s likely that you’ll need a few different types of treatment over months or years. Treatments include: Surgery – The goal of surgery is to take out the tumor and sometimes the surrounding tissue. Surgery procedures range from snipping a single tumor from the bladder lining to removing the entire bladder and other organs. Intravesical therapy – Intravesical therapy involves filling the bladder with a liquid medication that helps destroy cancer cells. Systemic therapy – Systemic therapy is typically an intravenous (IV) treatment that treats cancer anywhere in the whole body. Types of systemic therapy include chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy. Radiation therapy – Radiation therapy is a local therapy, which means it affects a specific area of the body. Sometimes chemotherapy or another therapy is added to radiation therapy to enhance treatment. Clinical trial – Clinical trials are done to test experimental treatments. You may be able to join a clinical trial at any time. Surgery Types of surgery for bladder cancer include tumor removal and bladder removal. Tumor removal For bladder cancer, a surgical procedure called a resection removes the tumor but leaves the rest of the bladder in place. The full name of the procedure is called a transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT, sometimes pronounced tur-bit). Even though it has a complicated name, the concept of TURBT is simple. It’s a procedure that removes tumors through the urethra without having to cut into the abdomen. The tumor can then be tested to provide a more detailed diagnosis. TURBT is done in an operating room in a clinic or hospital. You’ll be given anesthesia to put you to sleep. The urologist then guides an instrument with a small cutting device through the urethra and into the bladder. The instrument is used to examine and remove the tumor from the bladder lining. The goals of TURBT are to: Confirm the initial bladder cancer diagnosis. Take a sample of the bladder wall to see if the tumor has invaded the muscle layer. Remove all the visible tumor. After the procedure, most people can go home the same day. But you’ll need a few days to rest and recover. You may feel pain or burning when you urinate and have blood in your urine for the following 2 weeks or so. Another TURBT procedure may be needed about 2 to 6 weeks after the first one. The second TURBT is done to make sure all the tumor is removed. Or it may be done to get a deeper biopsy sample for the pathologist to examine. A treatment called intravesical therapy is often done in combination with TURBT."

The liver is a large, vital organ located on the right side of the body under the rib cage, playing a central role in the digestive system. It performs numerous critical functions, including filtering blood, detoxifying chemicals and toxins, processing nutrients, producing bile, breaking down fats, helping regulate blood sugar, and synthesizing coagulation factors and other essential proteins. The liver also produces lymph and is the site where primary liver cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and intrahepatic bile duct cancer, can develop.

Given its extensive metabolic and filtration roles, the liver is a common and clinically significant site for distant metastasis from many types of cancer. It is frequently affected by metastatic spread from colon, rectal, anal, breast, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, stomach, esophageal, prostate, kidney, thyroid, throat (including nasopharyngeal), and lung cancers, as well as from leukemias (such as CLL and AML) and lymphomas (such as DLBCL). In many of these cancers, liver involvement indicates advanced or stage 4 disease (e.g., stage 4B for cervical and bladder cancers, stage IV for anal cancer) and significantly influences treatment decisions, often requiring systemic therapy or local interventions like stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or ablative techniques.

The liver's health and function are routinely assessed through blood tests, including liver function tests (LFTs), comprehensive metabolic panels (CMP), and chemistry profiles, which measure enzymes, proteins, and other markers (e.g., ALP). These tests are essential for monitoring potential damage from chemotherapy drugs (such as high-dose methotrexate) and for evaluating the impact of cancers like CLL, which can cause the liver to swell due to cancer cell buildup. Imaging modalities such as CT, MRI, and ultrasound are used to detect metastatic lesions in the liver and to assess its size and condition during physical examinations. Overall, the liver is a crucial organ whose health is integral to overall bodily function and whose involvement in cancer spread is a key factor in staging, prognosis, and therapeutic planning.

To solve this problem, cancer experts created the tumor, node, metastasis (TNM) system to describe any tumor. It’s based on the results of your imaging scans, biopsies, and blood tests. In this system, the letters T, N, and M stand for different areas of cancer growth: T (tumor) – Describes the size of the main (primary) tumor and if it has grown outside the prostate N (node) – Identifies whether cancer has spread to lymph nodes M (metastasis) – Indicates if cancer has spread (metastasized) to parts of the body outside of the pelvis Your provider will assign a number to each letter, based on your test results. The higher the number, the larger the tumor (T) or the more the cancer has spread (M). These scores are combined to assign a “stage” to the cancer. Staging is a way to describe how much cancer is in your body and how far it has spread. Knowing your stage is important for predicting the course of your disease and for making a treatment plan. Cancer staging is done when you’re first diagnosed. It may also be done after treatment to confirm that the stage hasn’t changed. How to read a TNM score Let’s say your prostate cancer is given a TNM score of T4, N1, MThis score means that the tumor has grown outside the prostate gland (T4) and has spread to nearby lymph nodes (N1) and to one or more distant parts of the body (M1). Why know your TNM score? For one, it lets you know the extent of your cancer. It also helps characterize your risk for the cancer to spread. Your level of risk helps indicate the most appropriate treatment for you. Measurements and assessments not covered in this book include PSA density, Gleason score, Grade Group, and risk groups. Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Targeted therapy is a form of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to precisely identify and attack specific molecules, genetic mutations, or abnormal proteins involved in the growth, progression, and spread of cancer cells. It is a type of systemic therapy, meaning it travels throughout the body, and is designed to focus on unique or specific features of cancer cells, thereby minimizing damage to normal, healthy cells compared to traditional chemotherapy.

This approach is used across a wide range of cancers, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML), cervical cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, squamous cell skin cancer, and breast cancer (such as HER2-positive cases). It is often guided by biomarker testing or specific genetic profiling, such as identifying mutations like PIK3CA, the BCR::ABL protein, or markers like PSMA. Examples of targeted therapy drugs include PARP inhibitors, Gemtuzumab ozogamicin, Gilteritinib, quizartinib, midostaurin, sorafenib, ivosidenib, bevacizumab, mirvetuximab soravtansine-gynx, tisotumab vedotin, and EGFR inhibitors.

Targeted therapy may be used in various scenarios, including for cancers that have returned, metastasized, or are resistant to other treatments, such as radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy for thyroid cancer. It can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments like chemotherapy. While it can be highly effective, it may also have side effects, which can include allergic reactions, fatigue, low platelet counts, body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding. Some serious side effects may affect the heart, skin, or digestive system. Additionally, targeted therapy can affect fertility, so it is important for patients to discuss this potential impact with their healthcare provider before starting treatment.

Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that occurs in the cervix, the lower part of the female reproductive system, and is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in cervical tissues. It is primarily caused by long-term (persistent) infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), and it is a common cancer of the female reproductive system. The disease can manifest in several histological types, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is often detected through screening methods such as Pap smears, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by cervical biopsy. The cancer is staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, and staging is crucial as it determines treatment options and prognosis. Treatment approaches vary and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy (such as chemotherapy), and chemoradiation, with the choice of treatment based on the cancer stage and risk factors such as lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). Cervical cancer can spread to lymph nodes and, if untreated or not diagnosed early, may recur locally or regionally or spread to distant organs; therefore, surveillance and follow-up care are critical for managing recurrence and metastasis. The disease is closely linked to HPV, and a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of anal cancer, as both share the same viral cause. Consequently, screening for cervical cancer is recommended for patients with anal cancer, and female survivors of anal cancer may also be screened for cervical cancer. Additionally, p16, a biomarker, can be found in cervical cancer tissues.

Treatment encompasses a broad range of medical interventions—such as surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies—used to manage, cure, or slow the progression of various cancers, including head and neck cancer, prostate cancer, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), primary CNS lymphoma, chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), breast cancer, bone cancer, basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, MGZL, and thyroid cancer. The specific approach is personalized based on diagnostic test results, cancer staging, biomarkers (e.g., BCR::ABL1 protein activity), and patient preferences, with options ranging from minimal or no treatment for low-risk cases to aggressive therapies for high-risk or advanced disease. Treatment aims to slow tumor growth, reduce symptoms, prolong life, and prevent the disease from causing problems, though it may have side effects on hearing, fertility, and other bodily functions. For certain cancers, such as CLL, monitoring may be an option, while for metastatic cancer, targeted therapy or immunotherapy may be employed. Clinical trials are also considered in some cases, and treatment plans are often guided by a multidisciplinary care team, with patient preferences playing a key role in decision-making.

Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy radiation—such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons—to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is planned and prescribed by a radiation oncologist and delivered by radiation therapists or other specialists. This treatment is often used as a local therapy to target specific areas of the body, and it may be combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation), surgery, or systemic therapies, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Radiation therapy is applicable to a wide range of cancers, including anal, bladder, brain (e.g., gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma), breast, cervical, prostate, rectal, skin (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), thyroid, and perianal cancers, as well as chordoma and metastatic anal cancer. It can be used as a primary treatment, an adjunct after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells, or as palliative care to relieve pain. Techniques include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), and brachytherapy (internal radioactive material).

Treatment is typically given over several weeks, with common schedules of five sessions per week, each session lasting 30 to 60 minutes. While effective, radiation therapy can cause side effects, which may appear during treatment or years later. These include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, tiredness, headaches, nausea, vision problems, cataracts, and long-term cognitive issues. Radiation to the head and neck can affect endocrine glands, hearing, and other functions, requiring pre- and post-treatment monitoring. Additionally, radiation therapy can impact fertility—for example, in rectal cancer it may damage ovarian and testicular function—and prior exposure to radiation, especially at a young age (e.g., to the chest), is a risk factor for certain cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer and small cell lung cancer.

For some cancers, radiation therapy is a preferred or standard treatment option. For instance, IMRT is often preferred for anal cancer, and radiation is a main treatment for gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma. In prostate cancer, it may be used in both early and advanced stages, though it may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients. For skin cancers like squamous cell carcinoma, radiation is used when surgery is not possible or as an adjunct to reduce recurrence
Treatments refer to medical interventions for cancer, including surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation.

Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Chemotherapy can be used alone or combined with other therapies, including radiation (chemoradiation), surgery, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially when PD-L1 or PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed). It is a standard treatment for many cancers, including AML, ALL, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, anal cancer, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and squamous cell skin cancer, among others. Specific regimens vary by cancer type and may include platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin), taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine), mitomycin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and anthracyclines. Chemotherapy can be delivered systemically (through the bloodstream), intravenously, orally, intraperitoneally, intravesically, intrathecally, or intraocularly, depending on the cancer and treatment goal. It may be used before surgery (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), as primary treatment for metastatic disease, or in high doses during stem cell rescue. Side effects are common and include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, fever, infection, and low blood cell counts. Chemotherapy can also affect fertility and other bodily functions, so preventive measures and birth control may be recommended during treatment. Smoking during chemotherapy can increase lung problems. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility. Chemotherapy is often a key component of treatment plans and may be recommended based on cancer stage, molecular markers (e.g., PD-L1 expression), and response to other treatments.

Immunotherapy is a type of systemic cancer treatment that leverages and boosts the body’s own immune system to find, reactivate, and destroy cancer cells. It is commonly administered by a medical oncologist and is considered a newer, non-hormone therapeutic approach that works alongside other systemic therapies like chemotherapy and targeted therapy. Immunotherapy is used across a wide range of cancers, including anal, cervical, bladder, ovarian, breast, prostate, colon, skin (squamous cell carcinoma), and primary CNS lymphoma, as well as for acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and metastatic disease.

The treatment often involves immune checkpoint inhibitors—such as pembrolizumab, nivolumab, and ipilimumab—which help reactivate the immune system against tumor cells. For certain cancers, including those with specific biomarkers like dMMR, MSI-H, or PD-1 expression, immunotherapy is a preferred option. It may be used to avoid surgery in anal cancer, to treat recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer with specific biomarkers, or as a recommended approach when cancer progresses during or after chemotherapy. In primary CNS lymphoma, the main immunotherapy drug is rituximab, a monoclonal antibody that targets CD20 proteins on cancer cells.

Eligibility for immunotherapy is often determined through biomarker testing, and it may be delivered systemically or directly into the bladder for certain bladder cancers. While generally effective, immunotherapy can cause side effects, including autoimmune reactions, fatigue, fever, nausea, diarrhea, drowsiness, and low blood cell counts. These side effects are addressed in clinical guidelines. Overall, immunotherapy aims to help patients live longer, manage symptoms, and improve outcomes across various cancer types, particularly in advanced or metastatic stages.

entities.description:
Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Genetic testing is a medical procedure that analyzes DNA from samples such as blood, saliva, urine, or tumor tissue to identify genetic mutations and abnormalities. It serves two primary purposes: detecting inherited (germline) mutations that increase cancer risk and guiding personalized treatment, prognosis, and preventive measures. In the context of cancer, genetic testing is distinct from tumor mutation testing, which only examines mutations within the tumor itself. For inherited risk assessment, it is often recommended for individuals with a family history of cancer, such as breast, ovarian, prostate, or other hereditary cancer syndromes, and can identify mutations in genes like BRCA1, BRCA2, and BCR::ABL1. In hematologic malignancies like acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), genetic testing looks for changes in leukemia cells—including mutations, deletions, insertions, inversions, amplifications, and translocations—to determine disease aggressiveness and guide treatment decisions. For ovarian cancer, genetic testing is recommended for all patients to assess hereditary risk and inform therapy. In some cases, genetic testing of biopsy samples may help diagnose specific cancers, such as follicular or oncocytic thyroid cancer, by identifying genetic markers. Overall, genetic testing is a versatile tool used across various cancers to identify inherited or somatic mutations, support family history assessment, and tailor prevention and treatment strategies.

A patient is an individual receiving medical care, diagnosis, testing, or treatment for a wide range of conditions, including various types of cancer (such as basal cell skin cancer, prostate cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), rectal cancer, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), actinic keratoses, colon cancer, cervical cancer, follicular lymphoma (FL), anal cancer, bone cancer, bladder cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), ovarian cancer, mouth cancer, inflammatory breast cancer, and throat cancer) as well as other medical conditions. The patient may be diagnosed with, at risk for, or being evaluated for these conditions, and may undergo various diagnostic procedures, imaging tests, biopsies, and treatments as part of their care.

Patients are encouraged to be active participants in their own healthcare, including advocating for themselves, asking questions, making shared decisions with their care team, and managing their own health records, treatment side effects, and emotional well-being. They may also be advised to follow recommended exam schedules and to seek support and information about survivorship. The care team, which may include doctors, radiologists, and other specialists, coordinates the patient’s diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up care. The patient’s physical, mental, and emotional well-being are considered important throughout the process, and they may experience side effects, recovery processes, or challenges related to their condition and treatment. In some cases, factors such as claustrophobia, allergies, or kidney issues may influence the choice of imaging tests or procedures. Ultimately, the patient is the individual undergoing diagnostic and treatment procedures, with the goal of managing their health and receiving appropriate medical support.

A care team is a multidisciplinary group of healthcare professionals who collaborate to provide comprehensive medical care, diagnosis, treatment, and support for patients, particularly those with cancer or other complex conditions. The team typically includes board-certified medical experts from various fields, such as doctors (e.g., pulmonologists, thoracic radiologists, thoracic surgeons, oncologists, hematologists, hematopathologists, breast specialists, gynecologists, radiologists, dietitians, and therapists), nurses, specialists, technologists, pharmacists, and support staff. They work together to plan and implement treatment, interpret test results (including imaging, CBC measurements, and other diagnostics), discuss treatment options and potential side effects (including effects on fertility), and guide patients through diagnostic and therapeutic processes. The care team is central to patient communication and support, encouraging patients to share information, ask questions, discuss preferences, and make shared decisions about their care. They also provide guidance on preparation for procedures (such as imaging tests and surgery), manage symptoms and side effects, and offer resources for issues like smoking cessation, claustrophobia, and emotional support. The team may specialize in specific conditions, including lung, breast, bladder, pancreatic, thyroid, prostate, glioma, CNS lymphoma, AML, ALL, CLL, NPC, and other cancers, and is responsible for coordinating all aspects of a patient's medical journey, from diagnosis through treatment and recovery.

Supportive care, also known as palliative care, is a comprehensive and integral part of cancer care designed to relieve symptoms caused by the disease and the side effects of its treatment, with the primary goal of improving quality of life for patients at any stage of illness. This type of care can be provided alone or alongside active cancer treatments such as chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery, and is always an option for patients whether they are in active treatment or not. Supportive care addresses a wide range of physical, emotional, and practical challenges, including pain management, nutritional support, and the management of treatment-related side effects. It also encompasses emotional support, counseling, and services that provide practical assistance, and may include hospice care for patients with advanced or metastatic cancer. The scope of supportive care extends across various cancer types, including lung cancer, breast cancer, AML (acute myeloid leukemia), ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia), and CLL (chronic lymphocytic leukemia), where it is used to manage symptoms, support patients through therapy, and enhance overall well-being. In some cases, supportive care may involve treatments such as radiation therapy to ease pain or discomfort caused by cancer. Ultimately, supportive care aims to extend and enhance life by addressing the multifaceted challenges of cancer, ensuring that patients receive holistic care that improves their comfort and quality of life throughout their cancer journey.

A patient is an individual receiving medical care, diagnosis, testing, or treatment for a wide range of conditions, including various types of cancer (such as basal cell skin cancer, prostate cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), rectal cancer, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), actinic keratoses, colon cancer, cervical cancer, follicular lymphoma (FL), anal cancer, bone cancer, bladder cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), ovarian cancer, mouth cancer, inflammatory breast cancer, and throat cancer) as well as other medical conditions. The patient may be diagnosed with, at risk for, or being evaluated for these conditions, and may undergo various diagnostic procedures, imaging tests, biopsies, and treatments as part of their care.

Patients are encouraged to be active participants in their own healthcare, including advocating for themselves, asking questions, making shared decisions with their care team, and managing their own health records, treatment side effects, and emotional well-being. They may also be advised to follow recommended exam schedules and to seek support and information about survivorship. The care team, which may include doctors, radiologists, and other specialists, coordinates the patient’s diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up care. The patient’s physical, mental, and emotional well-being are considered important throughout the process, and they may experience side effects, recovery processes, or challenges related to their condition and treatment. In some cases, factors such as claustrophobia, allergies, or kidney issues may influence the choice of imaging tests or procedures. Ultimately, the patient is the individual undergoing diagnostic and treatment procedures, with the goal of managing their health and receiving appropriate medical support.

entities.description: Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that occurs in the cervix, the lower part of the female reproductive system, and is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in cervical tissues. It is primarily caused by long-term (persistent) infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), and it is a common cancer of the female reproductive system. The disease can manifest in several histological types, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is often detected through screening methods such as Pap smears, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by cervical biopsy. The cancer is staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, and staging is crucial as it determines treatment options and prognosis. Treatment approaches vary and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy (such as chemotherapy), and chemoradiation, with the choice of treatment based on the cancer stage and risk factors such as lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). Cervical cancer can spread to lymph nodes and, if untreated or not diagnosed early, may recur locally or regionally or spread to distant organs; therefore, surveillance and follow-up care are critical for managing recurrence and metastasis. The disease is closely linked to HPV, and a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of anal cancer, as both share the same viral cause. Consequently, screening for cervical cancer is recommended for patients with anal cancer, and female survivors of anal cancer may also be screened for cervical cancer. Additionally, p16, a biomarker, can be found in cervical cancer tissues.

Immunotherapy is a type of systemic cancer treatment that leverages and boosts the body’s own immune system to find, reactivate, and destroy cancer cells. It is commonly administered by a medical oncologist and is considered a newer, non-hormone therapeutic approach that works alongside other systemic therapies like chemotherapy and targeted therapy. Immunotherapy is used across a wide range of cancers, including anal, cervical, bladder, ovarian, breast, prostate, colon, skin (squamous cell carcinoma), and primary CNS lymphoma, as well as for acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and metastatic disease.

The treatment often involves immune checkpoint inhibitors—such as pembrolizumab, nivolumab, and ipilimumab—which help reactivate the immune system against tumor cells. For certain cancers, including those with specific biomarkers like dMMR, MSI-H, or PD-1 expression, immunotherapy is a preferred option. It may be used to avoid surgery in anal cancer, to treat recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer with specific biomarkers, or as a recommended approach when cancer progresses during or after chemotherapy. In primary CNS lymphoma, the main immunotherapy drug is rituximab, a monoclonal antibody that targets CD20 proteins on cancer cells.

Eligibility for immunotherapy is often determined through biomarker testing, and it may be delivered systemically or directly into the bladder for certain bladder cancers. While generally effective, immunotherapy can cause side effects, including autoimmune reactions, fatigue, fever, nausea, diarrhea, drowsiness, and low blood cell counts. These side effects are addressed in clinical guidelines. Overall, immunotherapy aims to help patients live longer, manage symptoms, and improve outcomes across various cancer types, particularly in advanced or metastatic stages.

Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the ovaries, most commonly beginning in the epithelium (the outer lining of the ovaries), and can also start in the fallopian tubes. It encompasses a range of types, including high-grade serous carcinoma, high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and other less common ovarian cancers. The disease can be hereditary or sporadic, with inherited mutations in genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, as well as Lynch syndrome, significantly increasing the risk in affected individuals. Additionally, a family history of ovarian cancer in close blood relatives is associated with an increased risk of developing pancreatic and prostate cancers.

Symptoms of ovarian cancer commonly include bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, difficulty eating, feeling full quickly, and urinary urgency. The disease is staged from 1 to 4, with stages 2, 3, and 4 specifically mentioned, and requires clinical staging along with various diagnostic tests—such as biopsy, imaging, and blood tests—to determine the extent of spread and guide treatment. Treatment typically involves a multidisciplinary team of experts and may include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, with protocols also addressing recurrence management. Ovarian cancer is the central topic of the provided text, guiding discussions on diagnosis, treatment, and related health considerations.

Recurrence, also known as relapse, refers to the return of cancer after a period of treatment or remission. This phenomenon is common across various cancer types, including bladder, breast, cervical, ovarian, prostate, basal cell skin, primary CNS lymphoma, and head and neck cancers. Recurrence can manifest locally (at the original site), regionally (in nearby lymph nodes), or at distant sites in the body, depending on the cancer type.

For bladder cancer, recurrence is a frequent occurrence that necessitates ongoing monitoring and regular follow-up testing. In breast cancer, recurrence may be local or distant. Cervical cancer recurrence can occur locally, regionally, or at distant sites, and often requires imaging, exploratory surgery, and biomarker testing to guide further treatment. Ovarian cancer recurrence also demands further management and monitoring. Prostate cancer recurrence can be detected through imaging tests such as MRI or PSMA-PET scans, and is a key factor in risk assessment. Basal cell skin cancer recurrence involves the cancer returning to the original area or spreading to lymph nodes or distant parts of the body, indicating a need for continued surveillance.

Monitoring for recurrence typically involves imaging tests like MRI, PSMA-PET, and other surveillance methods, including regular physical exams and blood tests. In some cases, such as higher-risk thyroid cancer, TSH suppression is used as a monitoring strategy. Symptoms of recurrence can vary but may include pelvic pain, bloating, and fatigue, particularly in gynecologic cancers.

Treatment for recurrence depends on the location and extent of the disease and may involve additional therapies such as surgery, radiation therapy, radioactive iodine (RAI), or adjustments to chemotherapy regimens. Biomarker testing is often employed to guide treatment decisions. Certain cancer subtypes and features can increase the risk of recurrence, and radiation therapy may be used in high-risk patients to prevent it. Overall, recurrence requires vigilant follow-up and individualized management to address the return of disease effectively.

Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Chemotherapy can be used alone or combined with other therapies, including radiation (chemoradiation), surgery, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially when PD-L1 or PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed). It is a standard treatment for many cancers, including AML, ALL, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, anal cancer, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and squamous cell skin cancer, among others. Specific regimens vary by cancer type and may include platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin), taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine), mitomycin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and anthracyclines. Chemotherapy can be delivered systemically (through the bloodstream), intravenously, orally, intraperitoneally, intravesically, intrathecally, or intraocularly, depending on the cancer and treatment goal. It may be used before surgery (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), as primary treatment for metastatic disease, or in high doses during stem cell rescue. Side effects are common and include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, fever, infection, and low blood cell counts. Chemotherapy can also affect fertility and other bodily functions, so preventive measures and birth control may be recommended during treatment. Smoking during chemotherapy can increase lung problems. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility. Chemotherapy is often a key component of treatment plans and may be recommended based on cancer stage, molecular markers (e.g., PD-L1 expression), and response to other treatments.

At this time, chemotherapy regimens recommended for use with radiation therapy to treat stage I, II, and III anal cancer include: Mitomycin and capecitabine Mitomycin and 5-FU 5-FU and cisplatin While you undergo chemotherapy with one of the above regimens, you will also receive treatment with radiation therapy 5 days per week. These chemotherapy regimens are described in more detail next. Mitomycin and capecitabine is a commonly used regimen. Capecitabine is taken by mouth twice daily, Monday through Friday (on radiation days only), for 5 and a half to 6 weeks. You will be undergoing radiation therapy during the same time period. On the day you begin taking capecitabine, a single intravenous dose of mitomycin will be given. Another dose of mitomycin is usually given at the start of week Mitomycin and 5-FU is another regimen recommended for use with radiation therapy. 5-FU is given by continuous (constant) infusion over several days. You do not need to stay at a treatment center during this time, however. Before chemotherapy begins, a thin, flexible tube will be inserted into a vein in your upper chest, below the collarbone. This is referred to as a “port.” Using a small wire and often x-ray guidance, the tube is guided to a large vein above the right side of the heart. Some people receive a temporary PICC line instead. A PICC line is a deep IV that stays in the arm for the duration of treatment. The 5-FU is stored in a small, wearable pump connected to the catheter. The pump infuses the medicine into the body very slowly, over several days. The tube, called a central venous catheter, stays in place for the duration of treatment. It allows you to receive chemotherapy with 5-FU from home. The first 5-FU infusion starts when radiation therapy begins and lasts for 4 to 5 days. You will have another 4- to 5-day infusion at the start of week 5 of radiation therapy. The pump will be disconnected and removed between infusions. A single dose of mitomycin is given on the first day of the first 5-FU infusion. Another dose of mitomycin may be given when the second 5-FU infusion begins, towards the end of radiation therapy. Another option for chemotherapy is 5-FU and cisplatin. 5-FU is given as described above. Cisplatin is given intravenously on the first day of 5-FU infusions. Chemotherapy can kill normal, healthy cells in addition to cancer cells. The damage to healthy cells causes potentially harsh side effects. The most common side effects of the chemotherapy regimens discussed above are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, sores in the mouth and lining of the anus, and low blood cell counts. Low white blood cell counts can make you prone to infections. Talk to your treatment team about ways to prevent or lessen these side effects. Capecitabine can cause a side effect known as hand-foot syndrome. Symptoms include redness, swelling, and pain on the palms of the hands, bottoms of feet, or both. Sometimes blisters appear. Your dose of capecitabine may be changed at the earliest signs of hand-foot syndrome. Next steps See Follow-up and surveillance on page 23 for next steps. We want your feedback! Our goal is to provide helpful and easy-to-understand information on cancer. Take our survey to let us know what we got right and what we could do better: NCCN.org/patients/feedback Perianal cancer (stages I – III) This section provides treatment recommendations for stages I, II, and III perianal cancer. Stages I through III are nonmetastatic, meaning the cancer has not spread beyond the pelvis. See page 26 for information on metastatic anal cancer. Like anal canal cancer, most perianal cancers are treated with chemoradiation. However, local excision (surgery) may be an option for some early-stage, low-risk perianal cancers. Local excision involves removing only the tumor and a small area of surrounding tissue. Local excision Local excision is a recommended treatment option for some stage I and stage IIA perianal cancers. Stage I and II anal cancers have not invaded nearby lymph nodes. See page 13 for more information on cancer staging. For local excision to be an option, the cancer must not have invaded the sphincter muscle. The cancer grade is also important when determining if local excision is an option. The cancer grade is a rating of how fast the cancer is expected to grow and spread. It is based on how abnormal the cancer cells look when viewed under a microscope. Higher scores mean that the cancer is likely to grow and spread quickly. There are 5 possible grades: GX: Grade cannot be assessed (undetermined grade) G1: Well differentiated (low grade) G2: Moderately differentiated (intermediate grade) G3: Poorly differentiated (high grade) G4: Undifferentiated (high grade) Local excision should only be considered for low-grade (G1) and intermediate-grade (G2) perianal cancers. The normal tissue surrounding the lesion removed during surgery is called the surgical margin. If a margin of at least 1 cm is removed and it does not contain cancer cells,

after treatment. Consult your doctor for the best time to plan a pregnancy. Those with testicles Cancer and cancer treatment can damage sperm. Therefore, use contraception (birth control) such as condoms to prevent pregnancy during and immediately after cancer treatment. Create a medical binder A medical binder or notebook is a great way to organize all of your records in one place. Make copies of blood tests, imaging results, and reports about your specific type of cancer. It will be helpful when getting a second opinion. Choose a binder that meets your needs. Consider a zipper pocket to include a pen, small calendar, and insurance cards. Create folders for insurance forms, test types (ie, blood, imaging, pathology, radiology, genetics), treatments, and procedures. Organize items in the folder by date. Use online patient portals to view your test results and other records. Download or print the records to add to your binder. Add a section for questions and to take notes. Bring your medical binder to appointments. You never know when you might need it! Imaging tests Imaging tests take pictures of the inside of your body. Imaging tests show the primary tumor, or where the cancer started, and look for cancer in other parts of the body. A radiologist, an expert in interpreting imaging tests, will write a report and send this report to your health care provider (HCP). It is likely that the report will be sent directly to you through your patient portal or patient access system. You should discuss these results with your HCP. You will not have all of the following tests. Contrast material Contrast material is used to improve the pictures of the inside of the body. Contrast materials are not dyes, but substances that help enhance and improve the images of several organs and structures in the body. It is used to make the pictures clearer. The contrast is not permanent and will leave your body in your urine immediately after the test. The types of contrast vary and are different for CT and MRI. Tell your care team if you have had allergic reactions to contrast in the past. This is important. You might be given medicines to avoid the effects of those allergies. Contrast might not be used if you have a serious allergy or if your kidneys aren’t working well. CT scan A computed tomography (CT or CAT) scan uses x-rays and computer technology to take pictures of the inside of the body. It takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles. All the images are combined to make one detailed picture. A CT scan of your head, neck, and chest, may be one of the tests to look for cancer. In most cases, contrast will be used. MRI scan A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. It does not use x-rays. Because of the very strong magnets used in the MRI machine, tell the technologist if you have any metal in your body. During the test, you will likely be asked to hold your breath for 10 to 20 seconds as the technician collects the images. Contrast is often used. A closed MRI has a capsule-like design where the magnet surrounds you. An open MRI has a magnetic top and bottom, which allows for an opening on each end. Closed MRIs are more common than open MRIs, so if you have claustrophobia (a dread or fear of enclosed spaces), be sure to talk to your care team about it. PET scan A positron emission tomography (PET) scan uses a radioactive drug called a tracer. A tracer is a substance injected into a vein to see where cancer cells are in the body and if they are using sugar produced by your body to grow. Cancer cells show up as bright spots on PET scans. However, not all tumors will appear on a PET scan. Also, not all bright spots are cancer. It is normal for the brain, base of the tongue or tonsil lymphoid tissue, heart, kidneys, and bladder to be bright on PET. Inflammation or infection can also show up as a bright spot. When a PET scan is combined with CT, it is called a PET/CT scan. FDG-PET/CT An FDG-PET/CT uses a radiotracer called fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG). It is made of fluoride and a simple form of sugar called glucose. You cannot eat or drink for at least 4 hours before the scan. This scan is most helpful when other imaging results are unclear. It may help find cancer in lymph nodes and distant sites. If it clearly shows cancer in the bone, a bone scan and sodium fluoride PET/ CT may not be needed. FDG-PET/CT can be done at the same time as a CT used for diagnosis. Ultrasound Ultrasound (US) uses high-energy sound waves to form pictures of the inside of the body. This is similar to the sonogram used for pregnancy. A wand-like probe (transducer) will be held and moved on your neck using gel. Ultrasound is painless and does not use x-rays, so it can be repeated as needed. Ultrasound is good at showing small areas of cancer that are near the skin. Sometimes, an ultrasound or CT is used to guide a biopsy. Panoramic dental x-ray A panoramic dental -ray or panoramic x-ray (Panorex) uses a very small dose of radiation to capture the entire mouth in one image, including the teeth, upper and lower jaws, and surrounding structures and tissues. It is commonly performed by dentists and oral surgeons in everyday practice and may be used to plan treatment for dentures, braces, extractions, and implants. If you smoke or vape, seek help to quit A history of smoking or vaping nicotine increases your chances of developing head and neck, lung, and other cancers. Smoking and vaping can limit how well cancer treatment works and prevent wound healing. They also greatly increase your chances of having side effects

Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Chemotherapy can be used alone or combined with other therapies, including radiation (chemoradiation), surgery, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially when PD-L1 or PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed). It is a standard treatment for many cancers, including AML, ALL, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, anal cancer, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and squamous cell skin cancer, among others. Specific regimens vary by cancer type and may include platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin), taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine), mitomycin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and anthracyclines. Chemotherapy can be delivered systemically (through the bloodstream), intravenously, orally, intraperitoneally, intravesically, intrathecally, or intraocularly, depending on the cancer and treatment goal. It may be used before surgery (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), as primary treatment for metastatic disease, or in high doses during stem cell rescue. Side effects are common and include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, fever, infection, and low blood cell counts. Chemotherapy can also affect fertility and other bodily functions, so preventive measures and birth control may be recommended during treatment. Smoking during chemotherapy can increase lung problems. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility. Chemotherapy is often a key component of treatment plans and may be recommended based on cancer stage, molecular markers (e.g., PD-L1 expression), and response to other treatments.

Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy radiation—such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons—to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is planned and prescribed by a radiation oncologist and delivered by radiation therapists or other specialists. This treatment is often used as a local therapy to target specific areas of the body, and it may be combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation), surgery, or systemic therapies, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Radiation therapy is applicable to a wide range of cancers, including anal, bladder, brain (e.g., gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma), breast, cervical, prostate, rectal, skin (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), thyroid, and perianal cancers, as well as chordoma and metastatic anal cancer. It can be used as a primary treatment, an adjunct after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells, or as palliative care to relieve pain. Techniques include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), and brachytherapy (internal radioactive material).

Treatment is typically given over several weeks, with common schedules of five sessions per week, each session lasting 30 to 60 minutes. While effective, radiation therapy can cause side effects, which may appear during treatment or years later. These include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, tiredness, headaches, nausea, vision problems, cataracts, and long-term cognitive issues. Radiation to the head and neck can affect endocrine glands, hearing, and other functions, requiring pre- and post-treatment monitoring. Additionally, radiation therapy can impact fertility—for example, in rectal cancer it may damage ovarian and testicular function—and prior exposure to radiation, especially at a young age (e.g., to the chest), is a risk factor for certain cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer and small cell lung cancer.

For some cancers, radiation therapy is a preferred or standard treatment option. For instance, IMRT is often preferred for anal cancer, and radiation is a main treatment for gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma. In prostate cancer, it may be used in both early and advanced stages, though it may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients. For skin cancers like squamous cell carcinoma, radiation is used when surgery is not possible or as an adjunct to reduce recurrence

Treatment encompasses a broad range of medical interventions—such as surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies—used to manage, cure, or slow the progression of various cancers, including head and neck cancer, prostate cancer, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), primary CNS lymphoma, chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), breast cancer, bone cancer, basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, MGZL, and thyroid cancer. The specific approach is personalized based on diagnostic test results, cancer staging, biomarkers (e.g., BCR::ABL1 protein activity), and patient preferences, with options ranging from minimal or no treatment for low-risk cases to aggressive therapies for high-risk or advanced disease. Treatment aims to slow tumor growth, reduce symptoms, prolong life, and prevent the disease from causing problems, though it may have side effects on hearing, fertility, and other bodily functions. For certain cancers, such as CLL, monitoring may be an option, while for metastatic cancer, targeted therapy or immunotherapy may be employed. Clinical trials are also considered in some cases, and treatment plans are often guided by a multidisciplinary care team, with patient preferences playing a key role in decision-making.

Imaging tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, locate, and evaluate tumors, assess cancer extent, and check for cancer spread. These tests are essential for staging cancer, planning treatment, monitoring tumor response during chemotherapy, and detecting recurrence during surveillance. They are also used to visualize internal structures, guide biopsies, and identify abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, organ involvement, or areas of infection or bleeding.

Imaging tests include a wide range of techniques such as CT scans, MRI, PET scans, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, X-rays, mammograms, and bone scans. These modalities are applied across various cancer types, including breast, prostate, colon, rectal, esophageal, liver, kidney, ovarian, thyroid, adrenal, bone, and throat cancers, as well as leukemias like ALL and AML, and lymphomas such as CBCL and NPC. For example, mammograms, ultrasounds, and MRIs are used to visualize breast tissue; CT and MRI are primary methods for colon cancer staging; and ultrasound is used to detect thyroid nodules and cancer.

Imaging tests are interpreted by a radiologist and are used to reveal a tumor’s location, size, and other features, as well as to detect cancer spread to distant sites. In certain cancers, such as early-stage prostate cancer, imaging may not be necessary, but in others, like leukemia, they help detect spread outside the bone marrow to areas such as the brain, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and skin. Overall, imaging tests are indispensable diagnostic and monitoring tools in oncology, providing detailed visual information that guides clinical decisions across the cancer care continuum.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped glands distributed throughout the body, including the neck, armpits, groin, pelvis, near the rectum, stomach, thyroid, bladder, and colon. They are part of the lymphatic and immune systems, containing immune cells such as lymphocytes, and function to filter lymph fluid, remove foreign particles, germs, and harmful substances, and help fight infection and disease. There are over 300 lymph nodes in the head and neck alone.

Lymph nodes play a critical role in the body’s immune response and are a primary site where many cancers—such as breast, prostate, lung, colorectal, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, kidney, thyroid, anal, stomach, esophageal, skin (including basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), and head and neck cancers—may spread. Their involvement is a key factor in cancer staging (e.g., the N score in the TNM system) and prognosis, and they are often examined during physical exams for enlargement, which may indicate infection or cancer spread.

Lymph nodes can be assessed through imaging tests such as MRI, CT, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, PSMA/PET, and EUS, and may be biopsied (including sentinel or axillary lymph node biopsy) or removed during surgery (e.g., colectomy, neck dissection, or transabdominal surgery) to determine whether cancer has spread. Enlarged lymph nodes may also result from the buildup of cancerous cells, as seen in conditions like chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), follicular lymphoma, B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, and mediastinal gray zone lymphoma. In some cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), spread to nearby lymph nodes is uncommon.

Lymph nodes are also involved in defining specific cancer stages, such as stage 3C cervical cancer (involvement of pelvic or para-aortic nodes) and stage 3 bladder cancer (nodes near the bladder). In lymphomas, cancer originating in lymph nodes can weaken the immune system, and involvement outside the nodes is termed extranodal disease. Overall, lymph nodes are essential immune organs whose status is crucial in diagnosing, staging, and treating many diseases, particularly cancers.
