contexts: Tumor staging Tumors come in different shapes and sizes. So it’s not easy to compare one tumor to another. To solve this problem, cancer experts created the tumor, node, metastasis (TNM) system to describe any tumor. It’s based on the results of your imaging scans, biopsies, and blood tests. In this system, the letters T, N, and M stand for different areas of cancer growth: T (tumor) – Describes the size of the main (primary) tumor and if it has grown outside the prostate N (node) – Identifies whether cancer has spread to lymph nodes M (metastasis) – Indicates if cancer has spread (metastasized) to parts of the body outside of the pelvis Your provider will assign a number to each letter, based on your test results. The higher the number, the larger the tumor (T) or the more the cancer has spread (M). These scores are combined to assign a “stage” to the cancer. Staging is a way to describe how much cancer is in your body and how far it has spread. Knowing your stage is important for predicting the course of your disease and for making a treatment plan. Cancer staging is done when you’re first diagnosed. It may also be done after treatment to confirm that the stage hasn’t changed. How to read a TNM score Let’s say your prostate cancer is given a TNM score of T4, N1, MThis score means that the tumor has grown outside the prostate gland (T4) and has spread to nearby lymph nodes (N1) and to one or more distant parts of the body (M1). Why know your TNM score? For one, it lets you know the extent of your cancer. It also helps characterize your risk for the cancer to spread. Your level of risk helps indicate the most appropriate treatment for you. Measurements and assessments not covered in this book include PSA density, Gleason score, Grade Group, and risk groups. To learn more about these, see the NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Early-Stage Prostate Cancer, which can be found at NCCN.org/ patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. What’s next? After you’ve had all these tests to confirm you have prostate cancer, your care team will discuss your test results and will work with you to develop a plan for treatment. Though orchiectomy is a surgical procedure, it’s still considered hormone therapy because it removes the primary source of testosterone: the testicles. Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Blood tests are a broad category of diagnostic procedures and laboratory analyses performed on blood samples to assess overall health, evaluate organ function, and detect, diagnose, and monitor various diseases—particularly cancer. These tests are used across a wide range of cancers, including liver, bladder, AML (acute myeloid leukemia), CML (chronic myeloid leukemia), ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia), cervical, bone, pancreatic, esophageal, FL (follicular lymphoma), ovarian, stomach, kidney, prostate, colon, adrenal tumors, primary CNS lymphoma, and NPC (nasopharyngeal carcinoma). They are also used in general health checks and to guide treatment planning, with results often included in medical records and binders for patient reference.

Blood tests measure various blood components, such as blood cell counts, blood chemistry, and organ function markers (e.g., liver and kidney function). Common tests include the complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, liver function tests (LFTs), and chemistry profiles. Specific tests may also detect tumor markers or other indicators, such as carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) for colon cancer, CA-125 for ovarian cancer, PSA for prostate cancer, and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), thyroglobulin (Tg), and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (Tg ab) for monitoring cancer recurrence. Blood tests can also measure hormone levels to detect abnormalities related to adrenal tumors or assess endocrine function.

These tests are essential for establishing the extent of cancer, guiding treatment decisions, and monitoring for recurrence or response to therapy. They are performed by drawing a blood sample through a needle from a vein in the arm. Blood tests are used to detect markers or abnormalities related to cancer, evaluate blood cell counts, and rule out other conditions. They are often ordered as part of initial testing, during chemotherapy, or if recurrence is suspected, and are critical for patients to understand and keep copies of their results.

Imaging refers to a broad range of medical techniques used to create pictures of the inside of the body, including computed tomography (CT) scans, PET/CT scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasound, x-rays, and transvaginal ultrasound. These tests are essential for determining the extent and spread of cancer, which is critical for staging the disease and guiding treatment decisions. Imaging is used across various cancer types: for pancreatic cancer, it helps decide if surgery is an option; for cervical cancer, techniques such as FDG-PET/CT, CT with contrast, and MRI detect recurrence or spread, typically ordered based on symptoms or stage; for prostate cancer, imaging is used alongside PSA tests to evaluate presence and spread, visualizing the prostate and surrounding areas; for lymphoma, it identifies the location, size, and features of the disease; for adrenal tumors, it often detects them incidentally; for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), it assesses spread to lymph nodes and beyond; for bladder cancer, it visualizes the bladder and surrounding areas to stage and plan treatment; for brain tumors and gliomas, MRI and CT scans aid in diagnosis; and for anal cancers (stage II and III), imaging is used for surveillance after treatment, with yearly imaging recommended for three years to monitor for recurrence or further spread. Imaging is performed by specialists such as thoracic radiologists and is a key component of treatment planning and post-treatment monitoring across oncology.

A physical exam is a clinical assessment performed by a healthcare provider to evaluate a patient's overall health, detect signs of disease, and guide medical decisions. It is a routine medical check-up that includes measuring vital signs (such as blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature), checking body measurements (like height and weight), and listening to the lungs and heart. The exam also involves examining the eyes, ears, nose, and throat, as well as palpating (feeling) the abdomen, pelvis, and lymph nodes to assess organ size and detect abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, lumps, or swelling in the spleen or liver.

This examination is used across a wide range of medical contexts, including general health assessments, pre-anesthesia evaluations, and cancer screening or monitoring. It helps identify signs of various conditions, including breast abnormalities, basal cell skin cancer, and cancers such as ALL, AML, CLL, liver cancer, NPC, bladder cancer, and colon cancer. Physical exams are also performed periodically during chemotherapy (every 1 to 3 cycles) to monitor treatment effectiveness and side effects, and are part of short-term follow-up after procedures like total thyroidectomy, alongside blood tests. Additionally, they are included in surveillance schedules for stages 2 and 3 colon cancer to check for recurrence or spread.

The physical exam provides critical information to the care team about a patient's treatment readiness, overall health, and functional abilities, and is used to detect signs of cancer recurrence or other health issues. It is a general health test that may also include assessing the throat and airway, skin, and other body systems to ensure a comprehensive evaluation.

Ultrasound is a versatile, non-invasive diagnostic imaging technique that uses high-energy sound waves to create real-time pictures of the inside of the body. It is painless and does not involve exposure to x-rays, making it a safe and widely used tool across many medical fields. Ultrasound is commonly employed to visualize the size, shape, and location of thyroid nodules, helping to detect thyroid cancer and monitor tumor growth during active surveillance. It is also frequently used to examine lymph nodes, where it can detect small areas of cancer near the skin and guide fine-needle biopsies with real-time visualization for accurate sampling. In addition, ultrasound is used to evaluate breast tissue abnormalities found on mammograms, guide prostate biopsies, and serve as the first diagnostic step for suspected ovarian cancer, using both transabdominal and transvaginal approaches. It is also applied in renal ultrasound for non-invasive assessment of organs, in echocardiograms to examine the heart, and may be used to examine the testicles for lymphoma spread, though this is not always necessary. Overall, ultrasound is an effective imaging method for guiding procedures, detecting small superficial cancers, and providing real-time, detailed images of internal structures across a wide range of clinical applications.

The next chapter describes the different treatment options for advanced-stage prostate cancer. After that chapter, you’ll read about which of those treatments may be right for you and your particular type of cancer. Imaging tests are used to see where the cancer has spread beyond the prostate. Imaging also shows the size and location of the cancer. A biopsy is a procedure that removes samples of cells or tissue, which are tested for cancer. A genetic test is used to find abnormal changes (mutations) in your genes. An inherited genetic mutation occurs in every cell in your body. A somatic mutation occurs all by itself and is only found in the cells of a tumor. To find out if you have an inherited risk for cancer, talk to your doctor about germline testing or ask to be referred to a genetic counselor. 3 Prostate cancer treatments Hormone therapy Non-hormone therapy Clinical trials Supportive care What’s next? Key points There’s more than one treatment for advanced prostate cancer. This chapter describes the available treatment options and what you might expect from them. Talk with your care team about which treatment could be best for you. Prostate cancer is a complex disease with many treatment options. Treatments for advanced-stage prostate cancer include hormone therapy as well as non-hormone therapies like chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, and radiation therapy. Often, hormone therapy is combined with one or more other therapies. Combining therapies can be more effective than using either therapy alone. key word in ADT is “deprivation”—this therapy “deprives” (starves) the cancer of its main fuel: androgens. This can shrink the tumor or slow tumor growth for a while. You might hear the term “castration” used when describing prostate cancer or its treatment. This term describes a drastic reduction of testosterone. Castration can be done with hormone-lowering medication or by surgical removal of one or both testicles (orchiectomy). Though orchiectomy is a surgical procedure, it’s still considered hormone therapy because it removes the primary source of testosterone: the testicles. While drug hormone therapy can be reversed when the medication is stopped, orchiectomy is permanent and can’t be reversed. Surgical removal of the testicles is much less common these days because systemic Hormone therapy Hormone therapy is a systemic (whole-body) treatment that adds, blocks, or removes hormones. A hormone is a natural chemical made by a gland in the body. Its job is to activate cells or organs. Male hormones are called androgens. The main androgen is testosterone. Most of the testosterone in the body is made by the testicles. Testosterone helps produce sperm, among other functions. But testosterone also helps prostate cancer grow. A type of hormone therapy called androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) can stop your body from making testosterone or block cancer cells from using testosterone. The What is ADT? Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) brings testosterone down to a very low level. For example, patients with lower risk generally get minimal treatment or no treatment at all. Patients with higher risk usually get more aggressive treatment. Test results and calculations—PSA level, Grade Group, tumor stage, and biopsy results—are put together to determine your risk group. PSA level A simple blood test will tell you how much prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is in your bloodstream. A high PSA level may indicate a risk for prostate cancer. However, high PSA levels can vary by age, race, and other factors: Age – PSA level tends to increase with age. For people in their 40s, a PSA level above 5 ng/mL is very suspicious for disease. For those in their 60s, 5 ng/mL or higher is suspicious. A PSA level of 10 ng/mL or higher is a danger sign at any age. Race – Normal PSA levels tend to be higher in Black males than in white males—about 1 point higher on average among males of the same age. Researchers don’t know the reason for this difference, but they’re investigating it. Enlarged prostate – The larger the prostate, the more PSA it can make. Other health issues besides cancer can also cause an enlarged prostate. h Sex and exercise – PSA may increase after ejaculation or vigorous exercise. Your doctor may recommend avoiding sex and exercise for 2 or 3 days before a PSA test. This short break allows PSA to return to its usual level. Drugs and supplements – Some medicines, herbals, and supplements can also affect PSA level. Biopsy – PSA level rises temporarily after a biopsy of the prostate. 66 Now more than ever, those living with cancer are living better, longer lives thanks to the power of research and advancements in treatment.” PSA level doesn’t tell the whole story, though. There are other ways that PSA can be interpreted, such as PSA density. PSA density If you have a larger prostate, you’re also likely to have a higher PSA level. But that doesn’t mean you have a greater risk for prostate cancer. To adjust for this, care providers calculate PSA density. PSA density is the amount of PSA compared to the size of the prostate. PSA density is calculated by dividing the PSA level by the prostate size. The size of the prostate is measured by transrectal ultrasound or MRI scan. A higher PSA density (above 15 ng/ mL², for example) indicates a greater likelihood of cancer. PSA density also accounts for those with small and very small prostates, who could have prostate cancer even with low PSAs. Results from these tests may indicate that the cancer will grow and spread quickly, for example. A cancer cell pattern that looks more like normal and healthy cells is given a lower number. A cell pattern that looks more abnormal is assigned a higher number. Gleason patterns range from 1 to However, patterns 1 and 2 are so rarely found that they are no longer used. But prostate biopsies often contain more than one pattern of cells. To account for this, the two most common Gleason patterns found in the biopsy sample are combined into a single Gleason score. The pattern of cancer cells that takes up the largest area in the sample is assigned the first number. The pattern that accounts for the secondlargest area is given the second number. A higher Gleason score means the cancer is more likely to grow and spread quickly than a cancer with a lower Gleason score. Gleason scores range from 6 to 10, where 6 is the lowest score. A Gleason score of 7 is intermediate-grade, and 8 to 10 is high-grade. This can be confusing because 6 seems like it would be a medium score, not a low score. So cancer with a Gleason score of 6 is assigned as Grade Group 1 to show that it is the lowest score. Likewise, cancer with a Gleason score of 9 or 10 becomes Grade Group 5, the highest score. entities.description: Breast tissue is the tissue that makes up the breast, including milk ducts, fat, nerves, lymph and blood vessels, ligaments, and connective tissue. It is the site where breast cancer develops.

Breast cancer is a disease that originates in the cells of the breast, most commonly arising from the epithelial cells of the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs). It can be classified as ductal or lobular, and includes various subtypes such as inflammatory breast cancer. The disease is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of cells, which can spread through invasive growth into surrounding tissues and metastasize to distant parts of the body, including the bone, lungs, liver, brain, or distant lymph nodes. When breast cancer spreads to another organ, such as the lungs, it is still referred to as breast cancer, not as a new type of cancer.

Breast cancer can affect anyone, regardless of gender assigned at birth. It is associated with inherited germline mutations in genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, and a family history of the disease can increase the risk of other cancers, including pancreatic, prostate, and thyroid cancers. The disease is staged based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, metastasis, and biomarkers, and staging is often performed both before and after surgery. Unlike some cancers such as AML, breast cancer has distinct stages.

Breast cancer influences medical guidance, including birth control recommendations, and is a focus of preventive health measures. It may be screened for during regular checkups, including in populations such as anal cancer survivors. Biomarker testing, tumor markers, and genetic testing are commonly used in its diagnosis and management. A personal or family history of breast cancer is also relevant to assessing risks for other cancers, such as thyroid cancer.
A bile duct is a tube that carries bile, made up of several layers including inner and outer membranes, with muscle and connective tissue in between.

The liver is a large, vital organ located on the right side of the body under the rib cage, playing a central role in the digestive system. It performs numerous critical functions, including filtering blood, detoxifying chemicals and toxins, processing nutrients, producing bile, breaking down fats, helping regulate blood sugar, and synthesizing coagulation factors and other essential proteins. The liver also produces lymph and is the site where primary liver cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and intrahepatic bile duct cancer, can develop.

Given its extensive metabolic and filtration roles, the liver is a common and clinically significant site for distant metastasis from many types of cancer. It is frequently affected by metastatic spread from colon, rectal, anal, breast, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, stomach, esophageal, prostate, kidney, thyroid, throat (including nasopharyngeal), and lung cancers, as well as from leukemias (such as CLL and AML) and lymphomas (such as DLBCL). In many of these cancers, liver involvement indicates advanced or stage 4 disease (e.g., stage 4B for cervical and bladder cancers, stage IV for anal cancer) and significantly influences treatment decisions, often requiring systemic therapy or local interventions like stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or ablative techniques.

The liver's health and function are routinely assessed through blood tests, including liver function tests (LFTs), comprehensive metabolic panels (CMP), and chemistry profiles, which measure enzymes, proteins, and other markers (e.g., ALP). These tests are essential for monitoring potential damage from chemotherapy drugs (such as high-dose methotrexate) and for evaluating the impact of cancers like CLL, which can cause the liver to swell due to cancer cell buildup. Imaging modalities such as CT, MRI, and ultrasound are used to detect metastatic lesions in the liver and to assess its size and condition during physical examinations. Overall, the liver is a crucial organ whose health is integral to overall bodily function and whose involvement in cancer spread is a key factor in staging, prognosis, and therapeutic planning.
Hepatic ducts are thin tubes that drain bile from the liver, with left and right hepatic ducts joining to form the common hepatic duct.
Pancreatic ducts are tubes in the pancreas that can appear wider than normal on x-rays, indicating potential cancer.

Physical exam During a physical exam, a health care provider may: Check your temperature, blood pressure, pulse, and breathing rate. Check your height and weight. Listen to your lungs and heart. Look in your eyes, ears, nose, and throat. Feel and apply pressure to parts of your body to see if organs are of normal size, are soft or hard, or cause pain when touched. h Feel for enlarged lymph nodes in your neck, underarm, and groin. Testing takes time. It might take weeks for all your test results to come in. Please wait to discuss the results with your doctor. Family history Your care team will ask about the health history of family members who are blood relatives. This information is called a family history. Ask family members on both sides of your family about their health issues like heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, and at what age they were diagnosed. It’s important to know the specific type of cancer or where the cancer started, if it is in multiple locations, and if they had genetic testing. Blood tests Blood tests check for signs of disease and how well organs are working. They require a sample of blood, which is removed through a needle placed into a vein in your arm. Be prepared to have many blood tests during AML treatment and recovery to check treatment results, blood counts, and the health of organs like your liver and kidneys. Some possible tests are described next. The list starts with more common tests. Complete blood count and differential A complete blood count (CBC) measures the levels of red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs), and platelets (PLTs) in your blood. A CBC is a key test that gives a picture of your overall health. AML often causes low counts of healthy blood cells, but it can also present with a high number of abnormal, malignant (abnormal) white blood cells. There are several types of white blood cells. A differential counts the number of each type of white blood cell. It also checks if the counts are in balance with each other. This test may show a high number of blasts in the blood. Your care team will pay particular attention to the following CBC measurements: Hemoglobin (Hgb) is a measurement of how much oxygen can move through blood and if a red blood cell transfusion might be needed. Platelets (PLTs) are cells that make the clot, thus preventing or stopping the bleeding. h An absolute neutrophil count (ANC) measures cells that fight bacteria and protect us from infections Blasts or leukemia cells can sometimes be detected in the blood and usually are reported as a percentage of cells. Comprehensive metabolic panel A comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) measures substances in your blood. It provides important information about how well your kidneys and liver are working, among other things. Creatinine Creatinine is a waste produced in the muscles. Every person generates a fixed amount of creatinine every day based on how much muscle they have. It is filtered out of the blood by the kidneys. The level of creatinine in the blood tells how well the kidneys are working. Higher levels of creatinine mean the kidneys aren’t working as well as they were when someone had lower levels of creatinine. Blood urea nitrogen Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) is a waste product filtered out of the blood by the kidneys. A high level of BUN can be a sign your kidneys aren’t working well. Electrolytes Electrolytes help move nutrients into cells and help move waste out of cells. Electrolytes are ions or particles with electrical charges that help the nerves, muscles, heart, and brain work as they should. Your body needs electrolytes to function properly. Lactate dehydrogenase Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) or lactic acid dehydrogenase is an enzyme found in most cells. Dying cells release LDH into blood. Fastgrowing cells, such as tumor cells, also release LDH. Liver function tests Liver function tests (LFTs) look at the health of the liver by measuring chemicals that are made or processed by the liver. Levels that are too high or low signal that the liver is not working well or the bile ducts might be blocked. B12 and folic acid Vitamin B12 and folic acid (folate) help the body make new proteins. They are needed for normal red blood cell (RBC) and white blood cell (WBC) formation. B12 and folic acid levels will be monitored. You may

The hematopathologist and your oncologist will examine a drop of your blood using a microscope. This is called a blood smear. The way the abnormal cells look can be a clue as to what type of cancer you have. Your blood will also be tested using a method called flow cytometry. It can detect common patterns of proteins on the outside of cells. Most cells have an identifiable pattern of proteins, like a silhouette or a shape, called the immunophenotype. A CLL diagnosis requires at least 5,000 or more of the same white blood cells called monoclonal B lymphocytes to be found per microliter in your blood. Diagnosis by biopsy A biopsy is a procedure that removes samples from the body for testing. If the blood results aren’t clear, you’ll have a biopsy of your lymph nodes or bone marrow to confirm CLL. Tests of lymph nodes will also confirm small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL). An excisional biopsy is when a whole lymph node is removed by a surgeon, while an incisional biopsy removes only part of a lymph node. There are many lymph nodes throughout your body, so if you have a lymph node removed, you won’t lose your ability to fight infections and disease. Needle biopsies take a small sample of a lymph node using a needle. They can be done when other biopsies are not safe to perform. A lab test will be used to find the immunophenotype of the biopsied cells. A bone marrow biopsy removes a core sample of marrow. A bone marrow aspiration removes liquid and cells from the marrow. These procedures are usually done at the same time. They’re performed on the back of the hip bone. You may receive an injected pain blocker or light sedative to help you relax. Tests of bone marrow aren’t usually needed for diagnosis, so you might not get one. How is treatment planned? Lab results used for diagnosis are included in a report. This report will be sent to your hematologist-oncologist, an expert in blood cancers. You may be able to view the pathology report using an online patient portal, or you could ask for a copy. The report is used to plan your treatment. Your oncologist will review the results with you. Take notes and ask questions. What tests are needed for starting treatment? The tests used to provide care are listed in Guide 1 and are described next. Health history Expect your care team to review your health in detail. This is known as taking a medical history. They will want to know a lot about your past and current health. You will likely be asked about: Family history Illnesses, infections, and injuries Guide 1 Tests used to plan treatment of CLL Tests that are needed for planning • Medical history including B symptoms and family history • Physical exam including lymph nodes, spleen, and liver • Performance status score • Flow cytometry • Complete blood count (CBC) with differential • Comprehensive metabolic panel • Beta-2 microglobulin • FISH, DNA sequencing, and CpG-stimulated karyotype Tests that may be useful for planning, but not needed • LDH • Quantitative immunoglobulins • Reticulocyte count, haptoglobin, and direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test • Uric acid • Hepatitis B and hepatitis C test • Bone marrow biopsy and aspirate • Diagnostic CT scans of chest, abdomen, and pelvis • Pregnancy test Prescription and over-the-counter medicines and supplements, surgeries, and blood transfusions Lifestyle choices, like your diet, how active you are, and whether you smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol They’ll also ask if you’re having any symptoms and complications of CLL. These symptoms are called B symptoms and include: Fevers when you’re not sick Night sweats that drench your sheets Weight loss you didn’t expect Some cancers and other health problems can run in families. Be prepared to discuss the health of your close blood relatives, like your siblings, parents, and grandparents. These are your first- and second-degree relatives, as seen in the figure below. Relatives are 7 to 8 times more likely to develop CLL if there’s a family history. Physical exam Your hematologist/oncologist will perform a physical exam of your body. This exam will include: Checking your vital signs—blood pressure, heart rate, breathing rate, and body temperature—and assessing your overall appearance Feeling and listening to organs Assessing your level of pain, if any, when you are touched Checking for swelling Cancer cells can build up in lymph nodes, the spleen, and the liver causing them to swell. Your oncologist will look at and gently press on your body to assess their size. Areas that may be touched include your neck, armpit, belly, and groin. Performance status Performance status is your ability to do daily activities, like feeding yourself or bathing. Your oncologist will score your performance status based on your health history and exam. Blood tests Blood tests can measure blood cells, proteins, and chemicals in the bloodstream. If you haven’t had a blood test recently, you’ll get a complete blood count (CBC) with differential. A CBC measures parts of the blood including counts of white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. h A differential counts the most common types of white blood cells in your blood. It also checks if the cell counts are in balance with each other. White blood cell counts are often high at diagnosis of CLL. Other blood counts, such as red blood cells or platelets, may be low. A comprehensive metabolic panel is a screening test for many diseases. It often includes tests for up to 14 chemicals in the blood. Abnormal levels may mean your kidneys and liver are not working

A care team is a multidisciplinary group of healthcare professionals who collaborate to provide comprehensive medical care, diagnosis, treatment, and support for patients, particularly those with cancer or other complex conditions. The team typically includes board-certified medical experts from various fields, such as doctors (e.g., pulmonologists, thoracic radiologists, thoracic surgeons, oncologists, hematologists, hematopathologists, breast specialists, gynecologists, radiologists, dietitians, and therapists), nurses, specialists, technologists, pharmacists, and support staff. They work together to plan and implement treatment, interpret test results (including imaging, CBC measurements, and other diagnostics), discuss treatment options and potential side effects (including effects on fertility), and guide patients through diagnostic and therapeutic processes. The care team is central to patient communication and support, encouraging patients to share information, ask questions, discuss preferences, and make shared decisions about their care. They also provide guidance on preparation for procedures (such as imaging tests and surgery), manage symptoms and side effects, and offer resources for issues like smoking cessation, claustrophobia, and emotional support. The team may specialize in specific conditions, including lung, breast, bladder, pancreatic, thyroid, prostate, glioma, CNS lymphoma, AML, ALL, CLL, NPC, and other cancers, and is responsible for coordinating all aspects of a patient's medical journey, from diagnosis through treatment and recovery.

Imaging tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, locate, and evaluate tumors, assess cancer extent, and check for cancer spread. These tests are essential for staging cancer, planning treatment, monitoring tumor response during chemotherapy, and detecting recurrence during surveillance. They are also used to visualize internal structures, guide biopsies, and identify abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, organ involvement, or areas of infection or bleeding.

Imaging tests include a wide range of techniques such as CT scans, MRI, PET scans, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, X-rays, mammograms, and bone scans. These modalities are applied across various cancer types, including breast, prostate, colon, rectal, esophageal, liver, kidney, ovarian, thyroid, adrenal, bone, and throat cancers, as well as leukemias like ALL and AML, and lymphomas such as CBCL and NPC. For example, mammograms, ultrasounds, and MRIs are used to visualize breast tissue; CT and MRI are primary methods for colon cancer staging; and ultrasound is used to detect thyroid nodules and cancer.

Imaging tests are interpreted by a radiologist and are used to reveal a tumor’s location, size, and other features, as well as to detect cancer spread to distant sites. In certain cancers, such as early-stage prostate cancer, imaging may not be necessary, but in others, like leukemia, they help detect spread outside the bone marrow to areas such as the brain, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and skin. Overall, imaging tests are indispensable diagnostic and monitoring tools in oncology, providing detailed visual information that guides clinical decisions across the cancer care continuum.
Extramedullary disease refers to leukemia that has spread outside the blood and bone marrow, such as to organs or tissues, detected via imaging tests.

Bone marrow is the soft, spongy tissue found in the center of most bones, rich in blood vessels, and composed of red marrow (containing blood stem cells) and yellow marrow (mostly fat). It is a critical part of the body’s hematopoietic (blood-forming) and lymphatic systems, serving as the primary site where all blood cells—including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets—are produced. Blood (hematopoietic) stem cells within the bone marrow multiply and differentiate into these various cell types, including B cells and lymphocytes, which are essential for immune function.

In the context of blood cancers, bone marrow is the primary site where leukemias such as Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL), Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML), and Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) originate. In ALL, the bone marrow produces an excess of immature lymphocytes called lymphoblasts, and diagnosis is confirmed when 20% or more of these cells are present. In AML, there is a buildup of myeloblasts in the marrow, and examination via aspirate and biopsy is crucial for diagnosis. For CLL, bone marrow tests may be performed to investigate low blood cell counts, and mutations in marrow cells are linked to disease development. Bone marrow is also a site where tumors can form in other lymphomas, such as follicular lymphoma (as extranodal disease), diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), and non-mediastinal gray zone lymphomas, and it may be tested for cancer spread in primary CNS lymphoma.

Bone marrow samples are obtained through biopsy or aspiration and are used for various diagnostic tests, including karyotyping, FISH, and other genetic analyses, because the tissue contains actively growing cells that can reveal leukemia-specific chromosomal changes. Additionally, bone marrow is vulnerable to damage from cancer and its treatments, and stem cell rescue procedures aim to restore its function. Overall, bone marrow is essential for blood cell production, immune response, and is a central focus in the diagnosis and monitoring of hematologic malignancies.

Blood tests are a broad category of diagnostic procedures and laboratory analyses performed on blood samples to assess overall health, evaluate organ function, and detect, diagnose, and monitor various diseases—particularly cancer. These tests are used across a wide range of cancers, including liver, bladder, AML (acute myeloid leukemia), CML (chronic myeloid leukemia), ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia), cervical, bone, pancreatic, esophageal, FL (follicular lymphoma), ovarian, stomach, kidney, prostate, colon, adrenal tumors, primary CNS lymphoma, and NPC (nasopharyngeal carcinoma). They are also used in general health checks and to guide treatment planning, with results often included in medical records and binders for patient reference.

Blood tests measure various blood components, such as blood cell counts, blood chemistry, and organ function markers (e.g., liver and kidney function). Common tests include the complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, liver function tests (LFTs), and chemistry profiles. Specific tests may also detect tumor markers or other indicators, such as carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) for colon cancer, CA-125 for ovarian cancer, PSA for prostate cancer, and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), thyroglobulin (Tg), and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (Tg ab) for monitoring cancer recurrence. Blood tests can also measure hormone levels to detect abnormalities related to adrenal tumors or assess endocrine function.

These tests are essential for establishing the extent of cancer, guiding treatment decisions, and monitoring for recurrence or response to therapy. They are performed by drawing a blood sample through a needle from a vein in the arm. Blood tests are used to detect markers or abnormalities related to cancer, evaluate blood cell counts, and rule out other conditions. They are often ordered as part of initial testing, during chemotherapy, or if recurrence is suspected, and are critical for patients to understand and keep copies of their results.

A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Family history is a comprehensive record of the health conditions and diseases—such as cancer, heart disease, and diabetes—that have occurred in a patient's blood relatives. It is a critical tool used by healthcare providers to assess an individual's inherited or genetic risk for a wide range of illnesses, including various types of cancer and other chronic conditions. The information gathered typically includes the specific diseases present in relatives, the nature of the biological relationship, and the age at which these conditions were diagnosed.

This assessment is particularly important in oncology, where a family history of certain cancers can significantly elevate an individual's risk. For example, having a close relative with prostate cancer increases the chance of developing the disease, and a family history of related cancers (such as breast, ovarian, colon, or pancreatic) also raises this risk. Similarly, a family history of thyroid cancer or related syndromes increases the likelihood of developing thyroid cancer. In the context of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), relatives of affected individuals are 7 to 8 times more likely to develop the disease, and a family history of leukemia can influence treatment decisions and prompt testing for leukemia predisposition syndromes. Family history is also a recognized risk factor for bladder cancer, and it is used to assess hereditary risk for ovarian and stomach cancers. In cases of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), understanding family history is vital for identifying potential hereditary factors.

Beyond risk assessment, family history plays a crucial role in guiding clinical care. It informs genetic testing recommendations, such as germline testing when cancer occurrences in relatives indicate an inherited risk, and helps in diagnosing conditions like basal cell skin cancer. While some cancers, such as head and neck cancers, are not typically inherited, family history is still collected to rule out any rare genetic predispositions. Ultimately, this information is used to create personalized screening plans, guide treatment decisions, and determine whether further genetic evaluation is necessary for the patient and their family members.

Genetic testing is a medical procedure that analyzes DNA from samples such as blood, saliva, urine, or tumor tissue to identify genetic mutations and abnormalities. It serves two primary purposes: detecting inherited (germline) mutations that increase cancer risk and guiding personalized treatment, prognosis, and preventive measures. In the context of cancer, genetic testing is distinct from tumor mutation testing, which only examines mutations within the tumor itself. For inherited risk assessment, it is often recommended for individuals with a family history of cancer, such as breast, ovarian, prostate, or other hereditary cancer syndromes, and can identify mutations in genes like BRCA1, BRCA2, and BCR::ABL1. In hematologic malignancies like acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), genetic testing looks for changes in leukemia cells—including mutations, deletions, insertions, inversions, amplifications, and translocations—to determine disease aggressiveness and guide treatment decisions. For ovarian cancer, genetic testing is recommended for all patients to assess hereditary risk and inform therapy. In some cases, genetic testing of biopsy samples may help diagnose specific cancers, such as follicular or oncocytic thyroid cancer, by identifying genetic markers. Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

The liver is a large, vital organ located on the right side of the body under the rib cage, playing a central role in the digestive system. It performs numerous critical functions, including filtering blood, detoxifying chemicals and toxins, processing nutrients, producing bile, breaking down fats, helping regulate blood sugar, and synthesizing coagulation factors and other essential proteins. The liver also produces lymph and is the site where primary liver cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and intrahepatic bile duct cancer, can develop.

Given its extensive metabolic and filtration roles, the liver is a common and clinically significant site for distant metastasis from many types of cancer. It is frequently affected by metastatic spread from colon, rectal, anal, breast, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, stomach, esophageal, prostate, kidney, thyroid, throat (including nasopharyngeal), and lung cancers, as well as from leukemias (such as CLL and AML) and lymphomas (such as DLBCL). In many of these cancers, liver involvement indicates advanced or stage 4 disease (e.g., stage 4B for cervical and bladder cancers, stage IV for anal cancer) and significantly influences treatment decisions, often requiring systemic therapy or local interventions like stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or ablative techniques.

The liver's health and function are routinely assessed through blood tests, including liver function tests (LFTs), comprehensive metabolic panels (CMP), and chemistry profiles, which measure enzymes, proteins, and other markers (e.g., ALP). These tests are essential for monitoring potential damage from chemotherapy drugs (such as high-dose methotrexate) and for evaluating the impact of cancers like CLL, which can cause the liver to swell due to cancer cell buildup. Imaging modalities such as CT, MRI, and ultrasound are used to detect metastatic lesions in the liver and to assess its size and condition during physical examinations. Overall, the liver is a crucial organ whose health is integral to overall bodily function and whose involvement in cancer spread is a key factor in staging, prognosis, and therapeutic planning.

Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that occurs in the cervix, the lower part of the female reproductive system, and is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in cervical tissues. It is primarily caused by long-term (persistent) infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), and it is a common cancer of the female reproductive system. The disease can manifest in several histological types, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is often detected through screening methods such as Pap smears, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by cervical biopsy. The cancer is staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, and staging is crucial as it determines treatment options and prognosis. Treatment approaches vary and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy (such as chemotherapy), and chemoradiation, with the choice of treatment based on the cancer stage and risk factors such as lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). Cervical cancer can spread to lymph nodes and, if untreated or not diagnosed early, may recur locally or regionally or spread to distant organs; therefore, surveillance and follow-up care are critical for managing recurrence and metastasis. The disease is closely linked to HPV, and a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of anal cancer, as both share the same viral cause. Consequently, screening for cervical cancer is recommended for patients with anal cancer, and female survivors of anal cancer may also be screened for cervical cancer. Additionally, p16, a biomarker, can be found in cervical cancer tissues.

CT scan, also known as Computed Tomography scan, is a diagnostic imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer technology to create detailed, cross-sectional, and often three-dimensional (3D) images of the inside of the body. The procedure involves taking multiple X-ray images from different angles, which are then combined by a computer to produce comprehensive pictures. CT scans are frequently performed with the use of contrast material to enhance image clarity and are typically completed in under 30 minutes.

This imaging modality serves a wide range of medical purposes. It is commonly used as an alternative to MRI when MRI is unavailable or not recommended. In oncology, CT scans are essential for detecting various cancers, including breast, colon, and ovarian cancer, as well as for identifying cancer spread (metastasis) to organs such as the liver, lungs, and lymph nodes. They are also used to detect adrenal tumors, bleeding, leukemia spread, and abnormalities in the neck and chest. Additionally, CT scans are employed to determine the extent of cancer beyond primary sites, such as the bladder or ovaries, and for surveillance in stages 2 and 3 colon cancer to monitor for recurrence.

Beyond diagnosis, CT imaging plays a critical role in treatment and procedural guidance. It is used during radiation therapy simulation to create precise treatment plans by obtaining pictures of the cancer site. CT scans also guide biopsies, particularly lymph node biopsies, ensuring accurate sampling. Furthermore, CT scans can be combined with PET scans (PET/CT) to enhance cancer detection and are recommended for further evaluation when suspicious lymph nodes are found. Overall, CT scanning is a versatile and widely used diagnostic tool for detecting cancer, guiding interventions, and assessing disease extent.

Context: "have any of these symptoms: Urinating frequently, especially at night Weak or intermittent urine stream Trouble urinating or straining to urinate Trouble holding in urine Feeling like your bladder hasn’t fully emptied Dull pain in your groin or pelvis Erectile dysfunction (difficulty getting an erection) or painful ejaculation Where does the prostate fit in? The prostate is located deep inside the lower body. It makes semen and is important for sexual reproduction. Prostate: A gland in the male reproductive system. A gland is an organ that makes fluids or chemicals the body needs. The prostate gland makes a protein (prostate-specific antigen, or PSA) that nourishes and helps transmit semen. The prostate also contains muscles that help propel semen through the urethra during ejaculation. Semen: A fluid made up of liquids from the prostate and the seminal vesicles as well as sperm from the testicles. During ejaculation, semen is released from the body through the urethra and out through the penis. Urethra: A tube that carries urine from the bladder and out of the body. The prostate wraps around the urethra just beneath the bladder. Seminal vesicles: Two glands that make another part of the fluid that becomes semen. The seminal vesicles are located above the prostate and behind the bladder. Bladder: An organ that holds urine. What causes prostate cancer? Many people who develop prostate cancer wonder where it came from and how they got it. Cancer researchers don’t know exactly what causes prostate cells to grow out of control (become cancerous). The fact is, everyone with a prostate has a risk of getting prostate cancer. But several factors are linked to a higher risk of prostate cancer. These are called risk factors. A risk factor is anything that increases your chance of getting cancer. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause prostate cancer, but people with prostate cancer usually have one or more of these risk factors: Age The biggest risk factor for prostate cancer is age. Prostate cancer is diagnosed most often in those aged 65 years and above. Your chances of getting prostate cancer increase as you become older. Family history Your family health history is information about the diseases and health conditions in your family. A family history reflects a pattern of certain diseases among family members. Having a close family member with prostate cancer (a sibling or parent) increases the chance of getting it yourself. Those with a family history of certain other cancers (breast, ovarian, colon, pancreatic, and other cancers) may also be at a higher risk for prostate cancer. Genetic factors When cancer “runs in the family,” genetic testing can be done to find specific genetic changes (mutations) known to be linked with prostate cancer or other cancers. For instance, having an inherited genetic change in the BRCA2 gene increases the risk of getting prostate cancer. But genetic abnormalities that aren’t inherited can occur, too. Race In the United States, Black males are more likely than white males to develop prostate cancer. Prostate cancer in Black males is also more likely to occur at an earlier age and be more aggressive and more advanced when diagnosed. Black males are also twice as likely to die from prostate cancer compared with white males. Prostate cancer is diagnosed less often in Hispanic and Asian males than in white and Black males. Several things may contribute to these differences, such as barriers to accessing health care (including early detection screening), biological and genetic factors, and other causes. Specialists are researching each of these areas. In light of these issues, Black males may want to talk with their health care providers about getting screening tests earlier than what’s recommended for other males. What does aggressive mean? When health care professionals describe cancer as aggressive, they mean the cancer is likely to grow or spread more rapidly than average. Aggressive is also used to describe therapy that’s stronger or more intense than other treatment options. Diet and lifestyle No one particular diet has been found to prevent prostate cancer or to cause prostate cancer. However, eating food that’s high in fat, such as meat and dairy products, has been linked with an increased risk of prostate cancer. Eating more fruits and vegetables may reduce this risk. Exercise and losing weight may also decrease the aggressiveness of prostate cancer and the likelihood of dying from it. On the other hand, smoking and obesity increase the risks of developing and dying from prostate cancer. What is early-stage prostate cancer? Prostate cancer can be grouped into earlystage cancer or advanced-stage cancer. Early stage Early-stage prostate cancer has not spread beyond the prostate. The cancer usually grows slowly and stays in the prostate. Cancer that is contained entirely within the prostate is called localized prostate cancer. This book is all about early-stage (localized) prostate cancer. Advanced stage Advanced stage means that cancer cells have spread outside the prostate to other areas in the body. This spreading is called metastasis or metastatic cancer. Metastatic prostate cancer has spread to the lymph nodes, bones, liver, lungs, and other organs. Advanced-stage prostate cancer can be separated into two types: Cancer that grows from the prostate gland to nearby lymph nodes, but no farther, is called regional prostate cancer. Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that occurs in the cervix, the lower part of the female reproductive system, and is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in cervical tissues. It is primarily caused by long-term (persistent) infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), and it is a common cancer of the female reproductive system. The disease can manifest in several histological types, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is often detected through screening methods such as Pap smears, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by cervical biopsy. The cancer is staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, and staging is crucial as it determines treatment options and prognosis. Treatment approaches vary and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy (such as chemotherapy), and chemoradiation, with the choice of treatment based on the cancer stage and risk factors such as lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). Cervical cancer can spread to lymph nodes and, if untreated or not diagnosed early, may recur locally or regionally or spread to distant organs; therefore, surveillance and follow-up care are critical for managing recurrence and metastasis. The disease is closely linked to HPV, and a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of anal cancer, as both share the same viral cause. Consequently, screening for cervical cancer is recommended for patients with anal cancer, and female survivors of anal cancer may also be screened for cervical cancer. Additionally, p16, a biomarker, can be found in cervical cancer tissues.

The liver is a large, vital organ located on the right side of the body under the rib cage, playing a central role in the digestive system. It performs numerous critical functions, including filtering blood, detoxifying chemicals and toxins, processing nutrients, producing bile, breaking down fats, helping regulate blood sugar, and synthesizing coagulation factors and other essential proteins. The liver also produces lymph and is the site where primary liver cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and intrahepatic bile duct cancer, can develop.

Given its extensive metabolic and filtration roles, the liver is a common and clinically significant site for distant metastasis from many types of cancer. It is frequently affected by metastatic spread from colon, rectal, anal, breast, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, stomach, esophageal, prostate, kidney, thyroid, throat (including nasopharyngeal), and lung cancers, as well as from leukemias (such as CLL and AML) and lymphomas (such as DLBCL). In many of these cancers, liver involvement indicates advanced or stage 4 disease (e.g., stage 4B for cervical and bladder cancers, stage IV for anal cancer) and significantly influences treatment decisions, often requiring systemic therapy or local interventions like stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or ablative techniques.

The liver's health and function are routinely assessed through blood tests, including liver function tests (LFTs), comprehensive metabolic panels (CMP), and chemistry profiles, which measure enzymes, proteins, and other markers (e.g., ALP). These tests are essential for monitoring potential damage from chemotherapy drugs (such as high-dose methotrexate) and for evaluating the impact of cancers like CLL, which can cause the liver to swell due to cancer cell buildup. Imaging modalities such as CT, MRI, and ultrasound are used to detect metastatic lesions in the liver and to assess its size and condition during physical examinations. Overall, the liver is a crucial organ whose health is integral to overall bodily function and whose involvement in cancer spread is a key factor in staging, prognosis, and therapeutic planning.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped glands distributed throughout the body, including the neck, armpits, groin, pelvis, near the rectum, stomach, thyroid, bladder, and colon. They are part of the lymphatic and immune systems, containing immune cells such as lymphocytes, and function to filter lymph fluid, remove foreign particles, germs, and harmful substances, and help fight infection and disease. There are over 300 lymph nodes in the head and neck alone.

Lymph nodes play a critical role in the body’s immune response and are a primary site where many cancers—such as breast, prostate, lung, colorectal, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, kidney, thyroid, anal, stomach, esophageal, skin (including basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), and head and neck cancers—may spread. Their involvement is a key factor in cancer staging (e.g., the N score in the TNM system) and prognosis, and they are often examined during physical exams for enlargement, which may indicate infection or cancer spread.

Lymph nodes can be assessed through imaging tests such as MRI, CT, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, PSMA/PET, and EUS, and may be biopsied (including sentinel or axillary lymph node biopsy) or removed during surgery (e.g., colectomy, neck dissection, or transabdominal surgery) to determine whether cancer has spread. Enlarged lymph nodes may also result from the buildup of cancerous cells, as seen in conditions like chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), follicular lymphoma, B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, and mediastinal gray zone lymphoma. In some cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), spread to nearby lymph nodes is uncommon.

Lymph nodes are also involved in defining specific cancer stages, such as stage 3C cervical cancer (involvement of pelvic or para-aortic nodes) and stage 3 bladder cancer (nodes near the bladder). In lymphomas, cancer originating in lymph nodes can weaken the immune system, and involvement outside the nodes is termed extranodal disease. Overall, lymph nodes are essential immune organs whose status is crucial in diagnosing, staging, and treating many diseases, particularly cancers.

HRA typically takes place after a digital rectal exam (DRE) is performed. Digital rectal exam The digital rectal exam (DRE) is an important exam for diagnosis, staging, and follow-up. There is nothing high-tech about a DRE. Digit is another word for finger. In a DRE, your doctor inserts a gloved, lubricated finger into your anus and rectum. This finger exam can detect or assess growths or other abnormalities in the anal canal and nearby areas. A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Family history is a comprehensive record of the health conditions and diseases—such as cancer, heart disease, and diabetes—that have occurred in a patient's blood relatives. It is a critical tool used by healthcare providers to assess an individual's inherited or genetic risk for a wide range of illnesses, including various types of cancer and other chronic conditions. The information gathered typically includes the specific diseases present in relatives, the nature of the biological relationship, and the age at which these conditions were diagnosed.

This assessment is particularly important in oncology, where a family history of certain cancers can significantly elevate an individual's risk. For example, having a close relative with prostate cancer increases the chance of developing the disease, and a family history of related cancers (such as breast, ovarian, colon, or pancreatic) also raises this risk. Similarly, a family history of thyroid cancer or related syndromes increases the likelihood of developing thyroid cancer. In the context of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), relatives of affected individuals are 7 to 8 times more likely to develop the disease, and a family history of leukemia can influence treatment decisions and prompt testing for leukemia predisposition syndromes. Family history is also a recognized risk factor for bladder cancer, and it is used to assess hereditary risk for ovarian and stomach cancers. Ultimately, this information is used to create personalized screening plans, guide treatment decisions, and determine whether further genetic evaluation is necessary for the patient and their family members.

Family history is a comprehensive record of the health conditions and diseases—such as cancer, heart disease, and diabetes—that have occurred in a patient's blood relatives. It is a critical tool used by healthcare providers to assess an individual's inherited or genetic risk for a wide range of illnesses, including various types of cancer and other chronic conditions. The information gathered typically includes the specific diseases present in relatives, the nature of the biological relationship, and the age at which these conditions were diagnosed.

This assessment is particularly important in oncology, where a family history of certain cancers can significantly elevate an individual's risk. For example, having a close relative with prostate cancer increases the chance of developing the disease, and a family history of related cancers (such as breast, ovarian, colon, or pancreatic) also raises this risk. Similarly, a family history of thyroid cancer or related syndromes increases the likelihood of developing thyroid cancer. In the context of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), relatives of affected individuals are 7 to 8 times more likely to develop the disease, and a family history of leukemia can influence treatment decisions and prompt testing for leukemia predisposition syndromes. Family history is also a recognized risk factor for bladder cancer, and it is used to assess hereditary risk for ovarian and stomach cancers. In cases of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), understanding family history is vital for identifying potential hereditary factors.

Beyond risk assessment, family history plays a crucial role in guiding clinical care. It informs genetic testing recommendations, such as germline testing when cancer occurrences in relatives indicate an inherited risk, and helps in diagnosing conditions like basal cell skin cancer. While some cancers, such as head and neck cancers, are not typically inherited, family history is still collected to rule out any rare genetic predispositions. Ultimately, this information is used to create personalized screening plans, guide treatment decisions, and determine whether further genetic evaluation is necessary for the patient and their family members.
