A patient is an individual receiving medical care, diagnosis, testing, or treatment for a wide range of conditions, including various types of cancer (such as basal cell skin cancer, prostate cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), rectal cancer, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), actinic keratoses, colon cancer, cervical cancer, follicular lymphoma (FL), anal cancer, bone cancer, bladder cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), ovarian cancer, mouth cancer, inflammatory breast cancer, and throat cancer) as well as other medical conditions. The patient may be diagnosed with, at risk for, or being evaluated for these conditions, and may undergo various diagnostic procedures, imaging tests, biopsies, and treatments as part of their care.

Patients are encouraged to be active participants in their own healthcare, including advocating for themselves, asking questions, making shared decisions with their care team, and managing their own health records, treatment side effects, and emotional well-being. They may also be advised to follow recommended exam schedules and to seek support and information about survivorship. The care team, which may include doctors, radiologists, and other specialists, coordinates the patient’s diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up care. The patient’s physical, mental, and emotional well-being are considered important throughout the process, and they may experience side effects, recovery processes, or challenges related to their condition and treatment. In some cases, factors such as claustrophobia, allergies, or kidney issues may influence the choice of imaging tests or procedures. Ultimately, the patient is the individual undergoing diagnostic and treatment procedures, with the goal of managing their health and receiving appropriate medical support.

Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the ovaries, most commonly beginning in the epithelium (the outer lining of the ovaries), and can also start in the fallopian tubes. It encompasses a range of types, including high-grade serous carcinoma, high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and other less common ovarian cancers. The disease can be hereditary or sporadic, with inherited mutations in genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, as well as Lynch syndrome, significantly increasing the risk in affected individuals. Additionally, a family history of ovarian cancer in close blood relatives is associated with an increased risk of developing pancreatic and prostate cancers.

Symptoms of ovarian cancer commonly include bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, difficulty eating, feeling full quickly, and urinary urgency. The disease is staged from 1 to 4, with stages 2, 3, and 4 specifically mentioned, and requires clinical staging along with various diagnostic tests—such as biopsy, imaging, and blood tests—to determine the extent of spread and guide treatment. Treatment typically involves a multidisciplinary team of experts and may include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, with protocols also addressing recurrence management. Ovarian cancer is the central topic of the provided text, guiding discussions on diagnosis, treatment, and related health considerations.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Recurrence, also known as relapse, refers to the return of cancer after a period of treatment or remission. This phenomenon is common across various cancer types, including bladder, breast, cervical, ovarian, prostate, basal cell skin, primary CNS lymphoma, and head and neck cancers. Recurrence can manifest locally (at the original site), regionally (in nearby lymph nodes), or at distant sites in the body, depending on the cancer type.

For bladder cancer, recurrence is a frequent occurrence that necessitates ongoing monitoring and regular follow-up testing. In breast cancer, recurrence may be local or distant. Cervical cancer recurrence can occur locally, regionally, or at distant sites, and often requires imaging, exploratory surgery, and biomarker testing to guide further treatment. Ovarian cancer recurrence also demands further management and monitoring. Prostate cancer recurrence can be detected through imaging tests such as MRI or PSMA-PET scans, and is a key factor in risk assessment. Basal cell skin cancer recurrence involves the cancer returning to the original area or spreading to lymph nodes or distant parts of the body, indicating a need for continued surveillance.

Monitoring for recurrence typically involves imaging tests like MRI, PSMA-PET, and other surveillance methods, including regular physical exams and blood tests. In some cases, such as higher-risk thyroid cancer, TSH suppression is used as a monitoring strategy. Symptoms of recurrence can vary but may include pelvic pain, bloating, and fatigue, particularly in gynecologic cancers.

Treatment for recurrence depends on the location and extent of the disease and may involve additional therapies such as surgery, radiation therapy, radioactive iodine (RAI), or adjustments to chemotherapy regimens. Biomarker testing is often employed to guide treatment decisions. Certain cancer subtypes and features can increase the risk of recurrence, and radiation therapy may be used in high-risk patients to prevent it. Overall, recurrence requires vigilant follow-up and individualized management to address the return of disease effectively.

Treatment encompasses a broad range of medical interventions—such as surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies—used to manage, cure, or slow the progression of various cancers, including head and neck cancer, prostate cancer, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), primary CNS lymphoma, chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), breast cancer, bone cancer, basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, MGZL, and thyroid cancer. The specific approach is personalized based on diagnostic test results, cancer staging, biomarkers (e.g., BCR::ABL1 protein activity), and patient preferences, with options ranging from minimal or no treatment for low-risk cases to aggressive therapies for high-risk or advanced disease. Treatment aims to slow tumor growth, reduce symptoms, prolong life, and prevent the disease from causing problems, though it may have side effects on hearing, fertility, and other bodily functions. For certain cancers, such as CLL, monitoring may be an option, while for metastatic cancer, targeted therapy or immunotherapy may be employed. Clinical trials are also considered in some cases, and treatment plans are often guided by a multidisciplinary care team, with patient preferences playing a key role in decision-making.
Chemoimmunotherapy is a type of treatment that may be targeted based on certain biomarkers in CLL patients.

Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Chemotherapy can be used alone or combined with other therapies, including radiation (chemoradiation), surgery, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially when PD-L1 or PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed). It is a standard treatment for many cancers, including AML, ALL, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, anal cancer, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and squamous cell skin cancer, among others. Specific regimens vary by cancer type and may include platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin), taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine), mitomycin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and anthracyclines. Chemotherapy can be delivered systemically (through the bloodstream), intravenously, orally, intraperitoneally, intravesically, intrathecally, or intraocularly, depending on the cancer and treatment goal. It may be used before surgery (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), as primary treatment for metastatic disease, or in high doses during stem cell rescue. Side effects are common and include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, fever, infection, and low blood cell counts. Chemotherapy can also affect fertility and other bodily functions, so preventive measures and birth control may be recommended during treatment. Smoking during chemotherapy can increase lung problems. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility. Chemotherapy is often a key component of treatment plans and may be recommended based on cancer stage, molecular markers (e.g., PD-L1 expression), and response to other treatments.

Biomarker testing is a category of medical tests used to analyze genes, proteins, and other molecules in cancer cells, tumor tissue, or blood samples to identify specific mutations, markers, or molecular features that can guide cancer diagnosis, treatment decisions, and prognosis. Also known as molecular testing, tumor profiling, tumor sequencing, genomic testing, gene expression profiling, or precision oncology, this process helps determine whether a patient is eligible for targeted therapies, immunotherapies, or clinical trials, and can inform maintenance therapies.

The testing examines biological markers such as DNA mutations, protein expression levels, and features like PD-L1, MMR, MSI, TMB, NTRK, HER2, RET, p16, BCR::ABL1, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA. It is applied across various cancer types, including ovarian, kidney, thyroid, stomach, esophageal, leukemia (such as ALL and AML), and metastatic cancers, to personalize treatment plans. Biomarker testing is typically performed on biopsy samples or blood samples and is recommended to identify specific genetic or molecular alterations that may suggest effective treatment options, including targeted therapy or immunotherapy.
Maintenance therapies are treatments guided by biomarker status, such as BRCA and HRD.

Targeted therapy is a form of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to precisely identify and attack specific molecules, genetic mutations, or abnormal proteins involved in the growth, progression, and spread of cancer cells. It is a type of systemic therapy, meaning it travels throughout the body, and is designed to focus on unique or specific features of cancer cells, thereby minimizing damage to normal, healthy cells compared to traditional chemotherapy.

This approach is used across a wide range of cancers, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML), cervical cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, squamous cell skin cancer, and breast cancer (such as HER2-positive cases). It is often guided by biomarker testing or specific genetic profiling, such as identifying mutations like PIK3CA, the BCR::ABL protein, or markers like PSMA. Examples of targeted therapy drugs include PARP inhibitors, Gemtuzumab ozogamicin, Gilteritinib, quizartinib, midostaurin, sorafenib, ivosidenib, bevacizumab, mirvetuximab soravtansine-gynx, tisotumab vedotin, and EGFR inhibitors.

Targeted therapy may be used in various scenarios, including for cancers that have returned, metastasized, or are resistant to other treatments, such as radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy for thyroid cancer. It can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments like chemotherapy. While it can be highly effective, it may also have side effects, which can include allergic reactions, fatigue, low platelet counts, body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding. Some serious side effects may affect the heart, skin, or digestive system. Additionally, targeted therapy can affect fertility, so it is important for patients to discuss this potential impact with their healthcare provider before starting treatment.

Basal cell skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), is the most common type of skin cancer. About 3 million cases of basal cell skin cancer are diagnosed every year in the United States. The good news is it can be cured in most cases. Treatment usually involves surgery to remove the cancer. Keep reading to find out more. What is basal cell skin cancer? Basal cell skin cancer is the most common of all skin cancer types. If caught early, it is easily treatable and curable. This is because it rarely metastasizes (spreads). Skin cancers often occur in the top layer of the skin (epidermis) and less commonly in the middle layer of the skin (dermis). The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. This cancer usually develops in areas exposed to the sun, including the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. But it can occur anywhere on the body. Skin lesions Basal cell skin cancer is often found on the face, head, and neck. Here is a basal cell lesion pictured on a person's cheek. Skin basics Did you know that your skin is your body’s largest organ and if you measured it it would stretch to about 20 square feet? Working as a barrier, your skin protects you from bacteria and chemicals and helps control your body temperature. It has 3 layers: Epidermis – The top layer of skin provides a waterproof barrier and creates skin color (melanin). Dermis – The middle layer involves connective tissue, blood vessels, oil and sweat glands, nerves, and hair follicles. Hypodermis – The deepest tissue layer is made up of fat and connective tissue. Most skin cancers form in the cells of the epidermis. It has 3 main types of cells: Squamous cells – These cells are flat cells found in the upper part of the epidermis. Basal cells – Found in the lower part of the epidermis, basal cells constantly divide to form new cells that replace the squamous cells on the skin’s surface. Melanocytes – Melanocytes are cells located in the lower part of the epidermis that produce melanin. Melanin is responsible for our hair, skin, and eye color. It also protects our skin from harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays. This book is only about basal cell skin cancer. For more information on squamous cell skin cancer or melanoma, read the NCCN Guidelines for Patients, available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Signs and symptoms Basal cell skin cancer can happen to anyone but it’s most common in people with lighter skin, lighter hair, or lighter eyes. In lighter skin, its lesions can look like any of the following: h Flat, pale or yellow areas, like a scar h Red patches that might be itchy Small, pink or red, shiny bumps that may have blue, brown, or black areas Open sores that don’t heal and might bleed, or go away and come back In darker (brown and black) skin, basal cell skin cancer can appear as a brown or glossy black bump with a rolled border. It can be mistaken for a normal mole. Be sure to look out for any new, changing, bleeding, or unusual skin growths. Skin cancer is easier to cure when it is caught early. To find out how basal cell skin cancer is diagnosed, read Chapter 2: Testing for basal cell skin cancer. Causes and risk factors Basal cell skin cancer is caused by exposure to UV radiation from the sun or other sources like tanning beds. UV radiation can harm the DNA inside basal skin cells. DNA controls how cells grow and function. If the DNA inside cells becomes damaged, the cells can become abnormal and grow out of control. You’re more likely to have basal cell skin cancer if you have certain risk factors. A risk factor increases the chance of developing cancer. Risk factors for basal cell skin cancer include: UV light exposure – UV light (radiation) that comes from the sun or tanning beds increases your risk. Fair skin, red or blond hair, or light eye color – People with lighter-colored skin are at a higher risk of developing skin cancer because melanin (skin pigment) filters out the sun's harmful UV rays. Age – Risk increases with age because sun exposure builds up over time. But skin cancer is becoming more common in younger people. History of skin cancer – If you or someone in your family has had skin cancer, you’re more likely to develop any type of skin cancer. Radiation therapy – Radiation treatment for other conditions, especially at a young age, can cause skin cancer. Immune suppression – People with weakened immune systems from organ transplants or autoimmune diseases are at higher risk for basal cell skin cancer. How is basal cell skin cancer treated? Basal cell skin cancer is highly treatable and curable. Catching it and treating it early is key. Surgery is the most common treatment for basal cell skin cancer. In some cases, radiation therapy or systemic therapy might be used to treat it. Following your treatment, you will have full skin exams with your doctor at least once a year. Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy radiation—such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons—to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is planned and prescribed by a radiation oncologist and delivered by radiation therapists or other specialists. This treatment is often used as a local therapy to target specific areas of the body, and it may be combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation), surgery, or systemic therapies, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Radiation therapy is applicable to a wide range of cancers, including anal, bladder, brain (e.g., gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma), breast, cervical, prostate, rectal, skin (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), thyroid, and perianal cancers, as well as chordoma and metastatic anal cancer. It can be used as a primary treatment, an adjunct after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells, or as palliative care to relieve pain. Techniques include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), and brachytherapy (internal radioactive material).

Treatment is typically given over several weeks, with common schedules of five sessions per week, each session lasting 30 to 60 minutes. While effective, radiation therapy can cause side effects, which may appear during treatment or years later. These include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, tiredness, headaches, nausea, vision problems, cataracts, and long-term cognitive issues. For some cancers, radiation therapy is a preferred or standard treatment option. For instance, IMRT is often preferred for anal cancer, and radiation is a main treatment for gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma. In prostate cancer, it may be used in both early and advanced stages, though it may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients. Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Chemotherapy can be used alone or combined with other therapies, including radiation (chemoradiation), surgery, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially when PD-L1 or PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed). It is a standard treatment for many cancers, including AML, ALL, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, anal cancer, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and squamous cell skin cancer, among others. Specific regimens vary by cancer type and may include platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin), taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine), mitomycin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and anthracyclines. Chemotherapy can be delivered systemically (through the bloodstream), intravenously, orally, intraperitoneally, intravesically, intrathecally, or intraocularly, depending on the cancer and treatment goal. It may be used before surgery (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), as primary treatment for metastatic disease, or in high doses during stem cell rescue. Side effects are common and include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, fever, infection, and low blood cell counts. Chemotherapy can also affect fertility and other bodily functions, so preventive measures and birth control may be recommended during treatment. Smoking during chemotherapy can increase lung problems. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility. Chemotherapy is often a key component of treatment plans and may be recommended based on cancer stage, molecular markers (e.g., PD-L1 expression), and response to other treatments.

Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the ovaries, most commonly beginning in the epithelium (the outer lining of the ovaries), and can also start in the fallopian tubes. It encompasses a range of types, including high-grade serous carcinoma, high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and other less common ovarian cancers. The disease can be hereditary or sporadic, with inherited mutations in genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, as well as Lynch syndrome, significantly increasing the risk in affected individuals. Additionally, a family history of ovarian cancer in close blood relatives is associated with an increased risk of developing pancreatic and prostate cancers.

Symptoms of ovarian cancer commonly include bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, difficulty eating, feeling full quickly, and urinary urgency. The disease is staged from 1 to 4, with stages 2, 3, and 4 specifically mentioned, and requires clinical staging along with various diagnostic tests—such as biopsy, imaging, and blood tests—to determine the extent of spread and guide treatment. Treatment typically involves a multidisciplinary team of experts and may include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, with protocols also addressing recurrence management. Ovarian cancer is the central topic of the provided text, guiding discussions on diagnosis, treatment, and related health considerations.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive diagnostic imaging technique that uses a powerful magnetic field, radio waves, and a computer to create highly detailed pictures of the inside of the body. Unlike X-rays or CT scans, MRI does not use ionizing radiation, making it a safe option for many patients. The procedure often involves the use of a contrast dye (or contrast material) to enhance the visibility of specific tissues, blood vessels, or abnormalities. MRI machines are available in both closed and open designs, accommodating different patient needs and comfort levels.

MRI is widely utilized across various medical fields for diagnosis, staging, treatment planning, and monitoring. It is particularly effective for imaging soft tissues, including the brain, spine, breasts, prostate, pelvic structures, and the rectal wall. In oncology, MRI is used to detect and stage cancers such as primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and rectal cancer. It can also identify the depth of tumor invasion (DOI), assess the spread of cancer to nearby lymph nodes or other organs (e.g., liver, chest), and detect cancer recurrence or metastasis.

In specific clinical scenarios, MRI is recommended for further evaluation when suspicious lymph nodes are found, when ultrasound results are unclear, or when CT results are inconclusive. It is also used to guide biopsies, often in conjunction with computerized navigation systems, and to assist in the placement of brachytherapy applicators and the design of treatment plans. For certain cancers, such as primary CNS lymphoma, MRI is considered the most useful imaging technique for identifying the disease and guiding treatment decisions. In cases of spinal involvement, MRI findings may indicate the need for intrathecal chemotherapy. Additionally, MRI can be combined with PET (positron emission tomography) for more detailed visualization, and it is sometimes used in urography to assess the extent of bladder cancer.

Overall, MRI is a versatile and essential medical imaging tool that provides detailed soft tissue images, supports accurate diagnosis and staging, and plays a critical role in guiding therapeutic interventions across a wide range of conditions.

Ultrasound is a versatile, non-invasive diagnostic imaging technique that uses high-energy sound waves to create real-time pictures of the inside of the body. It is painless and does not involve exposure to x-rays, making it a safe and widely used tool across many medical fields. Ultrasound is commonly employed to visualize the size, shape, and location of thyroid nodules, helping to detect thyroid cancer and monitor tumor growth during active surveillance. It is also frequently used to examine lymph nodes, where it can detect small areas of cancer near the skin and guide fine-needle biopsies with real-time visualization for accurate sampling. In addition, ultrasound is used to evaluate breast tissue abnormalities found on mammograms, guide prostate biopsies, and serve as the first diagnostic step for suspected ovarian cancer, using both transabdominal and transvaginal approaches. It is also applied in renal ultrasound for non-invasive assessment of organs, in echocardiograms to examine the heart, and may be used to examine the testicles for lymphoma spread, though this is not always necessary. Overall, ultrasound is an effective imaging method for guiding procedures, detecting small superficial cancers, and providing real-time, detailed images of internal structures across a wide range of clinical applications.

A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

Cancer cells are abnormal cells that develop genetic mutations, allowing them to grow and divide uncontrollably, avoid normal cell death, and invade surrounding tissues. They can spread to other parts of the body through the blood or lymphatic system, forming new tumors and indicating metastasis. These cells differ from normal cells in behavior and can crowd out healthy cells, leading to damage and symptoms.

Cancer cells can be detected through various diagnostic methods, including biopsy samples, blood tests (such as ctDNA testing), urine cytology, and imaging techniques like PET scans, where they appear as bright spots due to their high uptake of radioactive sugar-based tracers. In specific contexts, such as prostate cancer, they may be targeted by tracers in PET and PSMA/PET imaging, and in cases of HPV presence, they show increased p16 expression, aiding in diagnosis.

These abnormal cells are central to many cancer types, including bladder, prostate, breast, ovarian, anal, and primary CNS lymphoma, where they can be found in the cerebrospinal fluid, brain, or eyes. They may block lymph vessels in the breast, leading to inflammatory breast cancer symptoms, or be filtered out by lymph nodes, as seen in Hodgkin lymphoma. Cancer cells can express proteins like PD-1/PD-L1 or have mutations that guide treatment decisions.

Treatment approaches targeting cancer cells include chemotherapy, high-dose chemotherapy, intravesical therapy, systemic therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, and radiation therapy, all aimed at killing or inhibiting these harmful cells. In biopsy samples, patterns of cancer cells, such as Gleason patterns in prostate cancer, are analyzed to determine aggressiveness and risk of spread to lymph nodes or other body parts.

Cancer is a broad category of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells, which can potentially spread to other parts of the body. It encompasses numerous specific types, including head and neck cancer, colon cancer, breast cancer and its subtypes, cervical cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), bladder cancer, ovarian cancer, skin cancer, blood cancers, primary CNS lymphoma, lymphoma, differentiated high-grade carcinoma of the thyroid, and cancers affecting the ovaries, adrenal glands, and other organs. Cancer can develop from precancerous conditions like adenomas, spread through organ walls, cause bone damage, appear as tumors, and affect various bodily functions, including fertility and pregnancy. The disease may run in families, making family health history an important factor in risk assessment and genetic predisposition. Diagnosis and monitoring involve a range of procedures, including imaging tests such as PET scans, bone scans, mammograms, MRIs, and cystoscopy, as well as biopsies and biomarker, tumor marker, and genetic testing. Cancer appears brighter in PET scans due to increased sugar metabolism. Treatment options include radiation therapy, systemic therapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy, and participation in clinical trials for new treatments, with considerations for side effects, emotional and physical impacts, fertility and bone health, and the importance of quitting smoking to improve outcomes. The disease can be local or metastatic, and its staging, grading, and treatment are tailored to the specific type and context.

Biomarker testing is a category of medical tests used to analyze genes, proteins, and other molecules in cancer cells, tumor tissue, or blood samples to identify specific mutations, markers, or molecular features that can guide cancer diagnosis, treatment decisions, and prognosis. A clinical trial is a type of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, therapies, procedures, or preventive measures—such as drugs, devices, chemopreventive agents, or tests like ctDNA—for diseases, particularly cancer. These studies aim to determine the safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits of investigational approaches, with the goal of advancing medical care and bringing new treatments to individuals. Clinical trials are conducted in phases: Phase 1 assesses safety and side effects, Phase 2 evaluates effectiveness against specific cancers, Phase 3 compares the new treatment to standard therapies, and Phase 4 monitors long-term safety after approval. If a drug, device, or treatment approach is found safe and effective, it may be approved by the U.S. FDA.

Trials are governed by specific protocols and eligibility criteria, which may include factors such as a patient's performance status, as determined by their care team. They are managed by a dedicated research team, and participation requires informed consent. Placebos are rarely used alone in cancer trials. There is no enrollment fee, and the sponsor covers research-related costs; however, standard care costs may be billed to insurance.

Clinical trials are recommended or strongly encouraged for patients with various cancers, including anal cancer (especially metastatic), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)—where they are the preferred treatment for certain subtypes like BCR::ABL1-negative and BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL—primary CNS lymphoma (recommended for all patients by NCCN experts), metastatic cervical cancer, thyroid cancer (particularly for recurrence or metastatic disease), gliomas, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), bladder cancer, breast cancer, ovarian cancer (persistent or recurrent), and lung cancer. They offer patients access to experimental therapies, including chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and systemic therapy, and may be an option when standard therapies are not available or appropriate. Participation allows patients to receive investigational treatments while contributing to medical knowledge, though outcomes may vary. Patients are encouraged to ask their care team about clinical trials and may join at any time.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Cancer cells are abnormal cells that develop genetic mutations, allowing them to grow and divide uncontrollably, avoid normal cell death, and invade surrounding tissues. They can spread to other parts of the body through the blood or lymphatic system, forming new tumors and indicating metastasis. Cancer cells are abnormal cells that develop genetic mutations, allowing them to grow and divide uncontrollably, avoid normal cell death, and invade surrounding tissues. Primary central nervous system lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that affects the central nervous system (CNS). Let’s break it down word by word to understand it better: Primary – Primary means first. When talking about cancer, primary refers to the place where cancer first started. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in the central nervous system. Central nervous system – The CNS is made up of the brain and spinal cord. Primary CNS lymphoma occurs more often in the brain than in the spinal cord, but it can also involve the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and/or the eyes. Lymphoma – Lymphoma is cancer that forms from lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are white blood cells that fight infections. Cancer is what happens when cells grow out of control. So, a lymphoma is an abnormal overgrowth of lymphocytes. Now let’s put it all together: Primary CNS lymphoma is a cancer that begins when lymphocytes in the brain and spinal cord grow out of control. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in lymphocytes in the immune system. The immune system is your body’s natural defense against infection and disease. Having an impaired immune system may increase the risk of developing this cancer. Primary CNS lymphoma can spread to other areas within the nervous system. For example, it may spread from the brain to the eyes. But it rarely spreads to other areas of the body. However, a different kind of lymphoma—called secondary CNS lymphoma—starts in another part of the body but then spreads to the brain or spinal cord. This book is only about primary CNS lymphoma. What is the CNS? The central nervous system (CNS) receives signals from your senses, processes information, and controls your body’s responses. The CNS includes: The brain, which controls functions of the body such as feeling, moving, thinking, and learning. The eyes are connected directly to the brain and are also part of the CNS. h The spinal cord, which transmits messages between the brain and the body. Because the CNS is so important, your body has parts that protect it. These include: Meninges, which are membranes that cover your brain and spinal cord. Cerebrospinal fluid, which is a liquid that surrounds your brain and spinal cord. h Bones including the skull that shields your brain and the vertebrae that surround your spinal cord. What causes primary CNS lymphoma? Every person diagnosed with cancer wants to know how they got it. Although no one knows exactly what causes a lymphoma, we do know that lymphomas often start with a genetic abnormality (mutation) in certain lymphocytes. This abnormality causes these lymphocytes to grow out of control (become cancerous). The abnormality occurs on its own. It’s not a mutation that occurs in other cells or organs in your body. And it’s not typically passed down in families (hereditary mutation). Although primary CNS lymphoma is rare, it could happen to almost anyone. However, some people with certain risk factors have a greater chance. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. For example, having a reduced immune system increases the risk of developing primary CNS lymphoma. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause a disease (and just because you have risk factors, it doesn’t mean you'll definitely get the disease). Although primary CNS lymphoma can occur at any age, the majority of people diagnosed with it are in their 60s or 70s. How is primary CNS lymphoma diagnosed? Primary CNS lymphoma is often found when a person develops symptoms. A symptom is a feeling or problem that may be a sign of disease. Symptoms usually develop over several weeks. Primary CNS lymphoma can cause a variety of symptoms. Symptoms are often related to the lymphoma’s location in the central nervous system. The most common location is in the central part of the brain. A lymphoma located here may cause specific nerve changes such as leg or arm weakness, or problems with coordination or movement. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Imaging tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, locate, and evaluate tumors, assess cancer extent, and check for cancer spread. These tests are essential for staging cancer, planning treatment, monitoring tumor response during chemotherapy, and detecting recurrence during surveillance. They are also used to visualize internal structures, guide biopsies, and identify abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, organ involvement, or areas of infection or bleeding.

Imaging tests include a wide range of techniques such as CT scans, MRI, PET scans, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, X-rays, mammograms, and bone scans. These modalities are applied across various cancer types, including breast, prostate, colon, rectal, esophageal, liver, kidney, ovarian, thyroid, adrenal, bone, and throat cancers, as well as leukemias like ALL and AML, and lymphomas such as CBCL and NPC. For example, mammograms, ultrasounds, and MRIs are used to visualize breast tissue; CT and MRI are primary methods for colon cancer staging; and ultrasound is used to detect thyroid nodules and cancer.

Imaging tests are interpreted by a radiologist and are used to reveal a tumor’s location, size, and other features, as well as to detect cancer spread to distant sites. In certain cancers, such as early-stage prostate cancer, imaging may not be necessary, but in others, like leukemia, they help detect spread outside the bone marrow to areas such as the brain, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and skin. Overall, imaging tests are indispensable diagnostic and monitoring tools in oncology, providing detailed visual information that guides clinical decisions across the cancer care continuum.

Cancer is a broad category of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells, which can potentially spread to other parts of the body. It encompasses numerous specific types, including head and neck cancer, colon cancer, breast cancer and its subtypes, cervical cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), bladder cancer, ovarian cancer, skin cancer, blood cancers, primary CNS lymphoma, lymphoma, differentiated high-grade carcinoma of the thyroid, and cancers affecting the ovaries, adrenal glands, and other organs. Cancer can develop from precancerous conditions like adenomas, spread through organ walls, cause bone damage, appear as tumors, and affect various bodily functions, including fertility and pregnancy. The disease may run in families, making family health history an important factor in risk assessment and genetic predisposition. Diagnosis and monitoring involve a range of procedures, including imaging tests such as PET scans, bone scans, mammograms, MRIs, and cystoscopy, as well as biopsies and biomarker, tumor marker, and genetic testing. Cancer appears brighter in PET scans due to increased sugar metabolism. Treatment options include radiation therapy, systemic therapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy, and participation in clinical trials for new treatments, with considerations for side effects, emotional and physical impacts, fertility and bone health, and the importance of quitting smoking to improve outcomes. The disease can be local or metastatic, and its staging, grading, and treatment are tailored to the specific type and context.

CT scan, also known as Computed Tomography scan, is a diagnostic imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer technology to create detailed, cross-sectional, and often three-dimensional (3D) images of the inside of the body. This imaging modality serves a wide range of medical purposes. It is commonly used as an alternative to MRI when MRI is unavailable or not recommended. Additionally, CT scans are employed to determine the extent of cancer beyond primary sites, such as the bladder or ovaries, and for surveillance in stages 2 and 3 colon cancer to monitor for recurrence.

entities.description: A care team is a multidisciplinary group of healthcare professionals who collaborate to provide comprehensive medical care, diagnosis, treatment, and support for patients, particularly those with cancer or other complex conditions. The team typically includes board-certified medical experts from various fields, such as doctors (e.g., pulmonologists, thoracic radiologists, thoracic surgeons, oncologists, hematologists, hematopathologists, breast specialists, gynecologists, radiologists, dietitians, and therapists), nurses, specialists, technologists, pharmacists, and support staff. They work together to plan and implement treatment, interpret test results (including imaging, CBC measurements, and other diagnostics), discuss treatment options and potential side effects (including effects on fertility), and guide patients through diagnostic and therapeutic processes. The care team is central to patient communication and support, encouraging patients to share information, ask questions, discuss preferences, and make shared decisions about their care. They also provide guidance on preparation for procedures (such as imaging tests and surgery), manage symptoms and side effects, and offer resources for issues like smoking cessation, claustrophobia, and emotional support. The team may specialize in specific conditions, including lung, breast, bladder, pancreatic, thyroid, prostate, glioma, CNS lymphoma, AML, ALL, CLL, NPC, and other cancers, and is responsible for coordinating all aspects of a patient's medical journey, from diagnosis through treatment and recovery.

Targeted therapy is a form of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to precisely identify and attack specific molecules, genetic mutations, or abnormal proteins involved in the growth, progression, and spread of cancer cells. It is a type of systemic therapy, meaning it travels throughout the body, and is designed to focus on unique or specific features of cancer cells, thereby minimizing damage to normal, healthy cells compared to traditional chemotherapy.

This approach is used across a wide range of cancers, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML), cervical cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, squamous cell skin cancer, and breast cancer (such as HER2-positive cases). It is often guided by biomarker testing or specific genetic profiling, such as identifying mutations like PIK3CA, the BCR::ABL protein, or markers like PSMA. Examples of targeted therapy drugs include PARP inhibitors, Gemtuzumab ozogamicin, Gilteritinib, quizartinib, midostaurin, sorafenib, ivosidenib, bevacizumab, mirvetuximab soravtansine-gynx, tisotumab vedotin, and EGFR inhibitors.

Targeted therapy may be used in various scenarios, including for cancers that have returned, metastasized, or are resistant to other treatments, such as radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy for thyroid cancer. It can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments like chemotherapy. While it can be highly effective, it may also have side effects, which can include allergic reactions, fatigue, low platelet counts, body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding. Some serious side effects may affect the heart, skin, or digestive system. Additionally, targeted therapy can affect fertility, so it is important for patients to discuss this potential impact with their healthcare provider before starting treatment.

The disease can be hereditary or sporadic, with inherited mutations in genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, as well as Lynch syndrome, significantly increasing the risk in affected individuals. Additionally, a family history of ovarian cancer in close blood relatives is associated with an increased risk of developing pancreatic and prostate cancers.

Imaging tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, locate, and evaluate tumors, assess cancer extent, and check for cancer spread. These tests are essential for staging cancer, planning treatment, monitoring tumor response during chemotherapy, and detecting recurrence during surveillance. They are also used to visualize internal structures, guide biopsies, and identify abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, organ involvement, or areas of infection or bleeding.

Imaging tests include a wide range of techniques such as CT scans, MRI, PET scans, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, X-rays, mammograms, and bone scans. These modalities are applied across various cancer types, including breast, prostate, colon, rectal, esophageal, liver, kidney, ovarian, thyroid, adrenal, bone, and throat cancers, as well as leukemias like ALL and AML, and lymphomas such as CBCL and NPC. For example, mammograms, ultrasounds, and MRIs are used to visualize breast tissue; CT and MRI are primary methods for colon cancer staging; and ultrasound is used to detect thyroid nodules and cancer.

Imaging tests are interpreted by a radiologist and are used to reveal a tumor’s location, size, and other features, as well as to detect cancer spread to distant sites. In certain cancers, such as early-stage prostate cancer, imaging may not be necessary, but in others, like leukemia, they help detect spread outside the bone marrow to areas such as the brain, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and skin. Overall, imaging tests are indispensable diagnostic and monitoring tools in oncology, providing detailed visual information that guides clinical decisions across the cancer care continuum.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Imaging refers to a broad range of medical techniques used to create pictures of the inside of the body, including computed tomography (CT) scans, PET/CT scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasound, x-rays, and transvaginal ultrasound. These tests are essential for determining the extent and spread of cancer, which is critical for staging the disease and guiding treatment decisions. Imaging is used across various cancer types: for pancreatic cancer, it helps decide if surgery is an option; for cervical cancer, techniques such as FDG-PET/CT, CT with contrast, and MRI detect recurrence or spread, typically ordered based on symptoms or stage; for prostate cancer, imaging is used alongside PSA tests to evaluate presence and spread, visualizing the prostate and surrounding areas; for lymphoma, it identifies the location, size, and features of the disease; for adrenal tumors, it often detects them incidentally; for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), it assesses spread to lymph nodes and beyond; for bladder cancer, it visualizes the bladder and surrounding areas to stage and plan treatment; for brain tumors and gliomas, MRI and CT scans aid in diagnosis; and for anal cancers (stage II and III), imaging is used for surveillance after treatment, with yearly imaging recommended for three years to monitor for recurrence or further spread. Imaging is performed by specialists such as thoracic radiologists and is a key component of treatment planning and post-treatment monitoring across oncology.

A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

Cancer cells are abnormal cells that develop genetic mutations, allowing them to grow and divide uncontrollably, avoid normal cell death, and invade surrounding tissues. They can spread to other parts of the body through the blood or lymphatic system, forming new tumors and indicating metastasis. These cells differ from normal cells in behavior and can crowd out healthy cells, leading to damage and symptoms.

Cancer cells can be detected through various diagnostic methods, including biopsy samples, blood tests (such as ctDNA testing), urine cytology, and imaging techniques like PET scans, where they appear as bright spots due to their high uptake of radioactive sugar-based tracers. In specific contexts, such as prostate cancer, they may be targeted by tracers in PET and PSMA/PET imaging, and in cases of HPV presence, they show increased p16 expression, aiding in diagnosis.

These abnormal cells are central to many cancer types, including bladder, prostate, breast, ovarian, anal, and primary CNS lymphoma, where they can be found in the cerebrospinal fluid, brain, or eyes. They may block lymph vessels in the breast, leading to inflammatory breast cancer symptoms, or be filtered out by lymph nodes, as seen in Hodgkin lymphoma. Cancer cells can express proteins like PD-1/PD-L1 or have mutations that guide treatment decisions.

Treatment approaches targeting cancer cells include chemotherapy, high-dose chemotherapy, intravesical therapy, systemic therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, and radiation therapy, all aimed at killing or inhibiting these harmful cells. Primary central nervous system lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that affects the central nervous system (CNS). Let’s break it down word by word to understand it better: Primary – Primary means first. When talking about cancer, primary refers to the place where cancer first started. Lymphoma – Lymphoma is cancer that forms from lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are white blood cells that fight infections. Cancer is what happens when cells grow out of control. So, a lymphoma is an abnormal overgrowth of lymphocytes. Now let’s put it all together: Primary CNS lymphoma is a cancer that begins when lymphocytes in the brain and spinal cord grow out of control. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in lymphocytes in the immune system. The immune system is your body’s natural defense against infection and disease. Having an impaired immune system may increase the risk of developing this cancer. Primary CNS lymphoma can spread to other areas within the nervous system. For example, it may spread from the brain to the eyes. But it rarely spreads to other areas of the body. However, a different kind of lymphoma—called secondary CNS lymphoma—starts in another part of the body but then spreads to the brain or spinal cord. This book is only about primary CNS lymphoma. What is the CNS? The central nervous system (CNS) receives signals from your senses, processes information, and controls your body’s responses. The CNS includes: The brain, which controls functions of the body such as feeling, moving, thinking, and learning. The eyes are connected directly to the brain and are also part of the CNS. h The spinal cord, which transmits messages between the brain and the body. Because the CNS is so important, your body has parts that protect it. These include: Meninges, which are membranes that cover your brain and spinal cord. Cerebrospinal fluid, which is a liquid that surrounds your brain and spinal cord. h Bones including the skull that shields your brain and the vertebrae that surround your spinal cord. What causes primary CNS lymphoma? Every person diagnosed with cancer wants to know how they got it. Although no one knows exactly what causes a lymphoma, we do know that lymphomas often start with a genetic abnormality (mutation) in certain lymphocytes. This abnormality causes these lymphocytes to grow out of control (become cancerous). The abnormality occurs on its own. It’s not a mutation that occurs in other cells or organs in your body. And it’s not typically passed down in families (hereditary mutation). Although primary CNS lymphoma is rare, it could happen to almost anyone. However, some people with certain risk factors have a greater chance. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. For example, having a reduced immune system increases the risk of developing primary CNS lymphoma. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause a disease (and just because you have risk factors, it doesn’t mean you'll definitely get the disease). Lymphocytes are a type of white blood cell found in blood, lymph tissue, and all organs of the body, where they play a critical role in the immune system by helping to fight and prevent infections and disease. They are also the primary cells of the lymphatic system and are contained in lymph nodes. There are three main types of lymphocytes: B lymphocytes (B cells), which produce antibodies to fight infections; T lymphocytes (T cells), which fight infections and kill tumor cells; and natural killer (NK) cells, which kill tumor cells or virus-infected cells. Lymphocytes normally mature from lymphoblasts and grow in response to infection or inflammation; however, uncontrolled or abnormal growth of these cells can lead to various cancers, including lymphoma (such as Hodgkin lymphoma and primary CNS lymphoma, where they grow out of control in the brain and spinal cord), as well as leukemias. In acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the bone marrow produces too many immature lymphocytes called lymphoblasts, and ALL most often affects B cells or T cells, with subtypes such as B-ALL and T-ALL. Lymphocytes are also involved in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), which typically affects B cells. Overall, lymphocytes are essential disease-fighting white blood cells whose dysregulation is central to understanding and diagnosing several hematologic and lymphatic malignancies.

The liver is a large, vital organ located on the right side of the body under the rib cage, playing a central role in the digestive system. It performs numerous critical functions, including filtering blood, detoxifying chemicals and toxins, processing nutrients, producing bile, breaking down fats, helping regulate blood sugar, and synthesizing coagulation factors and other essential proteins. The liver also produces lymph and is the site where primary liver cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and intrahepatic bile duct cancer, can develop.

Given its extensive metabolic and filtration roles, the liver is a common and clinically significant site for distant metastasis from many types of cancer. It is frequently affected by metastatic spread from colon, rectal, anal, breast, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, stomach, esophageal, prostate, kidney, thyroid, throat (including nasopharyngeal), and lung cancers, as well as from leukemias (such as CLL and AML) and lymphomas (such as DLBCL). In many of these cancers, liver involvement indicates advanced or stage 4 disease (e.g., stage 4B for cervical and bladder cancers, stage IV for anal cancer) and significantly influences treatment decisions, often requiring systemic therapy or local interventions like stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or ablative techniques.

The liver's health and function are routinely assessed through blood tests, including liver function tests (LFTs), comprehensive metabolic panels (CMP), and chemistry profiles, which measure enzymes, proteins, and other markers (e.g., ALP). These tests are essential for monitoring potential damage from chemotherapy drugs (such as high-dose methotrexate) and for evaluating the impact of cancers like CLL, which can cause the liver to swell due to cancer cell buildup. Imaging modalities such as CT, MRI, and ultrasound are used to detect metastatic lesions in the liver and to assess its size and condition during physical examinations. Overall, the liver is a crucial organ whose health is integral to overall bodily function and whose involvement in cancer spread is a key factor in staging, prognosis, and therapeutic planning.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Chemotherapy can be used alone or combined with other therapies, including radiation (chemoradiation), surgery, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially when PD-L1 or PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed). It is a standard treatment for many cancers, including AML, ALL, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, anal cancer, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and squamous cell skin cancer, among others. Specific regimens vary by cancer type and may include platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin), taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine), mitomycin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and anthracyclines. Chemotherapy can be delivered systemically (through the bloodstream), intravenously, orally, intraperitoneally, intravesically, intrathecally, or intraocularly, depending on the cancer and treatment goal. It may be used before surgery (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), as primary treatment for metastatic disease, or in high doses during stem cell rescue. Side effects are common and include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, fever, infection, and low blood cell counts. Chemotherapy can also affect fertility and other bodily functions, so preventive measures and birth control may be recommended during treatment. Smoking during chemotherapy can increase lung problems. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility. Chemotherapy is often a key component of treatment plans and may be recommended based on cancer stage, molecular markers (e.g., PD-L1 expression), and response to other treatments.

Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy radiation—such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons—to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is planned and prescribed by a radiation oncologist and delivered by radiation therapists or other specialists. This treatment is often used as a local therapy to target specific areas of the body, and it may be combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation), surgery, or systemic therapies, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Radiation therapy is applicable to a wide range of cancers, including anal, bladder, brain (e.g., gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma), breast, cervical, prostate, rectal, skin (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), thyroid, and perianal cancers, as well as chordoma and metastatic anal cancer. It can be used as a primary treatment, an adjunct after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells, or as palliative care to relieve pain. Techniques include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), and brachytherapy (internal radioactive material).

Treatment is typically given over several weeks, with common schedules of five sessions per week, each session lasting 30 to 60 minutes. While effective, radiation therapy can cause side effects, which may appear during treatment or years later. These include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, tiredness, headaches, nausea, vision problems, cataracts, and long-term cognitive issues. Radiation to the head and neck can affect endocrine glands, hearing, and other functions, requiring pre- and post-treatment monitoring. Additionally, radiation therapy can impact fertility—for example, in rectal cancer it may damage ovarian and testicular function—and prior exposure to radiation, especially at a young age (e.g., to the chest), is a risk factor for certain cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer and small cell lung cancer.

A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.
