Cancer is a broad category of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells, which can potentially spread to other parts of the body. It encompasses numerous specific types, including head and neck cancer, colon cancer, breast cancer and its subtypes, cervical cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), bladder cancer, ovarian cancer, skin cancer, blood cancers, primary CNS lymphoma, lymphoma, differentiated high-grade carcinoma of the thyroid, and cancers affecting the ovaries, adrenal glands, and other organs. Cancer can develop from precancerous conditions like adenomas, spread through organ walls, cause bone damage, appear as tumors, and affect various bodily functions, including fertility and pregnancy. The disease may run in families, making family health history an important factor in risk assessment and genetic predisposition. Diagnosis and monitoring involve a range of procedures, including imaging tests such as PET scans, bone scans, mammograms, MRIs, and cystoscopy, as well as biopsies and biomarker, tumor marker, and genetic testing. Cancer appears brighter in PET scans due to increased sugar metabolism. Treatment options include radiation therapy, systemic therapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy, and participation in clinical trials for new treatments, with considerations for side effects, emotional and physical impacts, fertility and bone health, and the importance of quitting smoking to improve outcomes. The disease can be local or metastatic, and its staging, grading, and treatment are tailored to the specific type and context.

Treatment encompasses a broad range of medical interventions—such as surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies—used to manage, cure, or slow the progression of various cancers, including head and neck cancer, prostate cancer, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), primary CNS lymphoma, chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), breast cancer, bone cancer, basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, MGZL, and thyroid cancer. The specific approach is personalized based on diagnostic test results, cancer staging, biomarkers (e.g., BCR::ABL1 protein activity), and patient preferences, with options ranging from minimal or no treatment for low-risk cases to aggressive therapies for high-risk or advanced disease. Treatment aims to slow tumor growth, reduce symptoms, prolong life, and prevent the disease from causing problems, though it may have side effects on hearing, fertility, and other bodily functions. For certain cancers, such as CLL, monitoring may be an option, while for metastatic cancer, targeted therapy or immunotherapy may be employed. Clinical trials are also considered in some cases, and treatment plans are often guided by a multidisciplinary care team, with patient preferences playing a key role in decision-making.
Biopsy of metastasis is a procedure to confirm cancer spread to areas like lymph nodes or lungs, with each suspected site potentially biopsied depending on location.

A tumor is an abnormal mass of tissue that forms when cells grow and divide uncontrollably, and it may be benign or malignant. Tumors can arise in virtually any part of the body, including the colon, bladder, brain, central nervous system, oral mucosa, prostate, kidney, cervix, lung, pancreas, skin, rectum, and anal area. They are central to cancer diagnosis and treatment planning, and their size (often measured in centimeters or millimeters), depth of invasion, and extent of spread are key components in staging various cancers, such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma, head and neck cancers, cervical cancer, prostate cancer, and anal cancer (using the TNM system). Tumors can be primary (the original site of cancer) or metastatic (spread from another location), and they may invade nearby tissues, block organs (e.g., the bowel), or spread to lymph nodes and other parts of the body. They are detected and characterized through imaging tests (e.g., x-rays, mammograms, PET scans), endoscopy, cystoscopy, and biopsy procedures, and samples may be analyzed for biomarkers (e.g., dMMR). Treatment approaches include surgery (such as TURBT for bladder tumors), radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, which aim to shrink, kill, or remove the tumor. In specific contexts, tumors may present as one or multiple masses (e.g., in primary CNS lymphoma) or as lesions (e.g., squamous cell skin cancer), and their behavior and management depend on the cancer type and stage.

Cancer cells are abnormal cells that develop genetic mutations, allowing them to grow and divide uncontrollably, avoid normal cell death, and invade surrounding tissues. They can spread to other parts of the body through the blood or lymphatic system, forming new tumors and indicating metastasis. These cells differ from normal cells in behavior and can crowd out healthy cells, leading to damage and symptoms.

Cancer cells can be detected through various diagnostic methods, including biopsy samples, blood tests (such as ctDNA testing), urine cytology, and imaging techniques like PET scans, where they appear as bright spots due to their high uptake of radioactive sugar-based tracers. In specific contexts, such as prostate cancer, they may be targeted by tracers in PET and PSMA/PET imaging, and in cases of HPV presence, they show increased p16 expression, aiding in diagnosis.

These abnormal cells are central to many cancer types, including bladder, prostate, breast, ovarian, anal, and primary CNS lymphoma, where they can be found in the cerebrospinal fluid, brain, or eyes. They may block lymph vessels in the breast, leading to inflammatory breast cancer symptoms, or be filtered out by lymph nodes, as seen in Hodgkin lymphoma. Cancer cells can express proteins like PD-1/PD-L1 or have mutations that guide treatment decisions.

Treatment approaches targeting cancer cells include chemotherapy, high-dose chemotherapy, intravesical therapy, systemic therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, and radiation therapy, all aimed at killing or inhibiting these harmful cells. In biopsy samples, patterns of cancer cells, such as Gleason patterns in prostate cancer, are analyzed to determine aggressiveness and risk of spread to lymph nodes or other body parts.

Metastasis is the process by which cancer cells spread from the primary tumor (the original site of cancer) to other parts of the body, forming secondary tumors. This spread can occur through the blood or lymphatic system, allowing cancer cells to travel to nearby lymph nodes (local metastasis) or to distant organs and tissues (distant metastasis), such as the bones, liver, lungs, or other internal organs. The specific sites of metastasis can vary depending on the type of primary cancer; for example, prostate cancer commonly spreads to lymph nodes and bones, while colon cancer may spread to the liver or lungs, and kidney cancer can lead to metastatic tumors outside the kidney. Metastasis is a key indicator of advanced-stage cancer, often defining stage 4 disease (e.g., stage 4B cervical cancer), and is a critical component of cancer staging systems, such as the TNM system, where the "M" category indicates whether metastasis has occurred. In some cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer, metastasis is rare but possible, especially in advanced cases, while in very high-risk cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), it is a recognized risk. To confirm the presence of metastatic cancer, a biopsy of the metastatic site may be required, with the type of biopsy depending on the location of the spread. Imaging techniques are also used to detect metastasis, particularly in cases like prostate cancer. Overall, metastasis signifies the spread of cancer from its original location to other body areas, such as lymph nodes or distant organs, and is a fundamental factor in determining prognosis and guiding treatment decisions.
Metastasis biopsy is a procedure to sample tissue from areas where cancer has spread, such as lymph nodes or bones, to assess the extent of disease.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Imaging tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, locate, and evaluate tumors, assess cancer extent, and check for cancer spread. These tests are essential for staging cancer, planning treatment, monitoring tumor response during chemotherapy, and detecting recurrence during surveillance. They are also used to visualize internal structures, guide biopsies, and identify abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, organ involvement, or areas of infection or bleeding.

Imaging tests include a wide range of techniques such as CT scans, MRI, PET scans, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, X-rays, mammograms, and bone scans. These modalities are applied across various cancer types, including breast, prostate, colon, rectal, esophageal, liver, kidney, ovarian, thyroid, adrenal, bone, and throat cancers, as well as leukemias like ALL and AML, and lymphomas such as CBCL and NPC. For example, mammograms, ultrasounds, and MRIs are used to visualize breast tissue; CT and MRI are primary methods for colon cancer staging; and ultrasound is used to detect thyroid nodules and cancer.

Imaging tests are interpreted by a radiologist and are used to reveal a tumor’s location, size, and other features, as well as to detect cancer spread to distant sites. In certain cancers, such as early-stage prostate cancer, imaging may not be necessary, but in others, like leukemia, they help detect spread outside the bone marrow to areas such as the brain, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and skin. Overall, imaging tests are indispensable diagnostic and monitoring tools in oncology, providing detailed visual information that guides clinical decisions across the cancer care continuum.

Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy radiation—such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons—to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is planned and prescribed by a radiation oncologist and delivered by radiation therapists or other specialists. This treatment is often used as a local therapy to target specific areas of the body, and it may be combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation), surgery, or systemic therapies, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Radiation therapy is applicable to a wide range of cancers, including anal, bladder, brain (e.g., gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma), breast, cervical, prostate, rectal, skin (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), thyroid, and perianal cancers, as well as chordoma and metastatic anal cancer. It can be used as a primary treatment, an adjunct after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells, or as palliative care to relieve pain. Techniques include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), and brachytherapy (internal radioactive material).

Treatment is typically given over several weeks, with common schedules of five sessions per week, each session lasting 30 to 60 minutes. While effective, radiation therapy can cause side effects, which may appear during treatment or years later. These include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, tiredness, headaches, nausea, vision problems, cataracts, and long-term cognitive issues. Radiation to the head and neck can affect endocrine glands, hearing, and other functions, requiring pre- and post-treatment monitoring. Additionally, radiation therapy can impact fertility—for example, in rectal cancer it may damage ovarian and testicular function—and prior exposure to radiation, especially at a young age (e.g., to the chest), is a risk factor for certain cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer and small cell lung cancer.

For some cancers, radiation therapy is a preferred or standard treatment option. For instance, IMRT is often preferred for anal cancer, and radiation is a main treatment for gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma. In prostate cancer, it may be used in both early and advanced stages, though it may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients. For skin cancers like squamous cell carcinoma, radiation is used when surgery is not possible or as an adjunct to reduce recurrence

Targeted therapy is a form of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to precisely identify and attack specific molecules, genetic mutations, or abnormal proteins involved in the growth, progression, and spread of cancer cells. It is a type of systemic therapy, meaning it travels throughout the body, and is designed to focus on unique or specific features of cancer cells, thereby minimizing damage to normal, healthy cells compared to traditional chemotherapy.

This approach is used across a wide range of cancers, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML), cervical cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, squamous cell skin cancer, and breast cancer (such as HER2-positive cases). It is often guided by biomarker testing or specific genetic profiling, such as identifying mutations like PIK3CA, the BCR::ABL protein, or markers like PSMA. Examples of targeted therapy drugs include PARP inhibitors, Gemtuzumab ozogamicin, Gilteritinib, quizartinib, midostaurin, sorafenib, ivosidenib, bevacizumab, mirvetuximab soravtansine-gynx, tisotumab vedotin, and EGFR inhibitors.

Targeted therapy may be used in various scenarios, including for cancers that have returned, metastasized, or are resistant to other treatments, such as radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy for thyroid cancer. It can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments like chemotherapy. While it can be highly effective, it may also have side effects, which can include allergic reactions, fatigue, low platelet counts, body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding. Some serious side effects may affect the heart, skin, or digestive system. Additionally, targeted therapy can affect fertility, so it is important for patients to discuss this potential impact with their healthcare provider before starting treatment.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped glands distributed throughout the body, including the neck, armpits, groin, pelvis, near the rectum, stomach, thyroid, bladder, and colon. They are part of the lymphatic and immune systems, containing immune cells such as lymphocytes, and function to filter lymph fluid, remove foreign particles, germs, and harmful substances, and help fight infection and disease. There are over 300 lymph nodes in the head and neck alone.

Lymph nodes play a critical role in the body’s immune response and are a primary site where many cancers—such as breast, prostate, lung, colorectal, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, kidney, thyroid, anal, stomach, esophageal, skin (including basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), and head and neck cancers—may spread. Their involvement is a key factor in cancer staging (e.g., the N score in the TNM system) and prognosis, and they are often examined during physical exams for enlargement, which may indicate infection or cancer spread.

Lymph nodes can be assessed through imaging tests such as MRI, CT, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, PSMA/PET, and EUS, and may be biopsied (including sentinel or axillary lymph node biopsy) or removed during surgery (e.g., colectomy, neck dissection, or transabdominal surgery) to determine whether cancer has spread. Enlarged lymph nodes may also result from the buildup of cancerous cells, as seen in conditions like chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), follicular lymphoma, B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, and mediastinal gray zone lymphoma. In some cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), spread to nearby lymph nodes is uncommon.

Lymph nodes are also involved in defining specific cancer stages, such as stage 3C cervical cancer (involvement of pelvic or para-aortic nodes) and stage 3 bladder cancer (nodes near the bladder). In lymphomas, cancer originating in lymph nodes can weaken the immune system, and involvement outside the nodes is termed extranodal disease. Overall, lymph nodes are essential immune organs whose status is crucial in diagnosing, staging, and treating many diseases, particularly cancers.

A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

Blood is a vital bodily fluid and tissue that circulates through the body, composed of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Its primary functions include transporting oxygen and nutrients throughout the body, carrying away waste products, supporting the immune system, and preventing bleeding through clotting. Blood also serves as a medium through which cancer cells can travel to form tumors in distant organs, contributing to metastasis.

As a biological sample, blood is extensively used in medical diagnostics and testing. It can be sampled for liquid biopsy to detect tumor DNA, and it may contain circulating tumor DNA or other biomarkers such as EBV DNA to guide cancer treatment. Blood is utilized for a wide range of tests, including complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) analysis, and genetic testing to identify germline mutations. It is also a sample source for karyotype testing, as it contains growing cells, and for tumor marker analysis.

In the context of hematologic malignancies, blood is the primary sample type for diagnosing and monitoring conditions such as acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). In ALL, the presence of too many lymphoblasts in the blood impairs its normal function; in AML, blast accumulation similarly affects blood's ability to work properly. Blood is also used for genetic testing and mutation analysis in leukemia diagnosis and monitoring. Additionally, stem cells can be harvested from blood for cell rescue therapies.

Blood is sometimes described as part of bone tissue, and it flows through the kidneys, carrying waste and nutrients. Overall, blood is a crucial fluid that supports bodily functions, enables disease detection, and plays a central role in cancer diagnosis, monitoring, and spread.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped glands distributed throughout the body, including the neck, armpits, groin, pelvis, near the rectum, stomach, thyroid, bladder, and colon. They are part of the lymphatic and immune systems, containing immune cells such as lymphocytes, and function to filter lymph fluid, remove foreign particles, germs, and harmful substances, and help fight infection and disease. There are over 300 lymph nodes in the head and neck alone.

Lymph nodes play a critical role in the body’s immune response and are a primary site where many cancers—such as breast, prostate, lung, colorectal, bladder, cervical, ovarian, pancreatic, kidney, thyroid, anal, stomach, esophageal, skin (including basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), and head and neck cancers—may spread. Their involvement is a key factor in cancer staging (e.g., the N score in the TNM system) and prognosis, and they are often examined during physical exams for enlargement, which may indicate infection or cancer spread.

Lymph nodes can be assessed through imaging tests such as MRI, CT, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, PSMA/PET, and EUS, and may be biopsied (including sentinel or axillary lymph node biopsy) or removed during surgery (e.g., colectomy, neck dissection, or transabdominal surgery) to determine whether cancer has spread. Enlarged lymph nodes may also result from the buildup of cancerous cells, as seen in conditions like chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), follicular lymphoma, B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, and mediastinal gray zone lymphoma. In some cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), spread to nearby lymph nodes is uncommon.

Lymph nodes are also involved in defining specific cancer stages, such as stage 3C cervical cancer (involvement of pelvic or para-aortic nodes) and stage 3 bladder cancer (nodes near the bladder). In lymphomas, cancer originating in lymph nodes can weaken the immune system, and involvement outside the nodes is termed extranodal disease. Overall, lymph nodes are essential immune organs whose status is crucial in diagnosing, staging, and treating many diseases, particularly cancers.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

The abdomen is a major body region that plays a central role in the diagnosis, staging, treatment, and surveillance of various cancers, as well as in certain surgical and imaging procedures. Anatomically, it is the belly area containing the digestive organs (such as the liver, stomach, and colon), the omentum, reproductive organs (in females), and the para-aortic lymph nodes. It is also the location where a colostomy opening or a stoma for an Indiana pouch may be created, allowing for waste or urine drainage, respectively.

In cancer care, the abdomen is frequently examined through physical exams and imaging modalities such as CT, MRI, and ultrasound. These scans are used to assess organs like the liver and stomach, detect swollen lymph nodes, evaluate fluid buildup (ascites), and check for cancer spread (metastasis) beyond the primary site. For example, in anal, bladder, cervical, ovarian, prostate, and lymphoma cancers, abdominal imaging is essential for staging and determining whether cancer has invaded nearby structures or spread to distant organs such as the liver. In stage 4B cervical cancer, the abdomen can be a site of metastasis, and para-aortic lymph nodes located there may be evaluated or treated. Similarly, in stage 4A bladder cancer, the abdomen may be invaded, and in ovarian cancer, the abdomen is a common site of spread, often requiring laparotomy incisions for surgical access.

The abdomen is also a focus during surveillance after cancer treatment, with CT or MRI scans performed to detect any recurrence or new spread. In certain procedures, such as TURBT for bladder cancer, the abdomen is not cut into, as the operation is performed through the urethra. However, in other surgeries, such as those for cervical cancer, para-aortic lymph nodes in the abdomen may be removed. Overall, the abdomen is a critical anatomical region for cancer detection, treatment planning, and follow-up across multiple cancer types.

The lungs are a pair of organs located in the chest, forming a critical part of the respiratory system. They are composed of lobes, bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli, and their primary function is to facilitate gas exchange—delivering oxygen to the blood and removing carbon dioxide. Lung cancer originates in the cells lining the airways, and the lungs themselves can be the site where various cancers originate and subsequently spread to other parts of the body, such as bone.

In the context of cancer, the lungs are a common and significant site for distant metastasis across multiple cancer types. They are frequently affected by metastatic breast cancer, where cancer cells can form secondary tumors, and are also a common site for spread in bladder cancer, where chest imaging is used to assess whether the disease has advanced. Metastatic thyroid cancer often spreads to the lungs, requiring ongoing monitoring and treatment. The lungs are also a distant organ to which throat cancer (including nasopharyngeal cancer) may metastasize, though this is a less frequent occurrence. In anal cancer, the lungs are a common site for metastatic spread, particularly in stage IV, and CT scans of the chest are used to detect such involvement. Similarly, rectal cancer can spread to the lungs, as detected by CT imaging, and this affects treatment and prognosis. For cervical cancer, the lungs are a potential site of distant metastasis, especially in stage 4B, and local therapies such as stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or ablative techniques may be used to target tumors in this location. Kidney cancer frequently metastasizes to the lungs, and stomach cancer can also spread there, though less commonly than to the liver or peritoneum. Colon cancer can spread to the lungs, and in metastatic cases, local therapies may be employed; this spread is a key factor in stage 4 classification and treatment decisions. The pelvis is a basin-shaped anatomical structure located in the lower part of the torso, between the hip bones, that supports the spinal column and protects abdominal organs. It contains and surrounds vital organs including the bladder, rectum, reproductive organs (such as the ovaries, uterus, cervix, and prostate), and the anus and anal canal. The pelvis is a critical region for many cancers: it is the primary site for anal, rectal, and perianal cancers, and it is where these cancers are initially confined in non-metastatic stages. Cancer spread beyond the pelvis indicates distant metastasis (e.g., stage IV for anal or prostate cancer). The pelvis is also a common site for cancer spread from other organs, including prostate cancer (to bones), bladder cancer (to lymph nodes or organs), ovarian cancer, and lymphoma. Imaging techniques such as CT, MRI, EUS, and bone scans are frequently used to examine the pelvis for abnormalities, tumor spread, or lymph node involvement. Physical exams, including pelvic exams, are used to assess the cervix, uterus, and other pelvic structures for tenderness or abnormalities, particularly in bladder cancer. The pelvis is also a common location for bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, typically performed on the hip bone. Additionally, the pelvis can be a site for primary bone tumors such as Ewing sarcoma, and swollen lymph nodes in this region may be detected on imaging scans. The pelvis serves as an anatomical boundary for treatment planning, including radiation targeting, and is a focus of surveillance imaging after cancer recurrence treatment.

A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

CT scan, also known as Computed Tomography scan, is a diagnostic imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer technology to create detailed, cross-sectional, and often three-dimensional (3D) images of the inside of the body. The procedure involves taking multiple X-ray images from different angles, which are then combined by a computer to produce comprehensive pictures. CT scans are frequently performed with the use of contrast material to enhance image clarity and are typically completed in under 30 minutes.

This imaging modality serves a wide range of medical purposes. It is commonly used as an alternative to MRI when MRI is unavailable or not recommended. In oncology, CT scans are essential for detecting various cancers, including breast, colon, and ovarian cancer, as well as for identifying cancer spread (metastasis) to organs such as the liver, lungs, and lymph nodes. They are also used to detect adrenal tumors, bleeding, leukemia spread, and abnormalities in the neck and chest. Additionally, CT scans are employed to determine the extent of cancer beyond primary sites, such as the bladder or ovaries, and for surveillance in stages 2 and 3 colon cancer to monitor for recurrence.

Beyond diagnosis, CT imaging plays a critical role in treatment and procedural guidance. It is used during radiation therapy simulation to create precise treatment plans by obtaining pictures of the cancer site. CT scans also guide biopsies, particularly lymph node biopsies, ensuring accurate sampling. Furthermore, CT scans can be combined with PET scans (PET/CT) to enhance cancer detection and are recommended for further evaluation when suspicious lymph nodes are found. Overall, CT scanning is a versatile and widely used diagnostic tool for detecting cancer, guiding interventions, and assessing disease extent.

A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

They work together to plan and implement treatment, interpret test results (including imaging, CBC measurements, and other diagnostics), discuss treatment options and potential side effects (including effects on fertility), and guide patients through diagnostic and therapeutic processes. The care team is central to patient communication and support, encouraging patients to share information, ask questions, discuss preferences, and make shared decisions about their care. They also provide guidance on preparation for procedures (such as imaging tests and surgery), manage symptoms and side effects, and offer resources for issues like smoking cessation, claustrophobia, and emotional support. The team may specialize in specific conditions, including lung, breast, bladder, pancreatic, thyroid, prostate, glioma, CNS lymphoma, AML, ALL, CLL, NPC, and other cancers, and is responsible for coordinating all aspects of a patient's medical journey, from diagnosis through treatment and recovery.

Cancer is a broad category of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells, which can potentially spread to other parts of the body. It encompasses numerous specific types, including head and neck cancer, colon cancer, breast cancer and its subtypes, cervical cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), bladder cancer, ovarian cancer, skin cancer, blood cancers, primary CNS lymphoma, lymphoma, differentiated high-grade carcinoma of the thyroid, and cancers affecting the ovaries, adrenal glands, and other organs. Cancer can develop from precancerous conditions like adenomas, spread through organ walls, cause bone damage, appear as tumors, and affect various bodily functions, including fertility and pregnancy. The disease may run in families, making family health history an important factor in risk assessment and genetic predisposition. Diagnosis and monitoring involve a range of procedures, including imaging tests such as PET scans, bone scans, mammograms, MRIs, and cystoscopy, as well as biopsies and biomarker, tumor marker, and genetic testing. Cancer appears brighter in PET scans due to increased sugar metabolism. Treatment options include radiation therapy, systemic therapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy, and participation in clinical trials for new treatments, with considerations for side effects, emotional and physical impacts, fertility and bone health, and the importance of quitting smoking to improve outcomes. The disease can be local or metastatic, and its staging, grading, and treatment are tailored to the specific type and context.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

There are ways to prevent or alleviate some of these effects. Clinical trials A clinical trial is a type of medical research study. After being developed and tested in a laboratory, potential new ways of fighting cancer need to be studied in people. If found to be safe and effective in a clinical trial, a drug, device, or treatment approach may be approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Everyone with cancer should carefully consider all of the treatment options available for their cancer type, including standard treatments and clinical trials. Talk to your doctor about whether a clinical trial may make sense for you. Phases Most cancer clinical trials focus on treatment. Treatment trials are done in phases. Phase 1 trials study the dose, safety, and side effects of an investigational drug or treatment approach. They also look for early signs that the drug or approach is helpful. Phase 2 trials study how well the drug or approach works against a specific type of cancer. Phase 3 trials test the drug or approach against a standard treatment. If the results are good, it may be approved by the FDA. Phase 4 trials study the long-term safety and benefit of an FDA-approved treatment. Who can enroll? Every clinical trial has rules for joining, called eligibility criteria. The rules may be about age, cancer type and stage, treatment history, or general health. These requirements ensure that participants are alike in specific ways and that the trial is as safe as possible for the participants. Informed consent Clinical trials are managed by a group of experts called a research team. The research team will review the study with you in detail, including its purpose and the risks and benefits of joining. All of this information is also provided in an informed consent form. Read the form carefully and ask questions before signing it. Take time to discuss it with family, friends, or others you trust. Keep in mind that you can leave and seek treatment outside of the clinical trial at any time. Start the conversation Don’t wait for your doctor to bring up clinical trials. Start the conversation and learn about all of your treatment options. If you find a study that you may be eligible for, ask your treatment team if you meet the requirements. If you have already started standard treatment, you may not be eligible for certain clinical trials. Try not to be discouraged if you cannot join. New clinical trials are always becoming available. Frequently asked questions There are many myths and misconceptions surrounding clinical trials. The possible benefits and risks are not well understood by many with cancer. Will I get a placebo? Placebos (inactive versions of real medicines) are almost never used alone in cancer clinical trials. It is common to receive either a placebo with a standard treatment or a new drug with a standard treatment. You will be informed, verbally and in writing, if a placebo is part of a clinical trial before you enroll. Are clinical trials free? There is no fee to enroll in a clinical trial. The study sponsor pays for research-related costs, including the study drug. You may, however, have costs indirectly related to the trial, such as the cost of transportation or child care due to extra appointments. During the trial, you will continue to receive standard cancer care. This care is billed to—and often covered by— insurance. You are responsible for copays and any costs for this care that are not covered by your insurance. entities.description: Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that occurs in the cervix, the lower part of the female reproductive system, and is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in cervical tissues. It is primarily caused by long-term (persistent) infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), and it is a common cancer of the female reproductive system. The disease can manifest in several histological types, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is often detected through screening methods such as Pap smears, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by cervical biopsy. The cancer is staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, and staging is crucial as it determines treatment options and prognosis. Treatment approaches vary and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy (such as chemotherapy), and chemoradiation, with the choice of treatment based on the cancer stage and risk factors such as lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). Cervical cancer can spread to lymph nodes and, if untreated or not diagnosed early, may recur locally or regionally or spread to distant organs; therefore, surveillance and follow-up care are critical for managing recurrence and metastasis. The disease is closely linked to HPV, and a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of anal cancer, as both share the same viral cause. Consequently, screening for cervical cancer is recommended for patients with anal cancer, and female survivors of anal cancer may also be screened for cervical cancer. Additionally, p16, a biomarker, can be found in cervical cancer tissues.

Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy radiation—such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons—to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is planned and prescribed by a radiation oncologist and delivered by radiation therapists or other specialists. This treatment is often used as a local therapy to target specific areas of the body, and it may be combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation), surgery, or systemic therapies, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Radiation therapy is applicable to a wide range of cancers, including anal, bladder, brain (e.g., gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma), breast, cervical, prostate, rectal, skin (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), thyroid, and perianal cancers, as well as chordoma and metastatic anal cancer. It can be used as a primary treatment, an adjunct after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells, or as palliative care to relieve pain. Techniques include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), and brachytherapy (internal radioactive material).

Treatment is typically given over several weeks, with common schedules of five sessions per week, each session lasting 30 to 60 minutes. While effective, radiation therapy can cause side effects, which may appear during treatment or years later. These include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, tiredness, headaches, nausea, vision problems, cataracts, and long-term cognitive issues. Radiation to the head and neck can affect endocrine glands, hearing, and other functions, requiring pre- and post-treatment monitoring. Additionally, radiation therapy can impact fertility—for example, in rectal cancer it may damage ovarian and testicular function—and prior exposure to radiation, especially at a young age (e.g., to the chest), is a risk factor for certain cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer and small cell lung cancer.

For some cancers, radiation therapy is a preferred or standard treatment option. For instance, IMRT is often preferred for anal cancer, and radiation is a main treatment for gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma. In prostate cancer, it may be used in both early and advanced stages, though it may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients. For skin cancers like squamous cell carcinoma, radiation is used when surgery is not possible or as an adjunct to reduce recurrence

Surgery is a broad medical procedure involving the physical removal of tumors, cancerous tissue, or other affected areas, and is a primary or common treatment option for many types of cancer. It is used across a wide range of cancers, including early-stage cervical cancer (with types like cone biopsy, trachelectomy, and hysterectomy), bladder cancer (ranging from minor tumor removal to radical cystectomy, which is full bladder removal), and local squamous cell skin cancer (including curettage and electrodesiccation, PDEMA/Mohs surgery, and standard surgical excision). For gliomas, surgery is a main treatment aimed at removing the tumor, though it is difficult due to the tumor's invasive nature; it is particularly effective for grade 1 tumors, often followed by additional therapy for higher grades. Surgery is also a primary treatment for ovarian cancer, performed by gynecologic oncologists to remove tumors, determine cancer stage, and may involve staging and cytoreduction, with the response to surgery and chemotherapy determining maintenance therapy options. For breast cancer, surgery may involve mastectomy (removal of the entire breast) or lumpectomy (removal of a portion), and clips may remain until surgery. Surgery is a common treatment for head and neck cancer, anal cancer (including APR and complete removal of SISCCA lesions), and chondrosarcoma and other bone cancers. It is a treatment option for early or locally advanced NSCLC, pancreatic cancer (for stages 1, 2, or 3, depending on staging viability), and prostate cancer (particularly early-stage, involving removal of the prostate gland or metastatic tumors, and may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients). For thyroid cancer, surgery is the most common and effective treatment, involving lobectomy or total thyroidectomy, though targeted therapy is used for cancers that cannot be treated with surgery. Surgery is also a primary treatment for CSCC (cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma), involving excision of cancerous lesions and nearby lymph nodes for regional cases, and is the most common treatment for basal cell skin cancer, highly effective when caught early. Surgery may involve biopsy procedures, such as excisional biopsy for lymph nodes, and allows for pathologic staging by examining removed tissue, which is essential for determining treatment options. However, surgery is not normally used for primary CNS lymphoma due to the risks of removing deep brain tumors. Fertility is the ability to conceive and have children, and it is a significant health consideration for individuals of all genders affected by cancer. Cancer treatments—including chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and treatments for specific cancers such as acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), bone cancer, head and neck cancer, cervical cancer, and anal cancer—can damage the organs and bodily functions necessary for conception and pregnancy. As a result, fertility may be impacted either temporarily or permanently, and this risk is addressed as part of comprehensive cancer care.

Fertility concerns are discussed before and during treatment planning, and patients are strongly encouraged to speak with their care team about potential risks. Fertility preservation options—such as egg, sperm, or embryo freezing—are often considered and may involve referrals to specialists for counseling. These discussions are relevant across all genders and are integrated into treatment protocols for various cancer types, including those affecting the head and neck, bones, blood, cervix, and anus. Long-term effects on fertility are particularly noted in treatments like radiation therapy for cervical and anal cancers.

Overall, fertility is a key aspect of cancer treatment planning, and patients are advised to proactively address their reproductive goals with their healthcare providers to explore available preservation options before beginning treatment.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Recurrence, also known as relapse, refers to the return of cancer after a period of treatment or remission. This phenomenon is common across various cancer types, including bladder, breast, cervical, ovarian, prostate, basal cell skin, primary CNS lymphoma, and head and neck cancers. Recurrence can manifest locally (at the original site), regionally (in nearby lymph nodes), or at distant sites in the body, depending on the cancer type.

For bladder cancer, recurrence is a frequent occurrence that necessitates ongoing monitoring and regular follow-up testing. In breast cancer, recurrence may be local or distant. Cervical cancer recurrence can occur locally, regionally, or at distant sites, and often requires imaging, exploratory surgery, and biomarker testing to guide further treatment. Ovarian cancer recurrence also demands further management and monitoring. Prostate cancer recurrence can be detected through imaging tests such as MRI or PSMA-PET scans, and is a key factor in risk assessment. Basal cell skin cancer recurrence involves the cancer returning to the original area or spreading to lymph nodes or distant parts of the body, indicating a need for continued surveillance.

Monitoring for recurrence typically involves imaging tests like MRI, PSMA-PET, and other surveillance methods, including regular physical exams and blood tests. In some cases, such as higher-risk thyroid cancer, TSH suppression is used as a monitoring strategy. Symptoms of recurrence can vary but may include pelvic pain, bloating, and fatigue, particularly in gynecologic cancers.

Treatment for recurrence depends on the location and extent of the disease and may involve additional therapies such as surgery, radiation therapy, radioactive iodine (RAI), or adjustments to chemotherapy regimens. Biomarker testing is often employed to guide treatment decisions. Certain cancer subtypes and features can increase the risk of recurrence, and radiation therapy may be used in high-risk patients to prevent it. Overall, recurrence requires vigilant follow-up and individualized management to address the return of disease effectively.

After total thyroidectomy Short-term follow-up after total thyroidectomy involves a physical exam and blood tests. A neck ultrasound is also recommended 6 to 12 months after surgery. More information on blood tests is provided on the next page. If you had RAI therapy after total thyroidectomy, you may have whole-body RAI imaging to look for cancer after treatment. It may be helpful for high-risk patients, those with metastases that took up iodine, or those with abnormal blood or ultrasound results. Blood tests Blood testing will measure the levels of the following: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) Thyroglobulin (Tg) h Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (Tg ab) Thyroglobulin (Tg) is only made by thyroid tissue. If the thyroid is removed, there shouldn’t be any Tg in the blood. Therefore, checking the Tg level can serve as a way to monitor for the return of cancer. If the Tg level rises, it could be a sign that further testing is needed to check for recurrence. A small number of people with thyroid cancer make antibodies in response to Tg. These antiTg antibodies in blood can interfere with the Tg level. If the anti-Tg antibody level goes down, it may be a sign that treatment is working. If Neck ultrasound Neck ultrasound is used to monitor for the return of thyroid cancer. Talk to your care team about how often you need to have ultrasounds. it goes up, further testing should be done to check for cancer recurrence. Long-term monitoring If follow-up test results are normal, it is considered no evidence of disease (NED). In those with NED, longer-term surveillance includes physical exams, blood tests (TSH, Tg, and Tg ab), and periodic neck ultrasound. If there is reason to suspect the cancer has returned, you may have additional lab work, additional neck ultrasounds, TSH-stimulated testing (testing while thyroid hormone is stopped), or imaging procedures such as CT or MRI. After lobectomy Short-term follow-up after lobectomy involves a physical exam and TSH blood test. A neck ultrasound is also recommended 6 to 12 months after surgery. Unlike after total thyroidectomy, Tg testing isn’t helpful after lobectomy. If there is no evidence of disease, longer-term surveillance includes physical exams, TSH blood tests, and neck ultrasound. Talk to your care team about how often you need to have ultrasounds. Survivorship In addition to surveillance testing, a range of other care is important for cancer survivors. See Chapter 7: Survivorship for more information. Recurrence Although the thyroid has been removed, cancer can return to the neck or to areas far from the neck. The return of cancer after treatment is called recurrence. Biomarker testing Biomarkers are targetable features of a cancer. Many are mutations (changes) in the DNA of the cancer cells. For thyroid cancers with 1 or more specific biomarkers, targeted therapy or immunotherapy may be a treatment option if needed. Biomarker testing involves analyzing a piece of tumor tissue in a lab or testing a sample of blood. Testing for the following biomarkers is recommended for recurrent, advanced, or metastatic cancers that can't be treated with RAI therapy: h ALK gene fusion NTRK gene fusion BRAF gene mutations RET gene fusion (found in some medullary thyroid cancers) Mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR) Microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) Tumor mutational burden-high (TMB-H) Your provider may test for these individually or as part of a group. Testing for many biomarkers at one time is called nextgeneration sequencing (NGS). Cancer that returns to the neck If the cancer can be removed based on its size and location, surgery is the preferred treatment. For cancers that take up iodine, treatment with RAI therapy will also be considered. But, treatment isn't always needed. If the cancer isn't getting worse and isn't close to any critical structures, your provider may recommend close monitoring instead of treatment. If the cancer can't be removed with surgery, doesn’t take up iodine, and is getting worse (progressing), treatment with radiation therapy, targeted therapy, or both may be an option. The preferred targeted therapy for cancer that can’t be removed with surgery and is progressing is lenvatinib (Lenvima). Another recommended option is sorafenib (Nexavar). If the cancer gets worse after treatment with 1 or both of these, cabozantinib (Cabometyx) is recommended. For cancers with certain gene mutations or other features, biomarker-based therapy may also be an option for recurrence. See Guide 1 on the next page. If the therapies discussed above aren’t available or appropriate, joining a clinical trial is strongly encouraged. Metastatic cancer Thyroid cancer that spreads to areas far from the neck is known as metastatic. Metastatic tumors can form anywhere but are most common in the lungs, liver, muscles, bones, brain, and spinal cord. If the cancer takes up iodine, RAI therapy is recommended to treat metastatic papillary, follicular, or oncocytic thyroid cancers. Local therapies, such as radiation therapy, may also be used to treat areas of cancer directly. If RAI therapy isn’t an option If the cancer doesn't take up iodine, targeted therapy may be an option. But, if the metastatic tumors are growing slowly (or not at all) and aren't causing symptoms, monitoring the cancer may be a better option. Some people live with their thyroid cancer for months or years without needing treatment. You will continue to take levothyroxine to keep your TSH level down. Closed MRIs are more common than open MRIs, so if you have claustrophobia (a dread or fear of enclosed spaces), be sure to talk to your care team about it. PET scan A PET (positron emission tomography) scan uses a radioactive drug called a tracer. A tracer is a substance injected into a vein to see where cancer cells are in the body and how much sugar is being taken up by the cancer cells. This gives an idea about how fast the cancer cells are growing. Cancer cells show up as bright spots on PET scans. However, not all tumors will appear on a PET scan. Also, not all bright spots found on the PET scan are cancer. It is normal for the brain, heart, kidneys, and bladder to be bright on PET. Inflammation or infection can also show up as a bright spot. When a PET scan is combined with CT, it is called a PET/CT scan. An FDG-PET/CT uses a radiotracer called fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG). It is made of fluoride and a simple form of sugar called glucose. You cannot eat or drink for at least 4 hours before the scan. This scan is most helpful when other imaging results are unclear. Core needle biopsy removes tissue samples with a hollow needle that can grab a piece of tissue. This is frequently performed under light sedation by an interventional radiologist. Biomarker testing is a category of medical tests used to analyze genes, proteins, and other molecules in cancer cells, tumor tissue, or blood samples to identify specific mutations, markers, or molecular features that can guide cancer diagnosis, treatment decisions, and prognosis. Also known as molecular testing, tumor profiling, tumor sequencing, genomic testing, gene expression profiling, or precision oncology, this process helps determine whether a patient is eligible for targeted therapies, immunotherapies, or clinical trials, and can inform maintenance therapies.

The testing examines biological markers such as DNA mutations, protein expression levels, and features like PD-L1, MMR, MSI, TMB, NTRK, HER2, RET, p16, BCR::ABL1, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA. It is applied across various cancer types, including ovarian, kidney, thyroid, stomach, esophageal, leukemia (such as ALL and AML), and metastatic cancers, to personalize treatment plans. Biomarker testing is typically performed on biopsy samples or blood samples and is recommended to identify specific genetic or molecular alterations that may suggest effective treatment options, including targeted therapy or immunotherapy.

Immunotherapy is a type of systemic cancer treatment that leverages and boosts the body’s own immune system to find, reactivate, and destroy cancer cells. It is commonly administered by a medical oncologist and is considered a newer, non-hormone therapeutic approach that works alongside other systemic therapies like chemotherapy and targeted therapy. Immunotherapy is used across a wide range of cancers, including anal, cervical, bladder, ovarian, breast, prostate, colon, skin (squamous cell carcinoma), and primary CNS lymphoma, as well as for acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and metastatic disease.

The treatment often involves immune checkpoint inhibitors—such as pembrolizumab, nivolumab, and ipilimumab—which help reactivate the immune system against tumor cells. For certain cancers, including those with specific biomarkers like dMMR, MSI-H, or PD-1 expression, immunotherapy is a preferred option. It may be used to avoid surgery in anal cancer, to treat recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer with specific biomarkers, or as a recommended approach when cancer progresses during or after chemotherapy. In primary CNS lymphoma, the main immunotherapy drug is rituximab, a monoclonal antibody that targets CD20 proteins on cancer cells.

Eligibility for immunotherapy is often determined through biomarker testing, and it may be delivered systemically or directly into the bladder for certain bladder cancers. While generally effective, immunotherapy can cause side effects, including autoimmune reactions, fatigue, fever, nausea, diarrhea, drowsiness, and low blood cell counts. These side effects are addressed in clinical guidelines. Overall, immunotherapy aims to help patients live longer, manage symptoms, and improve outcomes across various cancer types, particularly in advanced or metastatic stages.

Cancer of the urothelium can start in these areas instead of the bladder, although it’s less common. Other (non-urothelial) types of bladder cancer are much less common. These include squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and small cell carcinoma. How is bladder cancer found? Bladder cancer is usually found when a person has symptoms. A symptom is a problem or feeling that may signal a disease or condition. The most common symptom of bladder cancer, and the one that usually appears first, is having blood in your urine (hematuria). How does blood get into urine? Bladder tumors are likely to release a little blood, which mixes with the urine in your bladder. The blood may turn your urine pink or bright red. Or, if there isn’t enough blood to be visible, your urine may look normal. But your clinical team can still detect blood by looking at a sample of the urine under a microscope. Blood in the urine can be caused by many other things besides bladder cancer. The most common cause is an infection in the urinary tract. So anyone with blood in their urine should see a health care provider to get their urine tested. Other symptoms of bladder cancer include: Frequent urination Urgency to urinate Painful urination Back pain Not every person with bladder cancer will have all these symptoms. Some people will have no symptoms. A person with one or more of these symptoms should visit a doctor or other health care provider who can recommend different tests. These tests are used to make a diagnosis. (A diagnosis means identifying an illness by using tests.) What does aggressive mean? Bladder cancer When health care professionals describe cancer as aggressive, they mean the cancer is likely to grow or spread more quickly than average. Bladder cancer is often described by how far it has spread into the muscle layer of the bladder. Here, the cancer tumor has grown through the inner lining (urothelial layer) and invaded the muscle layer in the bladder wall. This type of cancer is known as muscleinvasive bladder cancer. Aggressive can also be used to describe a treatment that’s stronger or more intense than other treatment options. Some people reading this book may have already been tested and given a diagnosis of bladder cancer. For those who haven’t been diagnosed yet, the only way to make sure you have bladder cancer is to have tests that: h Look inside your bladder (cystoscopy and imaging) Study your urine (urinalysis and cytology) Analyze a sample of surgically removed bladder tissue (resection and biopsy) We’ll talk about these and other tests in Chapter What causes bladder cancer? Many people wonder why they got cancer. Cancer experts don’t know exactly what causes bladder cells to grow out of control. What they do know is that bladder cancer and other cancers start with abnormal changes (mutations) in the genes of cells. Genes are tiny parts of a cell that carry the instructions for how cells behave. These instructions also control how new cells are made. Sometimes, mutations can mix up these instructions. This can turn normal cells into cancer cells. In most people with bladder cancer, these mutations aren’t passed down in families (hereditary mutation). They happen on their own and only in cancer cells. Still, you may have a higher risk for bladder cancer if another family member also had bladder cancer. In rare cases, mutations in these genes can be passed down in families. This results in an increased risk of getting bladder cancer. However, only some individuals with these genetic mutations go on to develop bladder cancer. What are the risk factors for bladder cancer? A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause bladder cancer. But people with bladder cancer often have one or more of these risk factors: Smoking – Smoking is the greatest risk factor for bladder cancer. It accounts for about half of all cases. Secondhand smoke increases bladder cancer risk, too. Quitting smoking, even after diagnosis, can still be helpful. Age – The risk of bladder cancer increases as you age. Family history – Your risk increases if you or anyone in your family has had bladder cancer. Also, people with an inherited condition called Lynch syndrome have a greater risk of cancer in the urinary tract, including bladder cancer. Chemical exposure – Some chemicals used in dyes, rubber, leather, printing materials, textiles, and paint products have been linked to an increased risk for bladder cancer. How advanced is my bladder cancer? Once bladder cancer is found, it’s important to know how far it has grown or spread. Bladder cancer advances in 3 phases: Non–muscle-invasive bladder cancer has grown on or in the bladder’s inner layer of urothelial cells, but not into the bladder’s muscle layer. Muscle-invasive bladder cancer has grown through the bladder’s inner urothelial layer and into its muscle layer. But it hasn’t grown anywhere else. Metastatic bladder cancer has spread outside the bladder to other areas of the body. Common areas of metastatic bladder cancer include the lymph nodes, bones, lungs, liver, and the inner wall of the abdomen. (Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped glands that transport a fluid called lymph and help fight infection. Lymph nodes are found around the urinary tract and all over the body.) Treatment is different for each of these three phases of bladder cancer. These phases are further divided into stages, which are explained in Chapter Bladder cancer treatment What’s the best treatment for bladder cancer? There’s no single treatment that’s best for everyone. The best treatment for bladder cancer is the treatment that’s best for you. You’ll work with your treatment team to choose which option makes the most sense for you. This choice is based on your cancer stage as well as your overall health and personal preferences. DOCTOR is a healthcare professional and provider who plays a central role in diagnosing, treating, and managing a wide range of medical conditions, particularly cancers and other serious diseases. They perform physical exams, ask about personal and family health history, and order or interpret diagnostic tests such as imaging (MRIs, CT scans), blood tests, biopsies, and scoping procedures (e.g., laryngoscopy, panendoscopy, polypectomy). Doctors discuss test results with patients, guide treatment decisions, and plan next steps in care, including recommending therapies such as systemic regimens, surgery, or procedures like excision, cone biopsy, or hysterectomy. They also provide guidance on lifestyle factors (exercise, diet, aspirin use, bone density monitoring, smoking cessation), fertility and pregnancy planning, birth control options, and managing side effects. In specific contexts, doctors specialize in conditions such as basal cell skin cancer, bladder cancer, bone cancer, cervical cancer, prostate cancer, anal cancer, ovarian cancer, and ALL, and may conduct full skin exams, pelvic exams, digital rectal exams, or monitor for recurrence or spread. They may also discuss germline testing or refer patients to genetic counselors for inherited cancer risk assessment, and they coordinate with radiologists and other specialists to ensure comprehensive care.

A tumor is an abnormal mass of tissue that forms when cells grow and divide uncontrollably, and it may be benign or malignant. Tumors can arise in virtually any part of the body, including the colon, bladder, brain, central nervous system, oral mucosa, prostate, kidney, cervix, lung, pancreas, skin, rectum, and anal area. They are central to cancer diagnosis and treatment planning, and their size (often measured in centimeters or millimeters), depth of invasion, and extent of spread are key components in staging various cancers, such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma, head and neck cancers, cervical cancer, prostate cancer, and anal cancer (using the TNM system). Tumors can be primary (the original site of cancer) or metastatic (spread from another location), and they may invade nearby tissues, block organs (e.g., the bowel), or spread to lymph nodes and other parts of the body. They are detected and characterized through imaging tests (e.g., x-rays, mammograms, PET scans), endoscopy, cystoscopy, and biopsy procedures, and samples may be analyzed for biomarkers (e.g., dMMR). Treatment approaches include surgery (such as TURBT for bladder tumors), radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, which aim to shrink, kill, or remove the tumor. In specific contexts, tumors may present as one or multiple masses (e.g., in primary CNS lymphoma) or as lesions (e.g., squamous cell skin cancer), and their behavior and management depend on the cancer type and stage.

A physical exam is a clinical assessment performed by a healthcare provider to evaluate a patient's overall health, detect signs of disease, and guide medical decisions. It is a routine medical check-up that includes measuring vital signs (such as blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature), checking body measurements (like height and weight), and listening to the lungs and heart. The exam also involves examining the eyes, ears, nose, and throat, as well as palpating (feeling) the abdomen, pelvis, and lymph nodes to assess organ size and detect abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, lumps, or swelling in the spleen or liver.

This examination is used across a wide range of medical contexts, including general health assessments, pre-anesthesia evaluations, and cancer screening or monitoring. It helps identify signs of various conditions, including breast abnormalities, basal cell skin cancer, and cancers such as ALL, AML, CLL, liver cancer, NPC, bladder cancer, and colon cancer. Physical exams are also performed periodically during chemotherapy (every 1 to 3 cycles) to monitor treatment effectiveness and side effects, and are part of short-term follow-up after procedures like total thyroidectomy, alongside blood tests. Additionally, they are included in surveillance schedules for stages 2 and 3 colon cancer to check for recurrence or spread.

The physical exam provides critical information to the care team about a patient's treatment readiness, overall health, and functional abilities, and is used to detect signs of cancer recurrence or other health issues. It is a general health test that may also include assessing the throat and airway, skin, and other body systems to ensure a comprehensive evaluation.
