A clinical trial is a type of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, therapies, procedures, or preventive measures—such as drugs, devices, chemopreventive agents, or tests like ctDNA—for diseases, particularly cancer. These studies aim to determine the safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits of investigational approaches, with the goal of advancing medical care and bringing new treatments to individuals. Clinical trials are conducted in phases: Phase 1 assesses safety and side effects, Phase 2 evaluates effectiveness against specific cancers, Phase 3 compares the new treatment to standard therapies, and Phase 4 monitors long-term safety after approval. If a drug, device, or treatment approach is found safe and effective, it may be approved by the U.S. FDA.

Trials are governed by specific protocols and eligibility criteria, which may include factors such as a patient's performance status, as determined by their care team. They are managed by a dedicated research team, and participation requires informed consent. Placebos are rarely used alone in cancer trials. There is no enrollment fee, and the sponsor covers research-related costs; however, standard care costs may be billed to insurance.

Clinical trials are recommended or strongly encouraged for patients with various cancers, including anal cancer (especially metastatic), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)—where they are the preferred treatment for certain subtypes like BCR::ABL1-negative and BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL—primary CNS lymphoma (recommended for all patients by NCCN experts), metastatic cervical cancer, thyroid cancer (particularly for recurrence or metastatic disease), gliomas, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), bladder cancer, breast cancer, ovarian cancer (persistent or recurrent), and lung cancer. They offer patients access to experimental therapies, including chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and systemic therapy, and may be an option when standard therapies are not available or appropriate. Participation allows patients to receive investigational treatments while contributing to medical knowledge, though outcomes may vary. Patients are encouraged to ask their care team about clinical trials and may join at any time.

Symptoms are physical or mental signs of illness or injury that patients may experience and should report to their care team or doctor. Symptoms may be specific to certain cancers or conditions—for example, breast issues may present as a lump, pain, nipple thickening or discharge, or changes in breast shape or size; bladder cancer may involve blood in urine; prostate cancer can cause urinary issues, bone pain, or blood in urine, especially in advanced stages; and primary CNS lymphoma or gliomas may cause headaches, nausea, vomiting, seizures, changes in eyesight, or muscle weakness due to pressure on the brain. Symptoms can also be signs of disease or treatment side effects, such as pain or nausea, which supportive care aims to relieve. It is important to note that screening is intended for individuals without symptoms, and patients are advised to report any symptoms to their care team. A physical exam is a clinical assessment performed by a healthcare provider to evaluate a patient's overall health, detect signs of disease, and guide medical decisions. It is a routine medical check-up that includes measuring vital signs (such as blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature), checking body measurements (like height and weight), and listening to the lungs and heart. The exam also involves examining the eyes, ears, nose, and throat, as well as palpating (feeling) the abdomen, pelvis, and lymph nodes to assess organ size and detect abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, lumps, or swelling in the spleen or liver.

This examination is used across a wide range of medical contexts, including general health assessments, pre-anesthesia evaluations, and cancer screening or monitoring. It helps identify signs of various conditions, including breast abnormalities, basal cell skin cancer, and cancers such as ALL, AML, CLL, liver cancer, NPC, bladder cancer, and colon cancer. Physical exams are also performed periodically during chemotherapy (every 1 to 3 cycles) to monitor treatment effectiveness and side effects, and are part of short-term follow-up after procedures like total thyroidectomy, alongside blood tests. Additionally, they are included in surveillance schedules for stages 2 and 3 colon cancer to check for recurrence or spread.

The physical exam provides critical information to the care team about a patient's treatment readiness, overall health, and functional abilities, and is used to detect signs of cancer recurrence or other health issues. It is a general health test that may also include assessing the throat and airway, skin, and other body systems to ensure a comprehensive evaluation.

A care team is a multidisciplinary group of healthcare professionals who collaborate to provide comprehensive medical care, diagnosis, treatment, and support for patients, particularly those with cancer or other complex conditions. The team typically includes board-certified medical experts from various fields, such as doctors (e.g., pulmonologists, thoracic radiologists, thoracic surgeons, oncologists, hematologists, hematopathologists, breast specialists, gynecologists, radiologists, dietitians, and therapists), nurses, specialists, technologists, pharmacists, and support staff. They work together to plan and implement treatment, interpret test results (including imaging, CBC measurements, and other diagnostics), discuss treatment options and potential side effects (including effects on fertility), and guide patients through diagnostic and therapeutic processes. The care team is central to patient communication and support, encouraging patients to share information, ask questions, discuss preferences, and make shared decisions about their care. They also provide guidance on preparation for procedures (such as imaging tests and surgery), manage symptoms and side effects, and offer resources for issues like smoking cessation, claustrophobia, and emotional support. The team may specialize in specific conditions, including lung, breast, bladder, pancreatic, thyroid, prostate, glioma, CNS lymphoma, AML, ALL, CLL, NPC, and other cancers, and is responsible for coordinating all aspects of a patient's medical journey, from diagnosis through treatment and recovery.

Examples of some tumor markers in breast cancer include carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), CA 15-3, and CA An increase in the level of certain tumor markers could mean that the cancer has grown or spread (progressed). However, not everyone has elevated levels of these markers and tumor markers alone are not a reliable method of detecting breast cancer. Tumor mutational burden When there are 10 or more mutations per million base pairs of tumor DNA, it is called tumor mutational burden-high (TMB-H). TMB-H can be used to help predict response to cancer treatment using immune checkpoint inhibitors that target the proteins called programmed death protein 1 (PD-1) and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1). Tumor mutation testing A sample of your tumor or blood may be used to see if the cancer cells have any specific DNA mutations. This is a different type of DNA testing than the genetic testing for mutations you may have inherited from your parents. In tumor mutation testing, only the tumor is tested and not the rest of your body. Certain mutations such as PIK3CA can be targeted with specific therapies. MSI-H/dMMR mutation Microsatellites are short, repeated strings of DNA. When errors or defects occur, they are fixed by mismatch repair (MMR) proteins. Some cancers have DNA mutations for changes that prevent these errors from being fixed. This is called microsatellite instability (MSI) or deficient mismatch repair (dMMR). When cancer cells have more than a normal number of microsatellites, it is called MSI-H (microsatellite instability-high). This is often due to dMMR genes. PD-1 and PD-L1 testing Programmed death protein 1 (PD-1) and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) are immune proteins. If either protein is expressed on the surface of cancer cells, it can cause your immune cells to ignore the cancer and suppress the anti-tumor immune response. If your cancer expresses either protein, you might have treatment that combines chemotherapy and a checkpoint inhibitor therapy. This is designed to activate your immune system to better fight off the cancer cells. FISH Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a testing method that involves special dyes called probes that attach to pieces of DNA, the genetic material in a person’s cells. Immunohistochemistry Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is a special staining process that involves adding a chemical marker to cancer or immune cells. The cells are then studied using a microscope. Next-generation sequencing Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a highthroughput method used to determine the DNA sequence or gene changes of cancer cells in your tumor. This method would only be used if enough tumor tissue remains after other biomarker testing has been completed. PCR A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a lab process that can make millions or billions of copies of your DNA (genetic information). PCR is very sensitive. It can find 1 abnormal cell among more than 100,000 normal cells. These copies called PCR product might be used for NGS. Genetic risk testing About 1 out of 10 breast cancers are hereditary. Depending on your family history or other features of your cancer, your health care provider might refer you for hereditary genetic testing to learn more about your cancer. A genetic counselor or trained provider will speak to you about the results. Tests results may be used to guide treatment planning. Genetic testing is done using blood or saliva (spitting into a cup or a cheek swab). The goal is to look for gene mutations inherited from your biological parents called germline mutations. Some mutations can put you at risk for more than one type of cancer. You can pass these genes on to your children. Also, other family members might carry these mutations. Tell your care team if there is a family history of cancer. BRCA tests Everyone has BRCA genes. Normal BRCA genes help to prevent tumor growth. They help fix damaged cells and help cells grow normally. BRCA mutations put you at risk for more than one type of cancer. Mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2 increase the risk of breast, ovarian, prostate, colorectal, pancreatic, and melanoma skin cancers. Mutated BRCA genes can also affect how well some treatments work. These tests might be repeated. What is your family cancer health history? Some cancers and other diseases run in families—those who are related to you through genes passed down from biological parent to child. This information is called a family health history. Ask blood relatives about their health issues like heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, and at what age they were diagnosed. For relatives who were diagnosed with cancer, ask them (or other relatives if they are no longer living) what type of cancer they had, if they died from the cancer, and at what age the cancer was diagnosed. Start by asking your parents, siblings, and children. Next, talk to half-siblings, aunts and uncles, nieces and nephews, grandparents, and grandchildren. Write down what you learn about your family history and share this information with your health care provider. Some of the questions to ask include: How old were you when each of these diseases and health conditions was diagnosed? It is primarily caused by long-term (persistent) infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), and it is a common cancer of the female reproductive system. The disease can manifest in several histological types, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is often detected through screening methods such as Pap smears, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by cervical biopsy. The cancer is staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, and staging is crucial as it determines treatment options and prognosis. Treatment approaches vary and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy (such as chemotherapy), and chemoradiation, with the choice of treatment based on the cancer stage and risk factors such as lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). Cervical cancer can spread to lymph nodes and, if untreated or not diagnosed early, may recur locally or regionally or spread to distant organs; therefore, surveillance and follow-up care are critical for managing recurrence and metastasis. The disease is closely linked to HPV, and a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of anal cancer, as both share the same viral cause. Consequently, screening for cervical cancer is recommended for patients with anal cancer, and female survivors of anal cancer may also be screened for cervical cancer. Additionally, p16, a biomarker, can be found in cervical cancer tissues.

Some cancers have DNA mutations for changes that prevent these errors from being fixed. This is called microsatellite instability (MSI) or deficient mismatch repair (dMMR). When cancer cells have more than a normal number of microsatellites, it is called MSI-H (microsatellite instability-high). This is often due to dMMR genes. entities.description: Surgery is a broad medical procedure involving the physical removal of tumors, cancerous tissue, or other affected areas, and is a primary or common treatment option for many types of cancer. It is used across a wide range of cancers, including early-stage cervical cancer (with types like cone biopsy, trachelectomy, and hysterectomy), bladder cancer (ranging from minor tumor removal to radical cystectomy, which is full bladder removal), and local squamous cell skin cancer (including curettage and electrodesiccation, PDEMA/Mohs surgery, and standard surgical excision). For gliomas, surgery is a main treatment aimed at removing the tumor, though it is difficult due to the tumor's invasive nature; it is particularly effective for grade 1 tumors, often followed by additional therapy for higher grades. Surgery is also a primary treatment for ovarian cancer, performed by gynecologic oncologists to remove tumors, determine cancer stage, and may involve staging and cytoreduction, with the response to surgery and chemotherapy determining maintenance therapy options. For breast cancer, surgery may involve mastectomy (removal of the entire breast) or lumpectomy (removal of a portion), and clips may remain until surgery. Surgery is a common treatment for head and neck cancer, anal cancer (including APR and complete removal of SISCCA lesions), and chondrosarcoma and other bone cancers. It is a treatment option for early or locally advanced NSCLC, pancreatic cancer (for stages 1, 2, or 3, depending on staging viability), and prostate cancer (particularly early-stage, involving removal of the prostate gland or metastatic tumors, and may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients). Surgery is also a primary treatment for CSCC (cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma), involving excision of cancerous lesions and nearby lymph nodes for regional cases, and is the most common treatment for basal cell skin cancer, highly effective when caught early. Surgery may involve biopsy procedures, such as excisional biopsy for lymph nodes, and allows for pathologic staging by examining removed tissue, which is essential for determining treatment options. A clinical trial is a type of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, therapies, procedures, or preventive measures—such as drugs, devices, chemopreventive agents, or tests like ctDNA—for diseases, particularly cancer. These studies aim to determine the safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits of investigational approaches, with the goal of advancing medical care and bringing new treatments to individuals. Clinical trials are conducted in phases: Phase 1 assesses safety and side effects, Phase 2 evaluates effectiveness against specific cancers, Phase 3 compares the new treatment to standard therapies, and Phase 4 monitors long-term safety after approval. If a drug, device, or treatment approach is found safe and effective, it may be approved by the U.S. FDA.

Trials are governed by specific protocols and eligibility criteria, which may include factors such as a patient's performance status, as determined by their care team. They are managed by a dedicated research team, and participation requires informed consent. Placebos are rarely used alone in cancer trials. There is no enrollment fee, and the sponsor covers research-related costs; however, standard care costs may be billed to insurance.

Clinical trials are recommended or strongly encouraged for patients with various cancers, including anal cancer (especially metastatic), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)—where they are the preferred treatment for certain subtypes like BCR::ABL1-negative and BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL—primary CNS lymphoma (recommended for all patients by NCCN experts), metastatic cervical cancer, thyroid cancer (particularly for recurrence or metastatic disease), gliomas, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), bladder cancer, breast cancer, ovarian cancer (persistent or recurrent), and lung cancer. They offer patients access to experimental therapies, including chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and systemic therapy, and may be an option when standard therapies are not available or appropriate. Participation allows patients to receive investigational treatments while contributing to medical knowledge, though outcomes may vary. Patients are encouraged to ask their care team about clinical trials and may join at any time.

entities.description: Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that occurs in the cervix, the lower part of the female reproductive system, and is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in cervical tissues. It is primarily caused by long-term (persistent) infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), and it is a common cancer of the female reproductive system. The disease can manifest in several histological types, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is often detected through screening methods such as Pap smears, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by cervical biopsy. The cancer is staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, and staging is crucial as it determines treatment options and prognosis. Treatment approaches vary and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy (such as chemotherapy), and chemoradiation, with the choice of treatment based on the cancer stage and risk factors such as lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). entities.description: Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Chemotherapy can be used alone or combined with other therapies, including radiation (chemoradiation), surgery, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially when PD-L1 or PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed). It is a standard treatment for many cancers, including AML, ALL, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, anal cancer, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and squamous cell skin cancer, among others. Specific regimens vary by cancer type and may include platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin), taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine), mitomycin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and anthracyclines. Chemotherapy can be delivered systemically (through the bloodstream), intravenously, orally, intraperitoneally, intravesically, intrathecally, or intraocularly, depending on the cancer and treatment goal. It may be used before surgery (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), as primary treatment for metastatic disease, or in high doses during stem cell rescue. Side effects are common and include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, fever, infection, and low blood cell counts. Chemotherapy can also affect fertility and other bodily functions, so preventive measures and birth control may be recommended during treatment. Smoking during chemotherapy can increase lung problems. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility. Chemotherapy is often a key component of treatment plans and may be recommended based on cancer stage, molecular markers (e.g., PD-L1 expression), and response to other treatments.

Surgery is a broad medical procedure involving the physical removal of tumors, cancerous tissue, or other affected areas, and is a primary or common treatment option for many types of cancer. It is used across a wide range of cancers, including early-stage cervical cancer (with types like cone biopsy, trachelectomy, and hysterectomy), bladder cancer (ranging from minor tumor removal to radical cystectomy, which is full bladder removal), and local squamous cell skin cancer (including curettage and electrodesiccation, PDEMA/Mohs surgery, and standard surgical excision). For gliomas, surgery is a main treatment aimed at removing the tumor, though it is difficult due to the tumor's invasive nature; it is particularly effective for grade 1 tumors, often followed by additional therapy for higher grades. Surgery is also a primary treatment for ovarian cancer, performed by gynecologic oncologists to remove tumors, determine cancer stage, and may involve staging and cytoreduction, with the response to surgery and chemotherapy determining maintenance therapy options. For breast cancer, surgery may involve mastectomy (removal of the entire breast) or lumpectomy (removal of a portion), and clips may remain until surgery. Surgery is a common treatment for head and neck cancer, anal cancer (including APR and complete removal of SISCCA lesions), and chondrosarcoma and other bone cancers. It is a treatment option for early or locally advanced NSCLC, pancreatic cancer (for stages 1, 2, or 3, depending on staging viability), and prostate cancer (particularly early-stage, involving removal of the prostate gland or metastatic tumors, and may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients). For thyroid cancer, surgery is the most common and effective treatment, involving lobectomy or total thyroidectomy, though targeted therapy is used for cancers that cannot be treated with surgery. Surgery is also a primary treatment for CSCC (cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma), involving excision of cancerous lesions and nearby lymph nodes for regional cases, and is the most common treatment for basal cell skin cancer, highly effective when caught early. Surgery may involve biopsy procedures, such as excisional biopsy for lymph nodes, and allows for pathologic staging by examining removed tissue, which is essential for determining treatment options. However, surgery is not normally used for primary CNS lymphoma due to the risks of removing deep brain tumors. Targeted therapy is a form of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to precisely identify and attack specific molecules, genetic mutations, or abnormal proteins involved in the growth, progression, and spread of cancer cells. It is a type of systemic therapy, meaning it travels throughout the body, and is designed to focus on unique or specific features of cancer cells, thereby minimizing damage to normal, healthy cells compared to traditional chemotherapy.

This approach is used across a wide range of cancers, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML), cervical cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, squamous cell skin cancer, and breast cancer (such as HER2-positive cases). It is often guided by biomarker testing or specific genetic profiling, such as identifying mutations like PIK3CA, the BCR::ABL protein, or markers like PSMA. Examples of targeted therapy drugs include PARP inhibitors, Gemtuzumab ozogamicin, Gilteritinib, quizartinib, midostaurin, sorafenib, ivosidenib, bevacizumab, mirvetuximab soravtansine-gynx, tisotumab vedotin, and EGFR inhibitors.

Targeted therapy may be used in various scenarios, including for cancers that have returned, metastasized, or are resistant to other treatments, such as radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy for thyroid cancer. It can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments like chemotherapy. While it can be highly effective, it may also have side effects, which can include allergic reactions, fatigue, low platelet counts, body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding. Some serious side effects may affect the heart, skin, or digestive system. Additionally, targeted therapy can affect fertility, so it is important for patients to discuss this potential impact with their healthcare provider before starting treatment.

Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy radiation—such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons—to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is planned and prescribed by a radiation oncologist and delivered by radiation therapists or other specialists. This treatment is often used as a local therapy to target specific areas of the body, and it may be combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation), surgery, or systemic therapies, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Radiation therapy is applicable to a wide range of cancers, including anal, bladder, brain (e.g., gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma), breast, cervical, prostate, rectal, skin (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), thyroid, and perianal cancers, as well as chordoma and metastatic anal cancer. It can be used as a primary treatment, an adjunct after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells, or as palliative care to relieve pain. Techniques include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), and brachytherapy (internal radioactive material).

Treatment is typically given over several weeks, with common schedules of five sessions per week, each session lasting 30 to 60 minutes. While effective, radiation therapy can cause side effects, which may appear during treatment or years later. These include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, tiredness, headaches, nausea, vision problems, cataracts, and long-term cognitive issues. Radiation to the head and neck can affect endocrine glands, hearing, and other functions, requiring pre- and post-treatment monitoring. Additionally, radiation therapy can impact fertility—for example, in rectal cancer it may damage ovarian and testicular function—and prior exposure to radiation, especially at a young age (e.g., to the chest), is a risk factor for certain cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer and small cell lung cancer.

For some cancers, radiation therapy is a preferred or standard treatment option. For instance, IMRT is often preferred for anal cancer, and radiation is a main treatment for gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma. In prostate cancer, it may be used in both early and advanced stages, though it may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients. For skin cancers like squamous cell carcinoma, radiation is used when surgery is not possible or as an adjunct to reduce recurrence

Talk to your doctor about whether a clinical trial may make sense for you. Phases Most cancer clinical trials focus on treatment. Treatment trials are done in phases. Phase 1 trials study the safety and side effects of an investigational drug or treatment approach. Phase 2 trials study how well the drug or approach works against a specific type of cancer. Phase 3 trials test the drug or approach against a standard treatment. If the results are good, it may be approved by the FDA. Phase 4 trials study the long-term safety and benefit of an FDA-approved treatment. Who can enroll? Every clinical trial has rules for joining, called eligibility criteria. These requirements ensure that participants are alike in specific ways and that the trial is as safe as possible for the participants. Informed consent Clinical trials are managed by a group of experts called a research team. Radiation therapy Radiation therapy most often uses highenergy x-rays to kill cancer cells. An advanced radiation technique called intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) is the preferred method for treating anal cancer. It is a type of external beam radiation therapy (EBRT). In EBRT, radiation is delivered from outside (external to) the body using a large machine Anal canal cancer (stages I – III) called a linear accelerator. The radiation passes through skin and other tissue to reach the tumor. All types of EBRT are conformal, which means that the radiation beams are shaped to the tumor. What makes IMRT unique compared to other forms of EBRT is that it uses many small beams of different intensities (strengths). This allows a high dose of radiation to be targeted at the tumor while limiting the amount of radiation to the surrounding normal tissue. With IMRT it is possible to reduce radiation to important nearby organs and structures, such as external genitalia and hip joints. This can help reduce treatment-related side effects. Radiation therapy is given in small doses, called fractions. Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the ovaries, most commonly beginning in the epithelium (the outer lining of the ovaries), and can also start in the fallopian tubes. It encompasses a range of types, including high-grade serous carcinoma, high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and other less common ovarian cancers. The disease can be hereditary or sporadic, with inherited mutations in genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, as well as Lynch syndrome, significantly increasing the risk in affected individuals. Additionally, a family history of ovarian cancer in close blood relatives is associated with an increased risk of developing pancreatic and prostate cancers.

Symptoms of ovarian cancer commonly include bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, difficulty eating, feeling full quickly, and urinary urgency. The disease is staged from 1 to 4, with stages 2, 3, and 4 specifically mentioned, and requires clinical staging along with various diagnostic tests—such as biopsy, imaging, and blood tests—to determine the extent of spread and guide treatment. Treatment typically involves a multidisciplinary team of experts and may include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, with protocols also addressing recurrence management. Ovarian cancer is the central topic of the provided text, guiding discussions on diagnosis, treatment, and related health considerations.

Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Breast cancer is a disease that originates in the cells of the breast, most commonly arising from the epithelial cells of the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs). It can be classified as ductal or lobular, and includes various subtypes such as inflammatory breast cancer. The disease is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of cells, which can spread through invasive growth into surrounding tissues and metastasize to distant parts of the body, including the bone, lungs, liver, brain, or distant lymph nodes. When breast cancer spreads to another organ, such as the lungs, it is still referred to as breast cancer, not as a new type of cancer.

Breast cancer can affect anyone, regardless of gender assigned at birth. It is associated with inherited germline mutations in genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, and a family history of the disease can increase the risk of other cancers, including pancreatic, prostate, and thyroid cancers. A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

Imaging refers to a broad range of medical techniques used to create pictures of the inside of the body, including computed tomography (CT) scans, PET/CT scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasound, x-rays, and transvaginal ultrasound. These tests are essential for determining the extent and spread of cancer, which is critical for staging the disease and guiding treatment decisions. Imaging is used across various cancer types: for pancreatic cancer, it helps decide if surgery is an option; for cervical cancer, techniques such as FDG-PET/CT, CT with contrast, and MRI detect recurrence or spread, typically ordered based on symptoms or stage; for prostate cancer, imaging is used alongside PSA tests to evaluate presence and spread, visualizing the prostate and surrounding areas; for lymphoma, it identifies the location, size, and features of the disease; for adrenal tumors, it often detects them incidentally; for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), it assesses spread to lymph nodes and beyond; for bladder cancer, it visualizes the bladder and surrounding areas to stage and plan treatment; for brain tumors and gliomas, MRI and CT scans aid in diagnosis; and for anal cancers (stage II and III), imaging is used for surveillance after treatment, with yearly imaging recommended for three years to monitor for recurrence or further spread. Imaging is performed by specialists such as thoracic radiologists and is a key component of treatment planning and post-treatment monitoring across oncology.
Imaging tests such as MRI or CT scans are used to detect tumors and confirm the presence of primary CNS lymphoma.

CT scan, also known as Computed Tomography scan, is a diagnostic imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer technology to create detailed, cross-sectional, and often three-dimensional (3D) images of the inside of the body. The procedure involves taking multiple X-ray images from different angles, which are then combined by a computer to produce comprehensive pictures. CT scans are frequently performed with the use of contrast material to enhance image clarity and are typically completed in under 30 minutes.

This imaging modality serves a wide range of medical purposes. It is commonly used as an alternative to MRI when MRI is unavailable or not recommended. In oncology, CT scans are essential for detecting various cancers, including breast, colon, and ovarian cancer, as well as for identifying cancer spread (metastasis) to organs such as the liver, lungs, and lymph nodes. They are also used to detect adrenal tumors, bleeding, leukemia spread, and abnormalities in the neck and chest. Additionally, CT scans are employed to determine the extent of cancer beyond primary sites, such as the bladder or ovaries, and for surveillance in stages 2 and 3 colon cancer to monitor for recurrence.

Beyond diagnosis, CT imaging plays a critical role in treatment and procedural guidance. It is used during radiation therapy simulation to create precise treatment plans by obtaining pictures of the cancer site. CT scans also guide biopsies, particularly lymph node biopsies, ensuring accurate sampling. Furthermore, CT scans can be combined with PET scans (PET/CT) to enhance cancer detection and are recommended for further evaluation when suspicious lymph nodes are found. Overall, CT scanning is a versatile and widely used diagnostic tool for detecting cancer, guiding interventions, and assessing disease extent.

Imaging tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, locate, and evaluate tumors, assess cancer extent, and check for cancer spread. These tests are essential for staging cancer, planning treatment, monitoring tumor response during chemotherapy, and detecting recurrence during surveillance. They are also used to visualize internal structures, guide biopsies, and identify abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, organ involvement, or areas of infection or bleeding.

Imaging tests include a wide range of techniques such as CT scans, MRI, PET scans, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, X-rays, mammograms, and bone scans. These modalities are applied across various cancer types, including breast, prostate, colon, rectal, esophageal, liver, kidney, ovarian, thyroid, adrenal, bone, and throat cancers, as well as leukemias like ALL and AML, and lymphomas such as CBCL and NPC. For example, mammograms, ultrasounds, and MRIs are used to visualize breast tissue; CT and MRI are primary methods for colon cancer staging; and ultrasound is used to detect thyroid nodules and cancer.

Imaging tests are interpreted by a radiologist and are used to reveal a tumor’s location, size, and other features, as well as to detect cancer spread to distant sites. In certain cancers, such as early-stage prostate cancer, imaging may not be necessary, but in others, like leukemia, they help detect spread outside the bone marrow to areas such as the brain, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and skin. Overall, imaging tests are indispensable diagnostic and monitoring tools in oncology, providing detailed visual information that guides clinical decisions across the cancer care continuum.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive diagnostic imaging technique that uses a powerful magnetic field, radio waves, and a computer to create highly detailed pictures of the inside of the body. Unlike X-rays or CT scans, MRI does not use ionizing radiation, making it a safe option for many patients. The procedure often involves the use of a contrast dye (or contrast material) to enhance the visibility of specific tissues, blood vessels, or abnormalities. MRI machines are available in both closed and open designs, accommodating different patient needs and comfort levels.

MRI is widely utilized across various medical fields for diagnosis, staging, treatment planning, and monitoring. It is particularly effective for imaging soft tissues, including the brain, spine, breasts, prostate, pelvic structures, and the rectal wall. In oncology, MRI is used to detect and stage cancers such as primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and rectal cancer. It can also identify the depth of tumor invasion (DOI), assess the spread of cancer to nearby lymph nodes or other organs (e.g., liver, chest), and detect cancer recurrence or metastasis.

In specific clinical scenarios, MRI is recommended for further evaluation when suspicious lymph nodes are found, when ultrasound results are unclear, or when CT results are inconclusive. It is also used to guide biopsies, often in conjunction with computerized navigation systems, and to assist in the placement of brachytherapy applicators and the design of treatment plans. For certain cancers, such as primary CNS lymphoma, MRI is considered the most useful imaging technique for identifying the disease and guiding treatment decisions. In cases of spinal involvement, MRI findings may indicate the need for intrathecal chemotherapy. Additionally, MRI can be combined with PET (positron emission tomography) for more detailed visualization, and it is sometimes used in urography to assess the extent of bladder cancer.

Overall, MRI is a versatile and essential medical imaging tool that provides detailed soft tissue images, supports accurate diagnosis and staging, and plays a critical role in guiding therapeutic interventions across a wide range of conditions.

entities.description: A care team is a multidisciplinary group of healthcare professionals who collaborate to provide comprehensive medical care, diagnosis, treatment, and support for patients, particularly those with cancer or other complex conditions. The team typically includes board-certified medical experts from various fields, such as doctors (e.g., pulmonologists, thoracic radiologists, thoracic surgeons, oncologists, hematologists, hematopathologists, breast specialists, gynecologists, radiologists, dietitians, and therapists), nurses, specialists, technologists, pharmacists, and support staff. They work together to plan and implement treatment, interpret test results (including imaging, CBC measurements, and other diagnostics), discuss treatment options and potential side effects (including effects on fertility), and guide patients through diagnostic and therapeutic processes. The care team is central to patient communication and support, encouraging patients to share information, ask questions, discuss preferences, and make shared decisions about their care. They also provide guidance on preparation for procedures (such as imaging tests and surgery), manage symptoms and side effects, and offer resources for issues like smoking cessation, claustrophobia, and emotional support. The team may specialize in specific conditions, including lung, breast, bladder, pancreatic, thyroid, prostate, glioma, CNS lymphoma, AML, ALL, CLL, NPC, and other cancers, and is responsible for coordinating all aspects of a patient's medical journey, from diagnosis through treatment and recovery.

A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. Biopsy is an invasive procedure and may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, and pain, particularly in procedures like prostate biopsy, which is typically performed by a urologist.

Once the tissue or fluid sample is removed, it is sent to a pathologist, who examines it for cancer cells and writes a pathology report. The results of a biopsy are crucial for confirming a cancer diagnosis, determining tumor characteristics such as Gleason patterns and scores (in prostate cancer), hormone and HER2 receptor status (in breast cancer), and molecular features, and for staging the cancer. Biopsy results also influence treatment plans, and patients are encouraged to understand and keep copies of their pathology reports. In some cases, a biopsy may be the only way to confirm a cancer diagnosis, and it is essential for guiding appropriate and timely treatment.

A pathologist is a specialized medical doctor and expert who examines cells, tissues, and organs—often from biopsy samples, removed lymph nodes, bone marrow, or surgical specimens—under a microscope to diagnose diseases, particularly cancer. They play a crucial role in confirming the presence of cancer, determining its type (tumor histology), grade (how abnormal the cells look and how fast the cancer is expected to grow), and extent (such as the percentage of cancer in each core or the involvement of lymph nodes). Pathologists analyze samples to diagnose various cancers, including cervical, breast, ovarian, prostate, squamous cell carcinoma, primary CNS lymphoma, and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and they may assign specific scores (e.g., Gleason patterns and Gleason scores for prostate cancer) to estimate aggressiveness. They also test blood, saliva, or tissue samples for gene mutations that cause inherited cancer syndromes and provide biomarker testing information. After examining samples, pathologists write detailed pathology reports that document their findings, which guide cancer staging and further treatment decisions. In some cases, a hematopathologist (a pathologist specializing in blood disorders) reviews bone marrow samples to diagnose conditions like AML. Overall, pathologists are essential medical professionals who analyze biopsy and tissue samples to provide accurate cancer diagnosis, staging, and biomarker information, ensuring that patients receive appropriate and timely care.

Imaging refers to a broad range of medical techniques used to create pictures of the inside of the body, including computed tomography (CT) scans, PET/CT scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasound, x-rays, and transvaginal ultrasound. These tests are essential for determining the extent and spread of cancer, which is critical for staging the disease and guiding treatment decisions. Imaging is used across various cancer types: for pancreatic cancer, it helps decide if surgery is an option; for cervical cancer, techniques such as FDG-PET/CT, CT with contrast, and MRI detect recurrence or spread, typically ordered based on symptoms or stage; for prostate cancer, imaging is used alongside PSA tests to evaluate presence and spread, visualizing the prostate and surrounding areas; for lymphoma, it identifies the location, size, and features of the disease; for adrenal tumors, it often detects them incidentally; for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), it assesses spread to lymph nodes and beyond; for bladder cancer, it visualizes the bladder and surrounding areas to stage and plan treatment; for brain tumors and gliomas, MRI and CT scans aid in diagnosis; and for anal cancers (stage II and III), imaging is used for surveillance after treatment, with yearly imaging recommended for three years to monitor for recurrence or further spread. Imaging is performed by specialists such as thoracic radiologists and is a key component of treatment planning and post-treatment monitoring across oncology.

A radiologist is a medical doctor and specialist trained to interpret a wide range of imaging tests—including mammograms, MRIs, CT, PET, bone scans, and ultrasounds—to diagnose, stage, and monitor various conditions such as breast, prostate, cervical, thyroid, and nervous system cancers. They analyze detailed images to identify areas of concern, assess the extent of disease, and evaluate diagnostic mammograms and other imaging results to guide further testing or treatment. Radiologists write detailed reports on their findings and send these results to the patient’s primary doctor, oncologist, or broader care team to aid in diagnosis, treatment planning, and next steps. In some contexts, they may also administer radiation treatments for cancer. Acting as medical experts, they convey imaging results clearly to healthcare providers and, in some cases, directly to patients, ensuring that all relevant information supports effective and coordinated patient care.

CT scan, also known as Computed Tomography scan, is a diagnostic imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer technology to create detailed, cross-sectional, and often three-dimensional (3D) images of the inside of the body. The procedure involves taking multiple X-ray images from different angles, which are then combined by a computer to produce comprehensive pictures. CT scans are frequently performed with the use of contrast material to enhance image clarity and are typically completed in under 30 minutes.

This imaging modality serves a wide range of medical purposes. It is commonly used as an alternative to MRI when MRI is unavailable or not recommended. In oncology, CT scans are essential for detecting various cancers, including breast, colon, and ovarian cancer, as well as for identifying cancer spread (metastasis) to organs such as the liver, lungs, and lymph nodes. They are also used to detect adrenal tumors, bleeding, leukemia spread, and abnormalities in the neck and chest. Additionally, CT scans are employed to determine the extent of cancer beyond primary sites, such as the bladder or ovaries, and for surveillance in stages 2 and 3 colon cancer to monitor for recurrence.

Beyond diagnosis, CT imaging plays a critical role in treatment and procedural guidance. It is used during radiation therapy simulation to create precise treatment plans by obtaining pictures of the cancer site. CT scans also guide biopsies, particularly lymph node biopsies, ensuring accurate sampling. Furthermore, CT scans can be combined with PET scans (PET/CT) to enhance cancer detection and are recommended for further evaluation when suspicious lymph nodes are found. Overall, CT scanning is a versatile and widely used diagnostic tool for detecting cancer, guiding interventions, and assessing disease extent.
Imaging tests such as MRI or CT scans are used to detect tumors and confirm the presence of primary CNS lymphoma.

Imaging tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, locate, and evaluate tumors, assess cancer extent, and check for cancer spread. These tests are essential for staging cancer, planning treatment, monitoring tumor response during chemotherapy, and detecting recurrence during surveillance. They are also used to visualize internal structures, guide biopsies, and identify abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, organ involvement, or areas of infection or bleeding.

Imaging tests include a wide range of techniques such as CT scans, MRI, PET scans, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, X-rays, mammograms, and bone scans. These modalities are applied across various cancer types, including breast, prostate, colon, rectal, esophageal, liver, kidney, ovarian, thyroid, adrenal, bone, and throat cancers, as well as leukemias like ALL and AML, and lymphomas such as CBCL and NPC. For example, mammograms, ultrasounds, and MRIs are used to visualize breast tissue; CT and MRI are primary methods for colon cancer staging; and ultrasound is used to detect thyroid nodules and cancer.

Imaging tests are interpreted by a radiologist and are used to reveal a tumor’s location, size, and other features, as well as to detect cancer spread to distant sites. In certain cancers, such as early-stage prostate cancer, imaging may not be necessary, but in others, like leukemia, they help detect spread outside the bone marrow to areas such as the brain, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and skin. Overall, imaging tests are indispensable diagnostic and monitoring tools in oncology, providing detailed visual information that guides clinical decisions across the cancer care continuum.

A patient is an individual receiving medical care, diagnosis, testing, or treatment for a wide range of conditions, including various types of cancer (such as basal cell skin cancer, prostate cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), rectal cancer, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), actinic keratoses, colon cancer, cervical cancer, follicular lymphoma (FL), anal cancer, bone cancer, bladder cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), ovarian cancer, mouth cancer, inflammatory breast cancer, and throat cancer) as well as other medical conditions. Ultimately, the patient is the individual undergoing diagnostic and treatment procedures, with the goal of managing their health and receiving appropriate medical support.

A physical exam is a clinical assessment performed by a healthcare provider to evaluate a patient's overall health, detect signs of disease, and guide medical decisions. It is a routine medical check-up that includes measuring vital signs (such as blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature), checking body measurements (like height and weight), and listening to the lungs and heart. The exam also involves examining the eyes, ears, nose, and throat, as well as palpating (feeling) the abdomen, pelvis, and lymph nodes to assess organ size and detect abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, lumps, or swelling in the spleen or liver.

This examination is used across a wide range of medical contexts, including general health assessments, pre-anesthesia evaluations, and cancer screening or monitoring. It helps identify signs of various conditions, including breast abnormalities, basal cell skin cancer, and cancers such as ALL, AML, CLL, liver cancer, NPC, bladder cancer, and colon cancer. Physical exams are also performed periodically during chemotherapy (every 1 to 3 cycles) to monitor treatment effectiveness and side effects, and are part of short-term follow-up after procedures like total thyroidectomy, alongside blood tests. Additionally, they are included in surveillance schedules for stages 2 and 3 colon cancer to check for recurrence or spread.

The physical exam provides critical information to the care team about a patient's treatment readiness, overall health, and functional abilities, and is used to detect signs of cancer recurrence or other health issues. It is a general health test that may also include assessing the throat and airway, skin, and other body systems to ensure a comprehensive evaluation.

They are part of the lymphatic and immune systems, containing immune cells such as lymphocytes, and function to filter lymph fluid, remove foreign particles, germs, and harmful substances, and help fight infection and disease. There are over 300 lymph nodes in the head and neck alone.

A biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose cancer and determine its characteristics. It is a key diagnostic tool used to confirm the presence of cancer cells, identify the specific type and histology of a tumor, and guide treatment decisions. Biopsies are performed on various organs and tissues, including the prostate, breast, lung, liver, brain (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma), ovary, thyroid, lymph nodes, bone, skin, bladder, kidney, esophagus, pancreas, adrenal gland, anal canal, and bone marrow, among others.

The procedure is often guided by imaging techniques such as ultrasound, CT, MRI, or EUS, or performed during scoping procedures like cystoscopy. Biopsies may be conducted after abnormal screening results, when a tumor is detected, or when follow-up examinations indicate growth or spread of cancer. In some cases, a biopsy is performed before starting chemotherapy or steroid therapy to avoid altering the appearance of cells, and it is sometimes combined with HPV testing or biomarker analysis to guide targeted therapy.

There are several types of biopsies, including fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), core needle biopsy (CNB), incisional biopsy, excisional biopsy, stereotactic biopsy, and skin biopsy. The choice of biopsy type depends on the location and nature of the suspected cancer. For example, excisional biopsy is preferred for Hodgkin lymphoma, while stereotactic biopsy is standard for primary CNS lymphoma. It identifies the presence or absence of mutations and certain proteins that might suggest treatment. This information is used to choose the best treatment for you. It is sometimes called molecular testing or tumor profiling, tumor sequencing, gene expression profiling, or genomic testing. Inside our cells are deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) molecules. These molecules are tightly packaged into what is called a chromosome. Chromosomes contain most of the genetic information in a cell. About basal cell skin cancer What is basal cell skin cancer? How is basal cell skin cancer treated? What can you do to get the best care? Basal cell skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), is the most common type of skin cancer. About 3 million cases of basal cell skin cancer are diagnosed every year in the United States. The good news is it can be cured in most cases. Treatment usually involves surgery to remove the cancer. Keep reading to find out more. What is basal cell skin cancer? Basal cell skin cancer is the most common of all skin cancer types. If caught early, it is easily treatable and curable. This is because it rarely metastasizes (spreads). Skin cancers often occur in the top layer of the skin (epidermis) and less commonly in the middle layer of the skin (dermis). The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. This cancer usually develops in areas exposed to the sun, including the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. But it can occur anywhere on the body. Skin lesions Basal cell skin cancer is often found on the face, head, and neck. Here is a basal cell lesion pictured on a person's cheek. Skin basics Did you know that your skin is your body’s largest organ and if you measured it it would stretch to about 20 square feet? Working as a barrier, your skin protects you from bacteria and chemicals and helps control your body temperature. It has 3 layers: Epidermis – The top layer of skin provides a waterproof barrier and creates skin color (melanin). Dermis – The middle layer involves connective tissue, blood vessels, oil and sweat glands, nerves, and hair follicles. Hypodermis – The deepest tissue layer is made up of fat and connective tissue. Most skin cancers form in the cells of the epidermis. It has 3 main types of cells: Squamous cells – These cells are flat cells found in the upper part of the epidermis. Basal cells – Found in the lower part of the epidermis, basal cells constantly divide to form new cells that replace the squamous cells on the skin’s surface. Melanocytes – Melanocytes are cells located in the lower part of the epidermis that produce melanin. Melanin is responsible for our hair, skin, and eye color. It also protects our skin from harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays. This book is only about basal cell skin cancer. For more information on squamous cell skin cancer or melanoma, read the NCCN Guidelines for Patients, available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Signs and symptoms Basal cell skin cancer can happen to anyone but it’s most common in people with lighter skin, lighter hair, or lighter eyes. In lighter skin, its lesions can look like any of the following: h Flat, pale or yellow areas, like a scar h Red patches that might be itchy Small, pink or red, shiny bumps that may have blue, brown, or black areas Open sores that don’t heal and might bleed, or go away and come back In darker (brown and black) skin, basal cell skin cancer can appear as a brown or glossy black bump with a rolled border. It can be mistaken for a normal mole. Be sure to look out for any new, changing, bleeding, or unusual skin growths. Skin cancer is easier to cure when it is caught early. To find out how basal cell skin cancer is diagnosed, read Chapter 2: Testing for basal cell skin cancer. Causes and risk factors Basal cell skin cancer is caused by exposure to UV radiation from the sun or other sources like tanning beds. UV radiation can harm the DNA inside basal skin cells. DNA controls how cells grow and function. If the DNA inside cells becomes damaged, the cells can become abnormal and grow out of control. You’re more likely to have basal cell skin cancer if you have certain risk factors. A risk factor increases the chance of developing cancer. Risk factors for basal cell skin cancer include: UV light exposure – UV light (radiation) that comes from the sun or tanning beds increases your risk. Fair skin, red or blond hair, or light eye color – People with lighter-colored skin are at a higher risk of developing skin cancer because melanin (skin pigment) filters out the sun's harmful UV rays. Age – Risk increases with age because sun exposure builds up over time. But skin cancer is becoming more common in younger people. History of skin cancer – If you or someone in your family has had skin cancer, you’re more likely to develop any type of skin cancer. Radiation therapy – Radiation treatment for other conditions, especially at a young age, can cause skin cancer. Immune suppression – People with weakened immune systems from organ transplants or autoimmune diseases are at higher risk for basal cell skin cancer. How is basal cell skin cancer treated? Basal cell skin cancer is highly treatable and curable. Catching it and treating it early is key. Surgery is the most common treatment for basal cell skin cancer. In some cases, radiation therapy or systemic therapy might be used to treat it. Following your treatment, you will have full skin exams with your doctor at least once a year. Between these periods, prevention is important. See Chapter 4: Treatment by risk and recurrence for more information. Recurrence is when basal cell skin cancer returns to the area where it was originally found, or it has metastasized (spread) to the lymph nodes or to distant parts of the body. Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Chemotherapy can be used alone or combined with other therapies, including radiation (chemoradiation), surgery, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially when PD-L1 or PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed). It is a standard treatment for many cancers, including AML, ALL, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, anal cancer, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and squamous cell skin cancer, among others. Specific regimens vary by cancer type and may include platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin), taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine), mitomycin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and anthracyclines. Chemotherapy can be delivered systemically (through the bloodstream), intravenously, orally, intraperitoneally, intravesically, intrathecally, or intraocularly, depending on the cancer and treatment goal. It may be used before surgery (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), as primary treatment for metastatic disease, or in high doses during stem cell rescue. Side effects are common and include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, fever, infection, and low blood cell counts. Chemotherapy can also affect fertility and other bodily functions, so preventive measures and birth control may be recommended during treatment. Smoking during chemotherapy can increase lung problems. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility. Chemotherapy is often a key component of treatment plans and may be recommended based on cancer stage, molecular markers (e.g., PD-L1 expression), and response to other treatments.

Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy radiation—such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons—to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is planned and prescribed by a radiation oncologist and delivered by radiation therapists or other specialists. This treatment is often used as a local therapy to target specific areas of the body, and it may be combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation), surgery, or systemic therapies, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Radiation therapy is applicable to a wide range of cancers, including anal, bladder, brain (e.g., gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma), breast, cervical, prostate, rectal, skin (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), thyroid, and perianal cancers, as well as chordoma and metastatic anal cancer. It can be used as a primary treatment, an adjunct after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells, or as palliative care to relieve pain. Techniques include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), and brachytherapy (internal radioactive material).

Treatment is typically given over several weeks, with common schedules of five sessions per week, each session lasting 30 to 60 minutes. While effective, radiation therapy can cause side effects, which may appear during treatment or years later. These include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, tiredness, headaches, nausea, vision problems, cataracts, and long-term cognitive issues. Radiation to the head and neck can affect endocrine glands, hearing, and other functions, requiring pre- and post-treatment monitoring. Additionally, radiation therapy can impact fertility—for example, in rectal cancer it may damage ovarian and testicular function—and prior exposure to radiation, especially at a young age (e.g., to the chest), is a risk factor for certain cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer and small cell lung cancer.

For some cancers, radiation therapy is a preferred or standard treatment option. For instance, IMRT is often preferred for anal cancer, and radiation is a main treatment for gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma. In prostate cancer, it may be used in both early and advanced stages, though it may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients. For skin cancers like squamous cell carcinoma, radiation is used when surgery is not possible or as an adjunct to reduce recurrence

It uses a scope called a laryngoscope placed in the back of your throat. This procedure allows the doctor to see deeper in the throat and to take a tissue sample for a biopsy. The purpose of direct laryngoscopy is to identify the primary (main) tumor and determine if it is resectable (can be removed with surgery). Esophagoscopy In an esophagoscopy, a device is guided down the throat into the esophagus. It is performed under anesthesia in an operating room. This allows the doctor to examine your esophagus (swallowing tube) for abnormal growths. Bronchoscopy During a bronchoscopy, a device is inserted through the nose or mouth to examine the inside of your airway, including the trachea and bronchi. Bronchoscopy may be used to detect cancer or to perform some treatment procedures. It is done under anesthesia to make you more comfortable. Panendoscopy During a panendoscopy, different types of endoscopes are passed down the mouth or nose to do a laryngoscopy, pharyngoscopy, esophagoscopy, or bronchoscopy. This allows a doctor to thoroughly examine the mouth, oropharynx, larynx (voice box), esophagus (tube leading to the stomach), and trachea (windpipe) and bronchi (breathing passages in the lungs). It is performed under anesthesia to make you more comfortable. This procedure might be done to look for other tumors if it is unclear where the cancer started, or if the lymph nodes in the bottom part of the neck seem abnormal. A biopsy of any tumors or other abnormal areas might be taken. Biopsies can be done with special tools that are used through the scopes. These molecules are tightly packaged into what is called a chromosome. Chromosomes contain most of the genetic information in a cell. Normal human cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes for a total of 46 chromosomes. Each chromosome contains thousands of genes. Genes are coded instructions for the proteins your cells make. About basal cell skin cancer What is basal cell skin cancer? How is basal cell skin cancer treated? What can you do to get the best care? Basal cell skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), is the most common type of skin cancer. About 3 million cases of basal cell skin cancer are diagnosed every year in the United States. The good news is it can be cured in most cases. Treatment usually involves surgery to remove the cancer. Keep reading to find out more. What is basal cell skin cancer? Basal cell skin cancer is the most common of all skin cancer types. If caught early, it is easily treatable and curable. This is because it rarely metastasizes (spreads). Skin cancers often occur in the top layer of the skin (epidermis) and less commonly in the middle layer of the skin (dermis). The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. This cancer usually develops in areas exposed to the sun, including the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. But it can occur anywhere on the body. Skin lesions Basal cell skin cancer is often found on the face, head, and neck. Here is a basal cell lesion pictured on a person's cheek. Skin basics Did you know that your skin is your body’s largest organ and if you measured it it would stretch to about 20 square feet? Working as a barrier, your skin protects you from bacteria and chemicals and helps control your body temperature. It has 3 layers: Epidermis – The top layer of skin provides a waterproof barrier and creates skin color (melanin). Dermis – The middle layer involves connective tissue, blood vessels, oil and sweat glands, nerves, and hair follicles. Hypodermis – The deepest tissue layer is made up of fat and connective tissue. Most skin cancers form in the cells of the epidermis. It has 3 main types of cells: Squamous cells – These cells are flat cells found in the upper part of the epidermis. Basal cells – Found in the lower part of the epidermis, basal cells constantly divide to form new cells that replace the squamous cells on the skin’s surface. Melanocytes – Melanocytes are cells located in the lower part of the epidermis that produce melanin. Melanin is responsible for our hair, skin, and eye color. It also protects our skin from harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays. This book is only about basal cell skin cancer. For more information on squamous cell skin cancer or melanoma, read the NCCN Guidelines for Patients, available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Signs and symptoms Basal cell skin cancer can happen to anyone but it’s most common in people with lighter skin, lighter hair, or lighter eyes. In lighter skin, its lesions can look like any of the following: h Flat, pale or yellow areas, like a scar h Red patches that might be itchy Small, pink or red, shiny bumps that may have blue, brown, or black areas Open sores that don’t heal and might bleed, or go away and come back In darker (brown and black) skin, basal cell skin cancer can appear as a brown or glossy black bump with a rolled border. It can be mistaken for a normal mole. Be sure to look out for any new, changing, bleeding, or unusual skin growths. Skin cancer is easier to cure when it is caught early. To find out how basal cell skin cancer is diagnosed, read Chapter 2: Testing for basal cell skin cancer. Causes and risk factors Basal cell skin cancer is caused by exposure to UV radiation from the sun or other sources like tanning beds. UV radiation can harm the DNA inside basal skin cells. DNA controls how cells grow and function. If the DNA inside cells becomes damaged, the cells can become abnormal and grow out of control. You’re more likely to have basal cell skin cancer if you have certain risk factors. A risk factor increases the chance of developing cancer. Risk factors for basal cell skin cancer include: UV light exposure – UV light (radiation) that comes from the sun or tanning beds increases your risk. Fair skin, red or blond hair, or light eye color – People with lighter-colored skin are at a higher risk of developing skin cancer because melanin (skin pigment) filters out the sun's harmful UV rays. Age – Risk increases with age because sun exposure builds up over time. But skin cancer is becoming more common in younger people. History of skin cancer – If you or someone in your family has had skin cancer, you’re more likely to develop any type of skin cancer. Radiation therapy – Radiation treatment for other conditions, especially at a young age, can cause skin cancer. Immune suppression – People with weakened immune systems from organ transplants or autoimmune diseases are at higher risk for basal cell skin cancer. How is basal cell skin cancer treated? Basal cell skin cancer is highly treatable and curable. Catching it and treating it early is key. Surgery is the most common treatment for basal cell skin cancer. In some cases, radiation therapy or systemic therapy might be used to treat it. Following your treatment, you will have full skin exams with your doctor at least once a year. Between these periods, prevention is important. See Chapter 4: Treatment by risk and recurrence for more information. Recurrence is when basal cell skin cancer returns to the area where it was originally found, or it has metastasized (spread) to the lymph nodes or to distant parts of the body. entities.description: A care team is a multidisciplinary group of healthcare professionals who collaborate to provide comprehensive medical care, diagnosis, treatment, and support for patients, particularly those with cancer or other complex conditions. The team typically includes board-certified medical experts from various fields, such as doctors (e.g., pulmonologists, thoracic radiologists, thoracic surgeons, oncologists, hematologists, hematopathologists, breast specialists, gynecologists, radiologists, dietitians, and therapists), nurses, specialists, technologists, pharmacists, and support staff. They work together to plan and implement treatment, interpret test results (including imaging, CBC measurements, and other diagnostics), discuss treatment options and potential side effects (including effects on fertility), and guide patients through diagnostic and therapeutic processes. The care team is central to patient communication and support, encouraging patients to share information, ask questions, discuss preferences, and make shared decisions about their care. They also provide guidance on preparation for procedures (such as imaging tests and surgery), manage symptoms and side effects, and offer resources for issues like smoking cessation, claustrophobia, and emotional support. The team may specialize in specific conditions, including lung, breast, bladder, pancreatic, thyroid, prostate, glioma, CNS lymphoma, AML, ALL, CLL, NPC, and other cancers, and is responsible for coordinating all aspects of a patient's medical journey, from diagnosis through treatment and recovery.
