Mouth sores Hair loss Fatigue Increased risk of infection Bleeding or bruising easily Nerve damage (neuropathy) Cisplatin can damage the kidneys. People whose kidneys do not work well may not be able to have cisplatin. An alternative chemotherapy drug may be used. Cisplatin can also cause ringing in the ears (tinnitus) or hearing problems or loss. Ask your treatment team for a list of common and rare side effects of each systemic therapy you are receiving. There are ways to prevent or alleviate some of these effects. Clinical trials A clinical trial is a type of medical research study. After being developed and tested in a laboratory, potential new ways of fighting cancer need to be studied in people. If found to be safe and effective in a clinical trial, a drug, device, or treatment approach may be approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Everyone with cancer should carefully consider all of the treatment options available for their cancer type, including standard treatments and clinical trials. Talk to your doctor about whether a clinical trial may make sense for you. Phases Most cancer clinical trials focus on treatment. Treatment trials are done in phases. Phase 1 trials study the dose, safety, and side effects of an investigational drug or treatment approach. They also look for early signs that the drug or approach is helpful. Phase 2 trials study how well the drug or approach works against a specific type of cancer. Phase 3 trials test the drug or approach against a standard treatment. If the results are good, it may be approved by the FDA. Phase 4 trials study the long-term safety and benefit of an FDA-approved treatment. Who can enroll? Every clinical trial has rules for joining, called eligibility criteria. The rules may be about age, cancer type and stage, treatment history, or general health. These requirements ensure that participants are alike in specific ways and that the trial is as safe as possible for the participants. Informed consent Clinical trials are managed by a group of experts called a research team. The research team will review the study with you in detail, including its purpose and the risks and benefits of joining. All of this information is also provided in an informed consent form. Read the form carefully and ask questions before signing it. Take time to discuss it with family, friends, or others you trust. Keep in mind that you can leave and seek treatment outside of the clinical trial at any time. Start the conversation Don’t wait for your doctor to bring up clinical trials. Start the conversation and learn about all of your treatment options. If you find a study that you may be eligible for, ask your treatment team if you meet the requirements. If you have already started standard treatment, you may not be eligible for certain clinical trials. Try not to be discouraged if you cannot join. New clinical trials are always becoming available. Frequently asked questions There are many myths and misconceptions surrounding clinical trials. The possible benefits and risks are not well understood by many with cancer. Will I get a placebo? Placebos (inactive versions of real medicines) are almost never used alone in cancer clinical trials. It is common to receive either a placebo with a standard treatment or a new drug with a standard treatment. You will be informed, verbally and in writing, if a placebo is part of a clinical trial before you enroll. Are clinical trials free? There is no fee to enroll in a clinical trial. The study sponsor pays for research-related costs, including the study drug. You may, however, have costs indirectly related to the trial, such as the cost of transportation or child care due to extra appointments. During the trial, you will continue to receive standard cancer care. This care is billed to—and often covered by— insurance. You are responsible for copays and any costs for this care that are not covered by your insurance. If there is more than one metastasis, each site may be biopsied. The type of biopsy used depends on the location of the suspected metastases and other factors. Biomarker testing Biomarker tumor testing includes tests of genes or their products (proteins). It identifies the presence or absence of mutations and certain proteins that might suggest treatment. This information is used to choose the best treatment for you. It is sometimes called molecular testing or tumor profiling, tumor sequencing, gene expression profiling, or genomic testing. Inside our cells are deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) molecules. These molecules are tightly packaged into what is called a chromosome. Chromosomes contain most of the genetic information in a cell. Normal human cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes for a total of 46 chromosomes. Each chromosome contains thousands of genes. Genes are coded instructions for the proteins your cells make. Most genes contain information about a specific protein. A mutation is when something goes wrong in the genetic code. Epstein-Barr virus Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a common virus that causes infectious mononucleosis. It remains dormant or inactive in most people. Cancer caused by EBV is called EBV-related cancer. Most nasopharyngeal cancers are EBV-related. A sample of your tumor and/or blood will be tested for EBV DNA before and after treatment. MSI-H/dMMR mutation Microsatellites are short, repeated strings of DNA. When errors or defects occur, they are fixed by mismatch repair (MMR) proteins. Some cancers have DNA mutations or changes that prevent these errors from being fixed. This is called microsatellite instability (MSI) or deficient mismatch repair (dMMR). When cancer cells have more than a normal number of microsatellites, it is called MSI-H (microsatellite instability-high). This is often due to dMMR genes. PD-L1 testing Programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) is an immune protein. If this protein is expressed on the surface of cancer cells, it can cause your immune cells to ignore the cancer and suppress the anti-tumor immune response. If your cancer expresses this protein, you might have treatment that combines chemotherapy and an immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. This is designed to activate your immune system to better fight off the cancer cells. Tumor HPV testing Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a group of viruses that infect the cells on the surface of skin or on the moist surfaces or inner linings of some organs and body cavities. HPV infection usually clears on its own. However, HPV infections can cause abnormal tissue growth (warts) and sometimes cancer. Cancer caused by HPV is called HPV-related cancer. In cancers of the head and neck, throat cancer is most often related to HPV. However, HPV testing might be done in some cases for nasopharyngeal cancer. More information on HPV can be found in NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Throat Cancer, available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Tumor mutational burden When there are 10 or more mutations per million base pairs of tumor DNA, it is called tumor mutational burden-high (TMB-H). Metastatic or unresectable TMB cancers are often treated using immunotherapy drugs that target the proteins called programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) or programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1). Tumor mutation testing Tumor mutation testing or tumor genomic aberration testing uses a sample of your tumor or blood to see if the cancer cells have any specific DNA mutations. This is a different type of DNA testing than the genetic testing for mutations you may have inherited from your biological parents. In tumor mutation testing, only the tumor is tested and not the rest of your body. Some mutations can be targeted with specific therapies. Online portals are a great way to access your test results. Please discuss your results with your health care provider. A medical history and physical exam inform your care team about your overall health. Your overall health may guide the best treatment for your cancer. Head and neck cancer and its treatment can affect the health of your jaw, teeth, and gums. Tell your dentist about your head and neck cancer and keep up with regular dental cleanings and checkups. Systemic therapy is a cancer treatment approach that uses drugs or substances that travel through the bloodstream to reach and affect cancer cells throughout the body. It is a whole-body treatment, typically administered intravenously, and includes a range of modalities such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, hormone therapy, and endocrine therapy. These treatments are used across various cancer types, including metastatic colon cancer, squamous cell skin cancer (CSCC), cervical cancer, bladder cancer, basal cell skin cancer, Ewing sarcoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), ovarian cancer, and MGZL, among others.

Systemic therapy may be used alone or in combination with other treatments, and is often indicated when cancer has spread (metastatic or recurrent disease), when surgery or radiation is not possible or insufficient, or when concerning amounts of cancer remain after surgery. It can also be part of maintenance therapy following initial treatment. The specific drugs used—such as platinum-based chemotherapy, HER2-targeted therapy, or inhibitors—are chosen based on the cancer type and receptor expression.

Administration is typically performed by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, often via a catheter or port. Goals of systemic therapy are discussed with patients before starting treatment. Side effects can include tiredness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, and low blood cell counts. Some side effects may appear years later, including secondary cancers, heart disease, or infertility. Systemic therapy can affect fertility, and preservation options are often discussed with patients.

Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that occurs in the cervix, the lower part of the female reproductive system, and is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in cervical tissues. It is primarily caused by long-term (persistent) infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), and it is a common cancer of the female reproductive system. The disease can manifest in several histological types, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is often detected through screening methods such as Pap smears, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by cervical biopsy. The cancer is staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, and staging is crucial as it determines treatment options and prognosis. Treatment approaches vary and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy (such as chemotherapy), and chemoradiation, with the choice of treatment based on the cancer stage and risk factors such as lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). Cervical cancer can spread to lymph nodes and, if untreated or not diagnosed early, may recur locally or regionally or spread to distant organs; therefore, surveillance and follow-up care are critical for managing recurrence and metastasis. The disease is closely linked to HPV, and a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of anal cancer, as both share the same viral cause. Consequently, screening for cervical cancer is recommended for patients with anal cancer, and female survivors of anal cancer may also be screened for cervical cancer. Additionally, p16, a biomarker, can be found in cervical cancer tissues.

Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Prostate cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled or abnormal growth of cells in the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ. This condition can manifest in two primary forms: early-stage (localized), where the cancer remains confined within the prostate, and advanced-stage (metastatic), where it spreads to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and may present no symptoms in its early stages, making it one of the most common types of cancer; however, it is highly treatable when detected early.

The disease can be influenced by a variety of risk factors, including age, family history, genetic factors (such as BRCA mutations), race, and lifestyle or dietary choices. Diagnosis and monitoring typically involve tests such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, digital rectal exams, and biopsies. The condition is further classified into risk groups and assessed using tools like Gleason scores and Grade Groups, which help determine prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Imaging is also utilized for staging and assessing the extent of the disease.

Treatment options for prostate cancer include hormone therapy (such as androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT, which aims to block or reduce testosterone levels), chemotherapy, radiation, and other therapeutic approaches. Prostate cancer may also be identified through screening during regular checkups or as part of cancer prevention efforts, including for specific populations such as male anal cancer survivors. Overall, the disease is managed through a combination of diagnostic, staging, and treatment strategies tailored to the individual's risk and disease progression.

Targeted therapy is a form of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to precisely identify and attack specific molecules, genetic mutations, or abnormal proteins involved in the growth, progression, and spread of cancer cells. It is a type of systemic therapy, meaning it travels throughout the body, and is designed to focus on unique or specific features of cancer cells, thereby minimizing damage to normal, healthy cells compared to traditional chemotherapy.

This approach is used across a wide range of cancers, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML), cervical cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, squamous cell skin cancer, and breast cancer (such as HER2-positive cases). It is often guided by biomarker testing or specific genetic profiling, such as identifying mutations like PIK3CA, the BCR::ABL protein, or markers like PSMA. Examples of targeted therapy drugs include PARP inhibitors, Gemtuzumab ozogamicin, Gilteritinib, quizartinib, midostaurin, sorafenib, ivosidenib, bevacizumab, mirvetuximab soravtansine-gynx, tisotumab vedotin, and EGFR inhibitors.

Targeted therapy may be used in various scenarios, including for cancers that have returned, metastasized, or are resistant to other treatments, such as radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy for thyroid cancer. It can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments like chemotherapy. While it can be highly effective, it may also have side effects, which can include allergic reactions, fatigue, low platelet counts, body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding. Some serious side effects may affect the heart, skin, or digestive system. Additionally, targeted therapy can affect fertility, so it is important for patients to discuss this potential impact with their healthcare provider before starting treatment.

Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that occurs in the cervix, the lower part of the female reproductive system, and is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in cervical tissues. It is primarily caused by long-term (persistent) infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), and it is a common cancer of the female reproductive system. The disease can manifest in several histological types, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is often detected through screening methods such as Pap smears, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by cervical biopsy. The cancer is staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, and staging is crucial as it determines treatment options and prognosis. Treatment approaches vary and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy (such as chemotherapy), and chemoradiation, with the choice of treatment based on the cancer stage and risk factors such as lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). Cervical cancer can spread to lymph nodes and, if untreated or not diagnosed early, may recur locally or regionally or spread to distant organs; therefore, surveillance and follow-up care are critical for managing recurrence and metastasis. The disease is closely linked to HPV, and a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of anal cancer, as both share the same viral cause. Consequently, screening for cervical cancer is recommended for patients with anal cancer, and female survivors of anal cancer may also be screened for cervical cancer. Additionally, p16, a biomarker, can be found in cervical cancer tissues.

Immunotherapy is a type of systemic cancer treatment that leverages and boosts the body’s own immune system to find, reactivate, and destroy cancer cells. It is commonly administered by a medical oncologist and is considered a newer, non-hormone therapeutic approach that works alongside other systemic therapies like chemotherapy and targeted therapy. Immunotherapy is used across a wide range of cancers, including anal, cervical, bladder, ovarian, breast, prostate, colon, skin (squamous cell carcinoma), and primary CNS lymphoma, as well as for acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and metastatic disease.

The treatment often involves immune checkpoint inhibitors—such as pembrolizumab, nivolumab, and ipilimumab—which help reactivate the immune system against tumor cells. For certain cancers, including those with specific biomarkers like dMMR, MSI-H, or PD-1 expression, immunotherapy is a preferred option. It may be used to avoid surgery in anal cancer, to treat recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer with specific biomarkers, or as a recommended approach when cancer progresses during or after chemotherapy. In primary CNS lymphoma, the main immunotherapy drug is rituximab, a monoclonal antibody that targets CD20 proteins on cancer cells.

Eligibility for immunotherapy is often determined through biomarker testing, and it may be delivered systemically or directly into the bladder for certain bladder cancers. While generally effective, immunotherapy can cause side effects, including autoimmune reactions, fatigue, fever, nausea, diarrhea, drowsiness, and low blood cell counts. These side effects are addressed in clinical guidelines. Overall, immunotherapy aims to help patients live longer, manage symptoms, and improve outcomes across various cancer types, particularly in advanced or metastatic stages.

entities.description: Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Chemotherapy can be used alone or combined with other therapies, including radiation (chemoradiation), surgery, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially when PD-L1 or PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed). It is a standard treatment for many cancers, including AML, ALL, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, anal cancer, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and squamous cell skin cancer, among others. Specific regimens vary by cancer type and may include platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin), taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine), mitomycin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and anthracyclines. Chemotherapy can be delivered systemically (through the bloodstream), intravenously, orally, intraperitoneally, intravesically, intrathecally, or intraocularly, depending on the cancer and treatment goal. It may be used before surgery (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), as primary treatment for metastatic disease, or in high doses during stem cell rescue. Side effects are common and include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, fever, infection, and low blood cell counts. Chemotherapy can also affect fertility and other bodily functions, so preventive measures and birth control may be recommended during treatment. Smoking during chemotherapy can increase lung problems. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility. Chemotherapy is often a key component of treatment plans and may be recommended based on cancer stage, molecular markers (e.g., PD-L1 expression), and response to other treatments.

Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses high-energy radiation—such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons—to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is planned and prescribed by a radiation oncologist and delivered by radiation therapists or other specialists. This treatment is often used as a local therapy to target specific areas of the body, and it may be combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation), surgery, or systemic therapies, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Radiation therapy is applicable to a wide range of cancers, including anal, bladder, brain (e.g., gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma), breast, cervical, prostate, rectal, skin (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), thyroid, and perianal cancers, as well as chordoma and metastatic anal cancer. It can be used as a primary treatment, an adjunct after surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells, or as palliative care to relieve pain. Techniques include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), and brachytherapy (internal radioactive material).

Treatment is typically given over several weeks, with common schedules of five sessions per week, each session lasting 30 to 60 minutes. While effective, radiation therapy can cause side effects, which may appear during treatment or years later. These include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, tiredness, headaches, nausea, vision problems, cataracts, and long-term cognitive issues. Radiation to the head and neck can affect endocrine glands, hearing, and other functions, requiring pre- and post-treatment monitoring. Additionally, radiation therapy can impact fertility—for example, in rectal cancer it may damage ovarian and testicular function—and prior exposure to radiation, especially at a young age (e.g., to the chest), is a risk factor for certain cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer and small cell lung cancer.

For some cancers, radiation therapy is a preferred or standard treatment option. For instance, IMRT is often preferred for anal cancer, and radiation is a main treatment for gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma. In prostate cancer, it may be used in both early and advanced stages, though it may be avoided or delayed for lower-risk patients. For skin cancers like squamous cell carcinoma, radiation is used when surgery is not possible or as an adjunct to reduce recurrence

Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that occurs in the cervix, the lower part of the female reproductive system, and is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in cervical tissues. It is primarily caused by long-term (persistent) infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), and it is a common cancer of the female reproductive system. The disease can manifest in several histological types, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Cervical cancer is often detected through screening methods such as Pap smears, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by cervical biopsy. The cancer is staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system, and staging is crucial as it determines treatment options and prognosis. Treatment approaches vary and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy (such as chemotherapy), and chemoradiation, with the choice of treatment based on the cancer stage and risk factors such as lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). Cervical cancer can spread to lymph nodes and, if untreated or not diagnosed early, may recur locally or regionally or spread to distant organs; therefore, surveillance and follow-up care are critical for managing recurrence and metastasis. The disease is closely linked to HPV, and a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of anal cancer, as both share the same viral cause. Consequently, screening for cervical cancer is recommended for patients with anal cancer, and female survivors of anal cancer may also be screened for cervical cancer. Additionally, p16, a biomarker, can be found in cervical cancer tissues.

Fertility is the ability to conceive and have children, and it is a significant health consideration for individuals of all genders affected by cancer. Cancer treatments—including chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and treatments for specific cancers such as acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), bone cancer, head and neck cancer, cervical cancer, and anal cancer—can damage the organs and bodily functions necessary for conception and pregnancy. As a result, fertility may be impacted either temporarily or permanently, and this risk is addressed as part of comprehensive cancer care.

Fertility concerns are discussed before and during treatment planning, and patients are strongly encouraged to speak with their care team about potential risks. Fertility preservation options—such as egg, sperm, or embryo freezing—are often considered and may involve referrals to specialists for counseling. These discussions are relevant across all genders and are integrated into treatment protocols for various cancer types, including those affecting the head and neck, bones, blood, cervix, and anus. Long-term effects on fertility are particularly noted in treatments like radiation therapy for cervical and anal cancers.

Overall, fertility is a key aspect of cancer treatment planning, and patients are advised to proactively address their reproductive goals with their healthcare providers to explore available preservation options before beginning treatment.

entities.description: A care team is a multidisciplinary group of healthcare professionals who collaborate to provide comprehensive medical care, diagnosis, treatment, and support for patients, particularly those with cancer or other complex conditions. The team typically includes board-certified medical experts from various fields, such as doctors (e.g., pulmonologists, thoracic radiologists, thoracic surgeons, oncologists, hematologists, hematopathologists, breast specialists, gynecologists, radiologists, dietitians, and therapists), nurses, specialists, technologists, pharmacists, and support staff. They work together to plan and implement treatment, interpret test results (including imaging, CBC measurements, and other diagnostics), discuss treatment options and potential side effects (including effects on fertility), and guide patients through diagnostic and therapeutic processes. The care team is central to patient communication and support, encouraging patients to share information, ask questions, discuss preferences, and make shared decisions about their care. They also provide guidance on preparation for procedures (such as imaging tests and surgery), manage symptoms and side effects, and offer resources for issues like smoking cessation, claustrophobia, and emotional support. The team may specialize in specific conditions, including lung, breast, bladder, pancreatic, thyroid, prostate, glioma, CNS lymphoma, AML, ALL, CLL, NPC, and other cancers, and is responsible for coordinating all aspects of a patient's medical journey, from diagnosis through treatment and recovery.

Fertility is the ability to conceive and have children, and it is a significant health consideration for individuals of all genders affected by cancer. Cancer treatments—including chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and treatments for specific cancers such as acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), bone cancer, head and neck cancer, cervical cancer, and anal cancer—can damage the organs and bodily functions necessary for conception and pregnancy. As a result, fertility may be impacted either temporarily or permanently, and this risk is addressed as part of comprehensive cancer care.

Fertility concerns are discussed before and during treatment planning, and patients are strongly encouraged to speak with their care team about potential risks. Fertility preservation options—such as egg, sperm, or embryo freezing—are often considered and may involve referrals to specialists for counseling. These discussions are relevant across all genders and are integrated into treatment protocols for various cancer types, including those affecting the head and neck, bones, blood, cervix, and anus. Long-term effects on fertility are particularly noted in treatments like radiation therapy for cervical and anal cancers.

Overall, fertility is a key aspect of cancer treatment planning, and patients are advised to proactively address their reproductive goals with their healthcare providers to explore available preservation options before beginning treatment.

Chemotherapy is a systemic cancer treatment that uses drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, particularly fast-dividing cells, throughout the body. It is administered by medical oncologists or oncology nurses, typically intravenously, orally, or topically, and is given in cycles (e.g., 14, 21, or 28 days). Chemotherapy can be used alone or combined with other therapies, including radiation (chemoradiation), surgery, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (especially when PD-L1 or PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed). It is a standard treatment for many cancers, including AML, ALL, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, anal cancer, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and squamous cell skin cancer, among others. Specific regimens vary by cancer type and may include platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin), taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel), antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine), mitomycin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and anthracyclines. Chemotherapy can be delivered systemically (through the bloodstream), intravenously, orally, intraperitoneally, intravesically, intrathecally, or intraocularly, depending on the cancer and treatment goal. It may be used before surgery (neoadjuvant), after surgery (adjuvant), as primary treatment for metastatic disease, or in high doses during stem cell rescue. Side effects are common and include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, fever, infection, and low blood cell counts. A clinical trial is a type of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, therapies, procedures, or preventive measures—such as drugs, devices, chemopreventive agents, or tests like ctDNA—for diseases, particularly cancer. These studies aim to determine the safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits of investigational approaches, with the goal of advancing medical care and bringing new treatments to individuals. Clinical trials are conducted in phases: Phase 1 assesses safety and side effects, Phase 2 evaluates effectiveness against specific cancers, Phase 3 compares the new treatment to standard therapies, and Phase 4 monitors long-term safety after approval. If a drug, device, or treatment approach is found safe and effective, it may be approved by the U.S. FDA.

Trials are governed by specific protocols and eligibility criteria, which may include factors such as a patient's performance status, as determined by their care team. They are managed by a dedicated research team, and participation requires informed consent. Placebos are rarely used alone in cancer trials. There is no enrollment fee, and the sponsor covers research-related costs; however, standard care costs may be billed to insurance.

They offer patients access to experimental therapies, including chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and systemic therapy, and may be an option when standard therapies are not available or appropriate. Participation allows patients to receive investigational treatments while contributing to medical knowledge, though outcomes may vary. Patients are encouraged to ask their care team about clinical trials and may join at any time.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive diagnostic imaging technique that uses a powerful magnetic field, radio waves, and a computer to create highly detailed pictures of the inside of the body. Unlike X-rays or CT scans, MRI does not use ionizing radiation, making it a safe option for many patients. The procedure often involves the use of a contrast dye (or contrast material) to enhance the visibility of specific tissues, blood vessels, or abnormalities. MRI machines are available in both closed and open designs, accommodating different patient needs and comfort levels.

MRI is widely utilized across various medical fields for diagnosis, staging, treatment planning, and monitoring. It is particularly effective for imaging soft tissues, including the brain, spine, breasts, prostate, pelvic structures, and the rectal wall. In oncology, MRI is used to detect and stage cancers such as primary CNS lymphoma, gliomas, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, and rectal cancer. It can also identify the depth of tumor invasion (DOI), assess the spread of cancer to nearby lymph nodes or other organs (e.g., liver, chest), and detect cancer recurrence or metastasis.

This book is organized into the following chapters: Chapter 2: Testing for bone cancer provides an overview of tests you might receive, how fertility might be impacted by treatment, and the role of biomarker and tumor mutation testing. Chapter 3: Bone cancer staging explains how bone cancer is staged and where bone tumors might be found in the body. Chapter 4: Types of treatment gives an overview of the types of different treatment and who might be on your treatment team. Chapter 5: Chondrosarcoma discusses chondrosarcoma treatment. Treatment is usually surgery to remove the tumor. Chapter 6: Chordoma discusses chordoma treatment. Treatment options include surgery or radiation therapy. Chapter 7: Ewing sarcoma discusses Ewing sarcoma treatment options. Treatment begins with systemic therapy. Chapter 8: Giant cell tumor of bone discusses GCTB treatment options. GCTB is usually not cancer, but needs aggressive treatment to prevent bone damage. Chapter 9: Osteosarcoma discusses osteosarcoma treatment options. Osteosarcoma is the more common type of bone cancer. Treatment is a combination of therapies. Chapter 10: Other resources provides information on patient advocacy groups and where to get help. What can you do to get the best care? Advocate for yourself. You have an important role to play in your care. In fact, you’re more likely to get the care you want by asking questions and making shared decisions with your care team. Consider seeking the opinion of a specialist in your type of bone cancer. The NCCN Guidelines for Patients will help you understand cancer care. With better understanding, you’ll be more prepared to discuss your care with your team and share your concerns. Many people feel more satisfied when they play an active role in their care. You may not know what to ask your care team. That’s common. Each chapter in this book ends with an important section called Questions to ask. These suggested questions will help you get more information on all aspects of your care. Take the next step and keep reading to learn what is the best care for you! 2 Testing for bone cancer General health tests Fertility (all genders) Performance status Blood tests Imaging tests Biopsy Genetic cancer risk testing Biomarker testing Key points Questions to ask Treatment planning starts with testing. Accurate testing is needed to diagnose and treat primary bone cancer. This chapter presents an overview of possible tests you might receive and what to expect. Bone cancer is very rare. Many health care providers are not experts in diagnosing or treating these tumors. Therefore, it is important to find a doctor, treatment center, or hospital that has experience in your type of bone cancer. Use resources on page 61 of this book to help you find an experienced doctor and treatment center. General health tests Some general health tests are described next. Medical history A medical history is a record of all health issues and treatments you have had in your life. Be prepared to list any illness or injury and when it happened. Bring a list of old and new medicines and any over-the-counter (OTC) medicines, herbals, or supplements you take. Some supplements interact with and affect medicines that your care team may prescribe. Tell your care team about any symptoms you have. A medical history, sometimes called a health history, will help determine which treatment is best for you. Family history Your care team will ask about the health history of family members who are blood relatives. This information is called a family history. Ask family members on both sides of your family about their health issues like heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, and at what age they were diagnosed. It’s important to know the specific type of cancer or where the cancer started, if it is in multiple locations, and if they had genetic testing. Physical exam During a physical exam, your health care provider may: Check your temperature, blood pressure, pulse, and breathing rate Check your height and weight Listen to your lungs and heart Look in your eyes, ears, nose, and throat Feel and apply pressure to parts of your body to see if organs are of normal size, are soft or hard, or cause pain when touched. h Feel for enlarged lymph nodes in your neck, underarm, and groin Examine your skeletal system Assess your ability to manage tasks and activities that are used in daily life called a functional assessment Fertility (all genders) Some types of treatment can affect your fertility, the ability to have children. If you think you want children in the future, ask your care team how cancer and cancer treatment might change your fertility. To preserve your fertility, you may need to take action before starting cancer treatment. Those who want to have children in the future should be referred to a fertility specialist to discuss the options before starting treatment. Fertility preservation is all about keeping your options open, whether you know you want to have children later in life or aren’t sure at the moment. Fertility and reproductive specialists can help you sort through what may be best for your situation. For more information on fertility preservation, see the NCCN Guidelines for Patients®: Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer at NCCN. org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Changes in fertility Treatment might cause your fertility to be temporarily or permanently impaired or interrupted. This loss of fertility is related to your age at time of diagnosis, treatment type(s), treatment dose, and treatment length. Talk to your care team about your concerns and if you are planning a pregnancy. Preventing pregnancy during treatment Preventing pregnancy during treatment is important. Cancer and cancer treatment can affect the ovaries and damage sperm. Therefore, becoming pregnant or having one's partner become pregnant during treatment should be avoided. Hormonal birth control may or may not be recommended, so ask your doctor about options such as intrauterine devices (IUDs)

After skeletal maturity, this leaves a physeal scar or line visible in the bone. TNM scores The tumor, node, metastasis (TNM) system is used to stage most bone cancers. In this system, the letters T, N, and M describe different areas of cancer growth. Based on imaging and biopsy results, your doctor will assign a score or number to each letter. The higher the number, the larger the tumor or the more the cancer has spread to lymph nodes or other organs. These scores will be combined to assign the cancer a stage. A TNM example might look like this: T1N0M0 or T1, N0, MThis might represent a stage 1 cancer. h T (tumor) – Size and depth of the main (primary) tumor N (node) – If cancer has spread to nearby (regional) lymph nodes M (metastasis) – If cancer has spread (metastasized) to distant parts of the body Cancer staging is often done twice. Clinical stage (c) is the rating given before any treatment. It is based on a physical exam, biopsy, and other tests. Pathologic stage (p) or surgical stage is determined by examining tissue removed during surgery such as in the removal of a lymph node. Pathologic features include size, shape, and type of cell. The spine The spinal or vertebral column includes a flexible column of bones called vertebrae. The spine includes the sacrum and tailbone (coccyx). There are 24 bones in the flexible spine: 7 cervical (neck), 12 thoracic (upper back), and 5 lumbar (lower back). T Tumor The primary (main) tumor size is measured in centimeters (cm). A large pea is 1 cm. A golf ball is 4 cm. A baseball is 7 cm. A grapefruit is . Tumors in limbs, torso, skull, and face Tumors are staged based on location. The appendicular skeleton is composed of 126 bones of the upper limbs, the lower limbs, the shoulder girdle, and the pelvic girdle. The shoulder girdle is a set of bones that connects the arm to the body. The pelvic girdle is a set of bones that connects the leg to the body. Staging for tumors found in the appendicular skeleton, torso, skull, and face are described next. TX – Primary tumor cannot be measured h T0 – Tumor cannot be found h T1 – Tumor is 8 cm or smaller T2 – Tumor is larger than 8 cm T3 – More than 1 tumor in the primary bone site Tumors in spine Staging for tumors found in the bones of the spine (vertebra) are described next. TX – Primary tumor cannot be measured T0 – Tumor cannot be found T1 – Tumor confined to 1 vertebra or 2 vertebrae next to one another (adjacent) T2 – Tumor confined to 3 adjacent vertebrae T3 – Tumor confined to 4 or more adjacent vertebrae, or any nonadjacent vertebrae T4 – Tumor has grown into spinal canal or large (great) vessels Tumors in pelvis Staging for tumors found in the pelvis are described below. TX – Primary tumor cannot be measured T0 – Tumor cannot be found T1 – Tumor is confined to 1 pelvic segment and has not grown outside the bone • T1a – Tumor is 8 cm or less • T1b – Tumor is larger than 8 cm T2 – Tumor is confined to 1 pelvic segment but has grown outside the bone or 2 segments that have not grown outside the bone • T2a – Tumor is 8 cm or less • T2b – Tumor is larger than 8 cm T3 – Tumor spans 2 pelvic segments and has grown outside the bone • T3a – Tumor is 8 cm or less • T3b – Tumor is larger than 8 cm T4 – Tumor spans 3 pelvic segments or crosses the sacroiliac joint (SIJ) • T4a – Tumor involves SIJ and extends into the spine • T4b – Tumor has grown into major blood vessels N = Node There are hundreds of lymph nodes throughout your body. They work as filters to help fight infection and remove harmful things from your body. Regional lymph nodes are those located near the tumor. Cancer in the lymph nodes is called nodal disease and is rare in bone cancer. NX – Cancer in nearby lymph nodes cannot be measured. N0 – There is no cancer in nearby lymph nodes. N1 – Cancer is found in the regional lymph nodes. M Metastasis Bone cancer can spread through blood or the lymphatic system. Cancer that has spread to distant parts of the body is defined as MWhen cancer is not metastatic it is labeled as MBone cancer can spread to the lung, other bones, or other parts of the body. Bone cancer that has metastasized to the lung is still called bone cancer. M0 – No distant metastasis M1 – Distant metastasis is found • M1a – Metastasis is in the lung • M1b – Metastasis is in the bone or other distant sites The pelvis The pelvis is a basin-shaped structure that supports the spinal column and protects the abdominal organs. G = Grade Another factor used in staging is the cancer grade. Grade describes how abnormal the tumor cells look under a microscope (histology). Imaging tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, locate, and evaluate tumors, assess cancer extent, and check for cancer spread. These tests are essential for staging cancer, planning treatment, monitoring tumor response during chemotherapy, and detecting recurrence during surveillance. They are also used to visualize internal structures, guide biopsies, and identify abnormalities such as enlarged lymph nodes, organ involvement, or areas of infection or bleeding.

Imaging tests include a wide range of techniques such as CT scans, MRI, PET scans, FDG-PET/CT, ultrasound, X-rays, mammograms, and bone scans. These modalities are applied across various cancer types, including breast, prostate, colon, rectal, esophageal, liver, kidney, ovarian, thyroid, adrenal, bone, and throat cancers, as well as leukemias like ALL and AML, and lymphomas such as CBCL and NPC. For example, mammograms, ultrasounds, and MRIs are used to visualize breast tissue; CT and MRI are primary methods for colon cancer staging; and ultrasound is used to detect thyroid nodules and cancer.

Imaging tests are interpreted by a radiologist and are used to reveal a tumor’s location, size, and other features, as well as to detect cancer spread to distant sites. In certain cancers, such as early-stage prostate cancer, imaging may not be necessary, but in others, like leukemia, they help detect spread outside the bone marrow to areas such as the brain, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and skin. Overall, imaging tests are indispensable diagnostic and monitoring tools in oncology, providing detailed visual information that guides clinical decisions across the cancer care continuum.

The specific approach is personalized based on diagnostic test results, cancer staging, biomarkers (e.g., BCR::ABL1 protein activity), and patient preferences, with options ranging from minimal or no treatment for low-risk cases to aggressive therapies for high-risk or advanced disease. Treatment aims to slow tumor growth, reduce symptoms, prolong life, and prevent the disease from causing problems, though it may have side effects on hearing, fertility, and other bodily functions. For certain cancers, such as CLL, monitoring may be an option, while for metastatic cancer, targeted therapy or immunotherapy may be employed. Clinical trials are also considered in some cases, and treatment plans are often guided by a multidisciplinary care team, with patient preferences playing a key role in decision-making.

Metastasis is the process by which cancer cells spread from the primary tumor (the original site of cancer) to other parts of the body, forming secondary tumors. This spread can occur through the blood or lymphatic system, allowing cancer cells to travel to nearby lymph nodes (local metastasis) or to distant organs and tissues (distant metastasis), such as the bones, liver, lungs, or other internal organs. The specific sites of metastasis can vary depending on the type of primary cancer; for example, prostate cancer commonly spreads to lymph nodes and bones, while colon cancer may spread to the liver or lungs, and kidney cancer can lead to metastatic tumors outside the kidney. Metastasis is a key indicator of advanced-stage cancer, often defining stage 4 disease (e.g., stage 4B cervical cancer), and is a critical component of cancer staging systems, such as the TNM system, where the "M" category indicates whether metastasis has occurred. In some cancers, such as basal cell skin cancer, metastasis is rare but possible, especially in advanced cases, while in very high-risk cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), it is a recognized risk. To confirm the presence of metastatic cancer, a biopsy of the metastatic site may be required, with the type of biopsy depending on the location of the spread. Imaging techniques are also used to detect metastasis, particularly in cases like prostate cancer. Overall, metastasis signifies the spread of cancer from its original location to other body areas, such as lymph nodes or distant organs, and is a fundamental factor in determining prognosis and guiding treatment decisions.

The pelvis is a basin-shaped anatomical structure located in the lower part of the torso, between the hip bones, that supports the spinal column and protects abdominal organs. It contains and surrounds vital organs including the bladder, rectum, reproductive organs (such as the ovaries, uterus, cervix, and prostate), and the anus and anal canal. The pelvis is a critical region for many cancers: it is the primary site for anal, rectal, and perianal cancers, and it is where these cancers are initially confined in non-metastatic stages. Cancer spread beyond the pelvis indicates distant metastasis (e.g., stage IV for anal or prostate cancer). The pelvis is also a common site for cancer spread from other organs, including prostate cancer (to bones), bladder cancer (to lymph nodes or organs), ovarian cancer, and lymphoma. Imaging techniques such as CT, MRI, EUS, and bone scans are frequently used to examine the pelvis for abnormalities, tumor spread, or lymph node involvement. Physical exams, including pelvic exams, are used to assess the cervix, uterus, and other pelvic structures for tenderness or abnormalities, particularly in bladder cancer. The pelvis is also a common location for bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, typically performed on the hip bone. Additionally, the pelvis can be a site for primary bone tumors such as Ewing sarcoma, and swollen lymph nodes in this region may be detected on imaging scans. The pelvis serves as an anatomical boundary for treatment planning, including radiation targeting, and is a focus of surveillance imaging after cancer recurrence treatment.
